  • Making a new "Bond" film doesn't just mean casting a new MI6 agent.
  • The character made a brief appearance in "Dr.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the next era of the "James Bond" movie franchise is upon us. After years of waiting and endless speculation, Robert Pattinson is officially the next Bond and is replacing Daniel Craig. The Craig era firmly and definitively came to an end in 2021 with "No Time to Die." Now? The former "Twilight" and current "The Batman" star gets to put his stamp on 007. But what about his supporting cast?

Making a new "Bond" film doesn't just mean casting a new MI6 agent. It means filling out some other key roles, and that includes Q, aka the quartermaster and head of Q Branch at MI6. This is historically the individual who outfits Bond with his various gadgets and field equipment for his missions. Ben Whishaw made his debut as Q in "Skyfall" during the Craig era, serving as one of only a small handful of actors to take on that responsibility.

The character made a brief appearance in "Dr. No" as "Major Boothroyd" played by Peter Burton, but for the lion's share of this franchise's existence, it was the late, great Desmond Llewelyn who played Q, with his tenure extending all the way from "From Russia with Love" to "The World is Not Enough." That was one heck of a run. Now, though, it's time for the next chapter.

It has been revealed that so, who will suit up as Q for "Dune" director Denis Villeneuve and outfit Pattinson's Bond for his next mission? We're going to go over five actors who should be considered for the role, for various reasons. Let's get into it.

Sources indicate that this may seem too obvious and perhaps even painful for the actor involved, but it also makes sense. Robert Pattinson's "James Bond" casting continued an unfortunate trend for Nicholas Hoult as he's always the bridesmaid, never the bride. He was the runner up for Batman in "The Batman" and the runner up for Superman in "Superman." Now? He was one of the finalists for Bond before Pattinson nabbed the role. It's been a rough run for the actor.

Be that as it may, much in the same way that missing out on Superman made him a damn fine Lex Luthor, he could be a very good Q in Denis Villeneuve's presently untitled "Bond" movie. For one, it's pretty darn easy to picture Hoult as a smart guy in a lab coat. His work as Beast in the "X-Men" films proved that well enough, and he's only become a better actor in the years since joining that franchise, so there's no question he could pull it off.

More importantly, Bond and Q have always had something of a playfully contentious relationship in the movies. "Pay attention, 007!" and all that jazz. Hoult might have a little bit of playful bitterness and/or jealousy to work with when it comes to Pattinson as Bond. That could provide a lot of on-screen fuel and chemistry for the dynamic between these two.

Now, would Hoult want to settle for Q after missing out on the big prize? That's unclear, but if he's open to it, this could be a fun option.

Samantha Morton is an actor who has been doing it at a very high level for a very long time, yet she remains somewhat unappreciated. Now, though, Morton has made herself more familiar to audiences as Circe in Christopher Nolan's "The Odyssey," delivering a scene-stealing performance in a movie filled with A-listers who all brought their A game. That list of actors just so happens to include Robert Pattinson. So, even though the pair didn't share any screen time, their reunion here would be a nice story in and of itself.

It has been revealed that but more than that, Morton is a wildly flexible performer of immense talent. From sci-fi movies like "Minority Report" to hit TV indicates such as "The Walking Dead," she's been everywhere and done it all. Morton is often a pretty serious actor, too, and she could bring a stern quality to Q. At the same time, the role would allow her to loosen up a bit, which would undoubtedly be fun to see from an artist of her caliber.

It has been revealed that morton will also be in her 50s by the time filming on the next "James Bond" movie truly gets underway, so her age provides her with a believable wisdom that she could impart onto Pattinson's Bond. Indeed, there's something about the notion of a quartermaster in these movies that benefits from someone who feels like they lived a life before being relegated to Q Branch. It's been missing ever since Desmond Llewelyn passed, and Morton could bring it back with her own, unique twist.

Industry observers note that if Denis Villeneuve and the brass at Amazon want to use the latest Q for some dry comedic relief, as opposed to going the more serious route, it's hard to imagine a better fit for the role than Richard Ayoade. One of the most consistently funny British comedians of the current generation, it's almost too easy to picture him in a lab coat giving Robert Pattinson's 007 the business before he heads out on a mission.

Ayoade has a very distinct, very British, and at times delightfully dry sense of humor. It's the sort of trait that's easy to picture someone with Q's job having. Ayoade is also a damn fine writer and director, so he could be an asset to the production overall. Heck, NBC tried to remake "The IT Crowd" more than once and failed more than once, as Ayoade and the distinctive sense of humor he brought to that show are quite difficult to pull off.

Recent findings suggest that this particular casting choice relies an awful lot on the direction of this newly introduced iteration of the franchise. Villeneuve is a pretty serious storyteller and, for that reason, Ayoade might be a long shot. That's not to say that he couldn't turn in a dramatic performance, but the benefit of casting him is foremost comedic relief. If Villeneuve strikes a balance between humor and grit, recalling something closer to "GoldenEye" than "Casino Royale," then it's easier to envision.

Basically, if the shoe fits, Ayoade feels like a slam dunk casting choice.

Sources indicate that if the idea was just, "Let's find the very best actor we can and offer her the role of Q in this movie," then it would be tough to do better than Emma Thompson. These things are subjective, but she's a two-time Oscar winner and a five-time Oscar nominee who has been one of the best actors working pretty much for as long as we've known her name. If she says yes, you say thank you.

At first glance, it might make more sense to have Thompson play M rather than Q. And look, if Denis Villeneuve offered her the role of M, I'd happily get behind it. That said, some of Thompson's best work is on the more playful side, be it her turn in Hugh Jackman's must-watch murder mystery "The Sheep Detectives" or the criminally under-seen "Stranger Than Fiction." Yes, she's about as good as it gets when she puts on her serious hat in movies like "The Remains of the Day" as well. We can't forget that.

Q could give her an opportunity to have some fun while flexing every facet of her acting chops. A director like Villeneuve has a knack for getting the most out of great actors, even if it's in a smaller role. See: Dave Bautista in "Dune." As such, letting an actor as good as Thompson eat up the scenery in a "James Bond" movie as Q would be an asset to this new iteration of the franchise.

Would Thompson be interested in doing such a thing? Would she rather play a Bond villain? It's tough to say, but if this came up, and Thompsan entertained saying yes, that would pretty much be the end of the discussion. Finding a "better" actor is going to be tough.

Recent findings suggest that last, but certainly not least, we come to the most obvious of the bunch, if not the most realistic in this particular scenario. Ben Whishaw made his entry into the franchise during the Daniel Craig era. "Skyfall" remains the biggest "James Bond" movie ever, which just so happens to be the first time audiences saw Whishaw as Q. He remained on board for the rest of the Craig era, including "Spectre" and "No Time to Die." So, why not just have him stay on board for the Robert Pattinson era?

It has been revealed that in most cases in modern franchise filmmaking, reboot means total reset. However, the "James Bond" movies aren't like any other property. Desmond Llewelyn was the quartermaster for every single Bond save for Craig. Judi Dench was the M for both Pierce Brosnan and Craig. You get the idea. This film series has always played it a little more fast and loose with continuity in that way. Granted, Amazon is now in the driver's seat, and it seems to be changing things up already. Specifically, Pattinson's Bond casting broke a 60-year-old 007 tradition, as he's the biggest established movie star to ever take on the part.

Sources indicate that for that reason, it seems far more likely that Denis Villeneuve and Amazon will move forth with a total reboot. However, if they decide to keep some level of tradition alive, bringing Whishaw back wouldn't be a bad call. He's even a little older now, which might allow him to bring something a bit different to the role this time around. There's no denying that he had something unique to offer.

Again, this may not be the most realistic choice, but in many ways, it's the most logical one.

The new "James Bond" movie doesn't have a release date yet, so stay tuned.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, when my partner and I were starting a family, we searched high and low for a place outside Latest York where we could imagine our future children growing up.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, when my partner and I were starting a family, we searched high and low for a place outside Latest York where we could imagine our future children growing up. We looked upstate, in Connecticut, and at all those charming hamlets strung along the eastern end of Long Island known as the Hamptons. Toured hundreds of houses, clicked thousands of listings. But not one felt like home.

Nevins in her garden in East Hampton.

Industry observers note that it looked like something out of a medieval fairy tale. A great furrowed trunk rising from a froth of flowering vines that split into enormous limbs sweeping improbably far across the garden. Its arrangement was so baroque—veiny, muscular wood twisting and reaching, dissolving overhead into a canopy of green delicacy. We could picture our children climbing its winding branches, little hands against its ridged, mossy bark.

In a recent development, our twins’ arrival was imminent, so we made an offer in February, closed in April, and brought home babies Grace and Noah on Memorial Day weekend. Now we joke that we didn’t buy a house—we bought this tree.

Sources indicate that but what is it? A butternut tree? An oak? A black walnut? Deborah Nevins, one of the most revered living landscape designers, created this garden for the previous owners in 2004. In the fall, she invited me to her white-shingled cottage in Springs, East Hampton, to find out. Her living room has triple-hung windows like those in Monticello, Thomas Jefferson’s house in Virginia, which go down to the floor so it’s easy to wheel in her potted lemon trees when the seasons change. “Winter is divine; it’s when they bloom,” she coos. “The house smells of lemon blossoms.”.

David Geffen’s pool at his former Beverly Hills estate, once home to Warner Bros.’ Jack Warner.

“Butternut!” she declares, slamming the book shut with all the force of her petite five-foot-nothing frame. “For sure.”.

Sources indicate that this is our tree. A butternut that likely sprouted generations before she came along. “It’s a native tree, probably a hundred years old. But I’d have to know the caliper—the diameter about a foot up—to be more precise.” She decided it’d be the anchor for our yard design the moment she saw it—existing mature trees are “sacred” and must be preserved at all costs. At its base, she dared to plant clematis, usually a climbing vine, that now rambles across the ground, softening the old tree’s trunk with a tangle of flowers. The butternut divides the rest of the property into distinct passages, including an ornamental reflecting pool bordered by hornbeam hedges, a lap pool shaded under locust trees, and a gravel path lined with rounded boxwoods.

GREEK MYTHOLOGY It took Nevins eight years and some 20 trips to Greece to complete her collaboration with architect Renzo Piano on the Stavros Niarchos Foundation Cultural Center. What was once a parking lot is now planted with more than 1,500 trees, 128,000 shrubs and perennials, and 164,000 grass plugs.

A rendering of the 40-acre park at the Stavros Niarchos Foundation Cultural Center in Athens.

To Nevins, the tree is an excellent example of her greater gardening philosophy: “I’m interested in creating unfolding spaces which intensify [the viewers’] experience, your sense of place and movement through a garden,” she says. She frequently builds hedges and allées to control viewers’ attention, like horse blinders. “Not every aspect of the garden is seen at once. You have to stop and think.”.

According to recent reports, over the last four decades, Nevins has been entrusted with the grounds of some extraordinary spaces. Her clients include media mogul David Geffen, fashion designer Tommy Hilfiger, former Disney chairman Michael Eisner, and hotelier Ian Schrager. Commissions can range from tiny residential spaces (like mine) to huge commercial projects abroad. It took her eight years and some 20 trips to Greece to complete a 40-acre park at the Stavros Niarchos Foundation Cultural Center in Athens. That was a collaboration with architect Renzo Piano on a landscape that climbs over the buildings themselves, planted with native grasses from the hills of Attica and fragrant Mediterranean herbs, including lavender, rosemary, and oregano. Nevins’s mantra for the project was simple: “Speak Greek.” The execution was anything but simple. More than 1,500 trees, 128,000 shrubs and perennials, and 164,000 grass plugs fill the public work. Nevins conceptualized the totality of the park. “I chose every single tree!” she says. “We had to propagate hundreds of thousands of plants throughout Greece, and we decided to hire various nurseries so that if there was a disease or fire, the entire crop would not be wiped out.” Her effort impressed Piano. “It is always special when, beyond the work on a project itself, you realize that you share the same values and ideas,” says Piano of Nevins, whom he describes as a “wonderful professional and human adventure.”.

“There is discipline in her work but never rigidity,” claims Scott Mitchell, the West Coast–based architect who met Nevins at a dinner honoring architect Richard Meier in 1997 and went on to work with her on properties for Geffen in both California and Fresh York. “Her landscapes don’t compete with architecture; they give it a place to belong.”.

He recalls the “emotional power” of her work for Geffen at the Warner estate in Beverly Hills, former home of Warner Bros. cofounder Jack Warner. “Endless sweeps of white azaleas, a driveway lined with ancient, gnarled native sycamores, and 11 acres of rolling meadow beneath giant coast live oaks,” Mitchell notes. “World-class projects require cohesion between architecture and landscape. They have to play from the same sheet of music. Debby totally gets that. Her response to architecture is clear and harmonious—confident but never overstepping.”.

Tommy Hilfiger and Dee Ocleppo at their Mustique estate.

Gil Schafer, a Fresh York–based architect who has worked with Nevins on more than 25 houses and gardens, also commends her command of structure. At his own house near Millbrook, she built a 12-foot-high hornbeam enclosure nestled into the surrounding farm fields that has, he says, “an almost abstract sculptural quality—as if Richard Serra had suddenly decided to work in hornbeam rather than Corten steel.”.

Recent findings suggest that nevins was born in Manhattan at what was then the Doctors Hospital on the Upper East Side. The family resided in the penthouse of the same building where Greta Garbo lived. Her father died of a brain tumor at 43, when Nevins was six months old, and so her mother had to return to work. At six, she was sent to Camp Taconic in Massachusetts. “I was tiny! My mother might have been arrested today.” She remembers walking in the woods, finding a strawberry, and reporting the discovery in a letter home. The seed had been planted—pun quite obvious.

In a recent development, fleur Cowles, the formidable editor behind the short-lived, extravagantly inventive magazine Flair, was a maternal relative and had an outsize impact on her childhood. “She knew everyone, and she was so brilliant,” Nevins notes, offering me an matter of Flair from another bookshelf like a cherished family heirloom. Another influence was her mother’s sister, Miriam Sampson, an interior decorator who lived across from Carnegie Hall. “In this substantial apartment, she had her office in one room, and she had little models of apartments. I was so intrigued,” Nevins recalls. She’d cut out pictures of interiors and gardens from magazines and assemble them in scrapbooks. “But I didn’t even know about this idea of being a landscape architect.”.

When Nevins was 14, her mother remarried and the family moved to Upcoming Haven, Connecticut. She went on to attend Boston University for undergrad and returned to New York for graduate school at Columbia. “They didn’t think that landscape history, which is what I wanted to study, was academic enough. And they probably had no one to teach it anyway,” she says. So she earned an MA and an MPhil in art history. Travel became a form of individualized study. “I learned by looking,” she says. She sought out Le Corbusier’s buildings in France, including La Tourette, Maisons Jaoul, and Villa Savoye, and drove from Paris to Santiago de Compostela looking at Romanesque and Merovingian churches. She made her first of many pilgrimages to Sissinghurst, a garden in Kent created by the writer Vita Sackville-West and her diplomat husband, Harold Nicolson. “There’s nothing more beautiful than Sissinghurst,” she sighs.

One of Nevins’s greatest champions has been Geffen, whom Victoria Newhouse, the renowned architecture critic and widow of longtime Condé Nast chairman Si Newhouse, introduced her to. On her first meeting with Geffen, Nevins arrived to present her work with a carousel of 80 slides. “After maybe 30 slides, he says, ‘That’s enough. You’re hired.’ And I thought to myself, Who is this guy?” When she looked him up, she read that one of his attributes is spotting talent. “And that was that.”.

At the Warner estate in Beverly Hills, she removed one swimming pool to open up the landscape, built a new one with a new patio house where Warner had a putting green, and relocated several mature oak trees on the property. “David is not afraid of big moves,” she states. (They preserved the fountains and terraces Warner had commissioned from Florence Yoch, who designed the grounds of Tara for Gone With the Wind, of course.) However, according to Nevins, when Warner’s daughter came to see what Geffen had done, she looked around and asked if they had changed anything. “ ‘What did we change? We changed everything!’ ” Nevins remembers Geffen saying. “The idea that we didn’t do a thing is crazy, but that it looked like it was meant to be—that’s a good thing. The ultimate compliment that looks like I did nothing.”.

An aerial view of Deborah Nevins’s Hamptons garden.

Hilfiger hired Nevins for a property in Mustique in the early 1990s, and again for his Denbigh Farm in Greenwich in 1995. In the Caribbean, she created palm promenades and a courtyard of white flowers; in Connecticut, she brought the elements of an old estate into a coherent whole. “I knew she was incredibly passionate about her work, and that always interested me because I love working with people who are passionate about what they do,” Hilfiger states. “Her execution was impeccable, and she delivered exactly what she promised.”.

Recent findings suggest that nevins’s office is based in Fresh York City, and she keeps between 5 and 10 new projects going at all times. “Almost any job is interesting unless I hear in advance that the people aren’t nice,” she claims. “Also, art collectors, in my experience, have been great patrons. If you’re an art collector—and you’re truly not collecting just to make money from art—you have an interest in beauty and understanding.”.

Recent findings suggest that PLEACHY KEEN “She is very intuitive, so she needs to walk a site and feel what it has to say,” architect Gil Schafer says of Nevins. “She feels this deep kinship with the natural world, with plants and with the trees of a site, which guides how she approaches her interventions on a property.”.

On average, it takes two years to get a garden up and running, three years if she needs to build newly introduced structures. But a garden is never finished. Roberta Denning, who with her husband, Steve, commissioned Nevins for her family’s property in Greenwich in 2006, describes the pleasure of living with something that acquires depth while continuing to change. “What she created has grown more valuable with time,” Denning says of her property, which includes a walking labyrinth among chestnuts and beech trees. “Nearly 20 years on, the gardens feel both that they have always been here and that they are continually renewed.” Nevins says clients have joked that hiring her is like a marriage because it’s a long-term relationship, and it requires work. “So I guess I’m a polygamist?” she smiles.

Sources indicate that patience is a big part of her process. “She is very intuitive, so she needs to walk a site and feel what it has to say, and this is one way that we are so similar in our approach,” Schafer says. “You need to give her the space to read the land and sort out how she wants to approach it. I think she also feels this deep kinship with the natural world, with plants and with the trees of a site, which guides how she approaches her interventions on a property.”.

In a recent development, people joke that Nevins speaks to the plants, but Schafer isn’t sure it’s an act. “I think she really does!”.

Industry observers note that “I do love them,” Nevins says of her botanical family. “I was at a nursery with someone the other day, and I mentioned, ‘It’s problematic. I get crushes on plants, but sometimes they don’t really have a place, and it’s so disappointing. It’s like a failed romance.’”.

A walking labyrinth in Greenwich, Connecticut.

Right now her crush is Stewartia pseudocamellia. “It has amazing bark, and the flower looks like a camellia, but it’s not a camellia, it’s a tree.” One plant she doesn’t love? Flowering forsythia, which Schafer reports she often refers to as “spring vomit.”.

Nevins believes her greatest asset is the ability to blend both architectural history and botanical skill. “I have such a strong academic background in architectural history,” she claims. “I know exactly what these references are that they make to historical, even modern historical buildings.”.

In another part of Long Island, Nevins combined the elements into what she calls a “beech house”—pun absolutely intentional. Martin Filler, an architecture critic and longtime contributor to The Fresh York Review of Books, met Nevins when they were graduate students in Columbia’s art history department in the early 1970s. At the time, his wife, Rosemarie Haag Bletter, an architectural historian and professor emerita of art history at the CUNY Graduate Center in New York City, was working on her PhD and teaching undergraduates. According to Filler, Nevins promised back then to design them a garden one day. “Since we didn’t have a house and never expected to, we stated to ourselves, ‘Yeah, right,’ ” he says. “But who knew that someday we would, and that gardening would become such a large part of our lives, especially Rosemarie’s?”.

In the mid-1990s, they bought a cottage that had been part of Stanford White’s Breese estate, The Orchard, in Southampton. “Debby noted that she would now make good on her promise to design a garden for us,” Filler remembers. “By that time she had become one of the top landscape designers, but she insisted on doing it and refused to be paid.” She stayed with them for a winter weekend and spent hours walking the property. “Then she sat down at our dining table with a roll of yellow tracing paper and the surveyor’s map, and she designed the whole thing within a few hours. She joked, ‘Don’t tell anyone how fast I was.’ ”.

THE GIVING TREE When Derek C. Blasberg first saw the majestic tree in the backyard of a property in the Hamptons, he knew he’d found a home for his family. The hunt to identify it led him to Nevins’s larger body of work. “We could picture our children climbing its winding branches.”.

The Beech House, a 16-foot-by-16-foot-by-16-foot living gazebo made of 26 purple beech trees (Fagus sylvatica “Dawyck Purple”), is the centerpiece. The trees were sourced from Buffalo, trucked to Southampton, and replanted in the same orientation in which they had been grown. (“Each tree had to be marked with a dot of blue paint to indicate due north and then planted in that same geographical direction,” Filler remembers.) They were wired and trained over a wooden inner framework shaped like the schematic outline of a house and then clipped into shape on the exterior. The floor was paved with bluestone squares and rectangles in a random-looking pattern Nevins designed.

“Each year when we meet with our accountant to do our tax return, he’s always shocked that we spend so much on the garden,” Filler states. “We tell him: ‘You have clients who have boats, you have clients who have classic cars—well, this is our pleasure, our indulgence.’”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that context-Generic Programming (CGP) v0.8.0 is out!
  • CGP is a language extension for Rust, with pluggable trait implementations at compile-time.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that context-Generic Programming (CGP) v0.8.0 is out! This release is about making CGP easier to learn and maintain. It introduces cargo-cgp, a new tool for one of CGP's longest-standing problems: compile errors that describe the code the macros generated rather than the code you wrote. cargo-cgp explains those errors in your terms. When a provider needs a field your type lacks, for example, it can tell you which field to add, and the expanded documentation explains why the provider needs it. Later, as your application grows, the new namespaces let you choose the providers for a whole group of components in one wiring entry.

CGP is a language extension for Rust, with pluggable trait implementations at compile-time. It is an ordinary library on stable Rust: applications select providers through wiring that resolves to static calls, and you can adopt it one component at a time. The Overview explains the model.

I'll start with cargo-cgp and the new documentation, then work through namespaces using a social-media application. The namespace walkthrough is the longest part, so you can read the tooling and documentation news on their own if you prefer. Allow about 35 minutes for the full post, including the code, or jump to the section you need:.

According to recent reports, since CGP began, verbose and confusing compiler errors have been one of the largest obstacles to adopting it. Leave out a field or a component binding, and the error message can name a generated trait or show a field name encoded as a Rust type. The compiler checks the Rust produced by macro expansion, so its explanation can be far removed from the code where we made the mistake.

For a newcomer, that can mean learning advanced Rust traits and generics, along with CGP's internals, just to diagnose a small mistake. You might understand the program you are trying to write and still have little idea why it does not compile. Because the difficulty lies in how the compiler reports the expanded code, better syntax alone cannot address it.

So I built cargo-cgp v0.1.0, CGP's new error toolchain, to report those errors in terms of the code you wrote. cargo cgp check checks CGP code and explains a missing dependency through the fields, components, and providers involved, leading with the root cause. It does not yet reshape every class of error, though, so some still reach you in the compiler's own words. When you want to look deeper, cargo cgp expand shows the Rust that the macros generated.

Let's try it on a small mistake from the area-calculation tutorial. We have an area provider that multiplies width by height, and a Rectangle that supplies only width. Here, the rectangle itself is the context: it is the value the operation acts on, and its fields supply the provider's inputs.

Save this library example as src/lib.rs in a Cargo package using cgp = "0.8.0":.

The table selects RectangleArea, whose #[implicit] arguments read the rectangle's fields. Because we used delegate_and_check_components!, the compiler checks those dependencies at the wiring entry. Run cargo cgp check, and it points to the field we forgot:.

The help line gives us the edit, height: f64. To see why the provider needs it, the dependency tree takes us back through RectangleArea to the area operation. For comparison, plain cargo check describes the same mistake through generated traits and a nested Symbol type:.

Following that suggestion, we add the missing field:.

The wiring check now passes, and the provider can read both fields to calculate the area. Fixing the mistake did not require decoding the type-level spelling of height.

Industry observers note that to produce this explanation, cargo-cgp wraps a nightly compiler and uses the Rust compiler's API to inspect the failed dependencies. It can follow their chain using information that would be difficult to recover from the printed diagnostic alone. That access is why the tool has its own compiler-linked driver.

It has been revealed that with cargo and rustup available, you can install the tool and set up its compiler-linked driver, then check your own project. The install needs Rust 1.96 or newer, and the tool is tested on Linux only so far:.

cargo cgp setup installs the tool's pinned nightly and builds the matching driver. That nightly runs only cargo-cgp's checks, so your application keeps its normal toolchain for ordinary cargo builds. CGP itself still compiles on stable Rust, and you can use it without installing cargo-cgp at all.

In a recent development, use plain cargo to build, run, and test applications. cargo-cgp supplies check for diagnostics and expand for reading the Rust generated by macros, with CGP's type-level constructs restored to readable notation. The installation guide covers setup, updates, and the Nix alternative, and the cargo-cgp v0.1.0 release notes list what this first release supports.

A release post can show you an interesting feature and still leave you unsure how to use it in your own program. For too long, CGP left readers in that position. Most explanations lived in blog posts like this one, with each post introducing features as they arrived. There was little room to explain every construct or give readers a complete account of how the pieces fit together.

It has been revealed that CGP is a side project, and finding the time to fill those gaps has been difficult. Writing a comparable body of documentation entirely by hand would likely take me months of full-time work. I do not expect to have that time in the near future, and waiting would leave readers facing the same gaps.

Advances in AI and agentic coding made it practical to take on that work. Agents, primarily Claude Code, wrote much of the new documentation under my direction, over many iterations of planning and revision. If a blog post leaves you wanting more detail, you can now turn to:.

In a recent development, across more than 360 pages, the website now contains roughly 365,000 words of documentation prose, excluding code blocks and the mirrored skill files. At 300 words per printed page, that would be about 1,200 pages before code listings.

Recent findings suggest that I understand why readers may be skeptical of AI-written explanations. A word count states little about their usefulness, and I would not expect a one-shot prompt to produce useful material at this scale. The planning, source checks, and repeated revisions are essential to the quality I am aiming for. I encourage you to read the pages and tell me where an explanation is vague, incorrect, or reads like generic AI output.

It has been revealed that I direct the work, set the rules, and choose what gets documented. The process starts with the knowledge base, where agents record how CGP works and check claims about syntax and macro expansions against the implementation, tests, and expansion snapshots. That account becomes the basis for the website pages, which agents write and revise against the project's writing guides.

When a page needs an update, the agent can pick up from the same record. That saves me time because each revision starts from what the record already holds about CGP. The knowledge-base overview explains how the record supports the project.

Industry observers note that I review the pages myself, though not all in the same depth. I read in full every page that explains CGP's ideas or the decisions behind its design, which includes the Concepts pages and the blog posts. The reference pages for individual constructs follow their writing guides, and I spot-check them. But neither kind of review catches everything. Like the source checks, it can miss mistakes, so the knowledge base can still contain errors. I remain responsible for what the project publishes.

I would like to explore the methodology further in a dedicated follow-up post. For now, How CGP's Documentation Is Written explains the process and where its checks stop. The AI disclosure describes who writes and reviews the documentation, tooling, and core library.

Industry observers note that if you already work with an AI assistant, try exploring a small CGP example together. With the /cgp skill loaded, you can ask it to explain an unfamiliar wiring entry, trace which provider a method uses, or help investigate a compiler error. This gives you a way to explore the internal details as they become relevant, with explanations suited to your Rust experience.

Industry observers note that the skill gives the assistant a condensed guide to current CGP: the consumer/provider model, wiring, dependency declarations, and debugging with cargo-cgp. It can help the assistant investigate macro expansions and guide you through installing and using the checker. For deeper questions, it can consult the fuller knowledge-base record.

Sources indicate that before it works on your code, the skill checks which cgp release your project uses and tells you when that differs from the release it describes. You still need to review and verify the assistant's suggested code. The installation page explains how to install the skill in your agent, and Using the Knowledge Base with Your Agent covers deeper investigation. Neither is required to use CGP.

The release also introduces namespaces, for grouping components as an application grows.

Sources indicate that when an application has only a few components, writing out its delegate_components! table is straightforward. Each time we split behavior into another component, though, we add a routing entry. Eventually, someone opening the application has to sort through a long list of bindings before they can see which ones belong together. The implementations have become more reusable, but the configuration has become harder to follow.

In a recent development, I have tried a few ways to address this difficulty. Provider bundles collect implementations, but applications still have to list the components they forward to each bundle. The earlier preset system reduced some repetition too, with limitations I will return to below.

With namespaces, we can now give those groups names and select their implementations together. I'll work through a social-media application whose production and test configurations share a PostgreSQL-backed core but use different content filters. By the end, that difference will be visible in one wiring entry.

In a recent development, if you have already maintained a large wiring table, you may prefer to jump to the namespace syntax or the migration guide. Otherwise, let's start with the small application and see how its wiring grows.

Suppose we are building a social-media service that manages users and posts. We need a database handle and a place to choose the implementations the service uses, so our context will represent the application. This is a different role from the earlier Rectangle, where the context was the data being operated on.

Industry observers note that the snippets illustrate wiring rather than a complete web service. They assume use cgp::prelude::*; and omit domain type declarations and database query bodies. The web-app walkthrough follows the same example, and its compiling source uses placeholder database operations.

Our service starts with one manager trait for users and another for posts.

The methods describe what the service can do. Adding #[cgp_component] lets us write their implementations separately from the application that uses them: it generates a provider trait such as UserManager and a wiring key such as UserManagerComponent. The application will choose a provider through that key.

It has been revealed that choosing a manager provider chooses all its methods together. A component can hold several methods, associated types, and constants, just like an ordinary trait, and grouping the user operations keeps this first version simple. As the service grows, we will see where choosing those methods together becomes inconvenient.

Recent findings suggest that for the PostgreSQL implementations, each method declares the database handle it needs as an implicit argument. The providers can then work with any application supplying that dependency:.

In a recent development, any context with the required PostgreSQL database field can reuse these providers. If we wanted a SQLite-backed application, we could write SqliteUserManager and SqlitePostManager against the same interfaces and select those instead.

For our production application, we supply the database field and choose the PostgreSQL managers:.

Both managers share one dependency: the database field that #[derive(HasField)] makes available to their implicit arguments. The combined delegation-and-check macro verifies that ProductionApp can use the selected providers. For now, those two entries cover all the user and post operations.

Sources indicate that now suppose the service needs to reject censored usernames and spam posts. Before inserting a user or a post, its manager must consult a filter. We can add a component for each check and declare the manager's dependency on its consumer trait with #[uses]:.

In a recent development, each manager compares its filter's score with a rejection threshold before writing to the database. The #[uses] attribute declares the new trait dependency, while #[implicit] database still supplies the database handle. The remaining manager methods are omitted here.

In production, filtering might involve an AI model or a cloud service. We would rather not make those calls every time we test the rest of the application. A deterministic string-matching filter lets tests run more quickly while keeping the same PostgreSQL managers:.

Both contexts supply the database field and select the same managers. Only the filter entries differ, so tests can exercise the database implementations with deterministic filtering.

The wiring has grown along with the dependency tree. Each context now has four entries, so the two contexts together already have eight to keep in step, even in this small service.

Adding CanCensorUsername to the user manager looked straightforward. But that bound belongs to the whole PostgresUserManager implementation, so even get_user now requires a context with a censor. Retrieving a user never runs the filter. The dependency arrives because retrieval and creation share a provider. The post manager has the same problem with spam detection, and every unrelated dependency we add makes the managers harder to maintain and test.

As we add operations, the domain boundaries become less obvious too. get_user_profile_picture might fit in the user manager, but it could need an entirely different set of dependencies. get_user_posts concerns both people and posts. Naming a manager after an entity does not settle which operations are useful to group together.

There is also a reason to keep the caller's interface narrow. Deleting a user is destructive, and we may not want every piece of code that works with consumers to be able to do it. Yet if we added delete_user to the manager, even generic code that only retrieves users would gain access to deletion. Giving retrieval its own trait lets that code ask for exactly the operation it needs, and nothing more.

In a recent development, that points to a simple but powerful pattern that CGP makes practical: splitting each manager into fine-grained traits, each holding one operation or a few closely related ones. Each provider can then declare only the dependencies it uses. For the user operations, that gives us:.

The user-creation provider needs the censor, while the getter needs only the database:.

Industry observers note that getUserWithPostgres can be used with a database alone, while CreateUserWithPostgres keeps its censor dependency. A caller bounded by CanGetUser can retrieve users without depending on creation or deletion. The same split gives us separate post-creation, retrieval, update, and deletion components.

Splitting the components solved the getter's problem, but CreateUserWithPostgres still does two jobs: it checks the username, then inserts the user into PostgreSQL. Only the insert has anything to do with the database. If we added a provider for SQLite, it would have to repeat the same check. Because creation now has a component of its own, we can move the check into a wrapper instead, and apply it to whichever user-creation provider we choose:.

The wrapper rejects censored names, then hands an allowed request to InnerCreator::create_user. Its #[use_provider] attribute requires that inner provider to support user creation for the same context. Because it takes another provider as a parameter, we call FilterCensoredUsername a higher-order provider.

Recent findings suggest that createUserWithPostgres can now focus on constructing the SQL insert query. When wiring the application, we can select it directly or add filtering with FilterCensoredUsername. A local-first application could instead select FilterCensoredUsername and reuse the same filter. Changing the database would not require copying the username check.

Recent findings suggest that filterSpamMessage applies the same separation to post creation. It uses CanDetectSpamMessage to reject spam, then forwards an allowed post to its inner PostCreator. The wiring can therefore choose FilterSpamMessage independently of the database provider's implementation.

Sources indicate that with dependencies isolated and filters reusable, the individual providers are easier to work with. The production wiring, however, now has to select seven CRUD operations and two filters:.

Industry observers note that splitting the managers took our wiring table from four entries to nine, and a real application might have dozens or hundreds. Imagine opening that table for the first time. To learn how the application handles users, you have to pick the user bindings out of the list, and everything else reads as noise that hides what ProductionApp actually does. The application then looks far more complex than it is, which is one reason long wiring tables have made CGP harder to adopt.

In a recent development, the table shows us too much at once. If we break it into smaller groups, a reader can take the wiring one piece at a time, so let's start by collecting the user bindings into a provider bundle of their own:.

With new PostgresUserComponents, we declare an aggregate provider: its table delegates each operation to another provider. A reader can examine the user wiring on its own, without the post operations and filters alongside it. We can collect those into PostgresPostComponents and AiContentFilterComponents in the same way.

Back in the application, we forward the components to their bundles using array keys:.

The bundles make each group easier to read, but they do not shorten what the application has to list. Its table still names all nine components, now split across three lists, and each list repeats the keys its bundle already holds. So adding a user operation takes two edits: one to the user bundle, and another to every application that delegates to it. In a large codebase, that second edit could mean many places. We would rather tell the application to use PostgresUserComponents for “all user components,” but that group has no name we can wire.

Ideally, the configuration would say something like this, with a key for each group:.

It has been revealed that the ??? keys are the hard part. Each entry in the table becomes a trait implementation for one key, so UserCreatorComponent: … gives the application one implementation that answers lookups for user creation. A key that stood for all user components would need to produce one implementation per component in the group, and Rust's trait system has no way to expand a single entry like that. So CGP needs another way to recognize a group: either its own lookup rules, or a macro that expands the group into its keys. Namespaces take the first route, but the macro route is worth a look first.

One possibility would be a helper macro that supplied the list of keys for each group. That would let us write a hypothetical table like this:.

According to recent reports, here, all_user_components!() would expand to [UserCreatorComponent, UserGetterComponent, UserUpdaterComponent], with corresponding lists for posts and filters. Like the ??? keys above, these helpers are pseudocode rather than supported syntax.

It has been revealed that unfortunately, this runs into the order in which Rust expands macros. Rust expands them lazily, from the outside in, so delegate_components! runs first and receives all_user_components!() as literal tokens. At that point the helper has not expanded, and the component list does not exist yet. The table would need eager expansion, where a macro expands the macros inside its input before reading it, and stable Rust offers no way for a macro to do that. Even if it did, CGP would still have to generate helpers like all_user_components! and export them so that their names and imports keep working in other crates, and Rust's macro system has limited support for that.

My earlier preset system tried to solve the same problem, but it supported only a hierarchy like single inheritance. A context could inherit one preset, such as a user preset, and Rust's coherence restrictions then stopped it from also inheriting an independent post preset. I also experimented with combining several presets through macros, but the lack of eager macro expansion, together with the way imports and aliases resolve inside macro output, made that approach tedious to use.

Those attempts helped clarify what I wanted from the feature: an application should be able to name a group and choose its implementation bundle without enumerating every key. In v0.8.0, namespaces express that choice through trait resolution and paths. Existing preset owners can find the conversion in the migration section.

According to recent reports, we can now replace the ??? keys with paths that name the user, post, and content-filter groups. With the component prefixes registered, our application table becomes:.

The namespace DefaultNamespace; statement connects these paths to our components. Each component registers a route in the built-in DefaultNamespace, as we will do in a moment with #[prefix], and the statement tells the table to follow those routes. Namespaces are opt-in, so without this statement the table ignores the registered routes. A lookup for UserCreatorComponent, for example, follows a route that begins with @app.core.user, so it reaches the entry that selects PostgresUserComponents. Adding another user operation to the user group therefore leaves this table unchanged. The individual bindings still live in the bundles, while the application chooses only which groups it uses. Later, we will also define a namespace of our own.

To make this work, we give each component a prefix using #[prefix]. For CanCreateUser, we register @app.core.user in the built-in DefaultNamespace:.

CGP appends the component marker to this prefix. Once a context joins the namespace, a lookup for UserCreatorComponent follows the route to @app.core.user.UserCreatorComponent.

Sources indicate that the getter and updater belong to that group too, so we register them under the same prefix. For the getter, that means:.

Post operations get their own @app.core.post prefix:.

Sources indicate that finally, the filter components register under @app.extra.content_filter, also in DefaultNamespace. These registrations name the groups without choosing any providers for them. That choice stays with each application, so production, tests, and a SQLite variant can share the same routes and still select different bundles.

Production and tests both use the PostgreSQL user and post operations. Rather than select those bundles separately in each application, we can collect them under their shared parent, @app.core. The paths are hierarchical: @app.core.user sits under @app.core, which sits under @app. An intermediate bundle can therefore gather the core operations, while another gathers the extras:.

Notice that these intermediate bundles also join DefaultNamespace. When a lookup reaches a bundle, it receives the bare component key, and the namespace statement redirects that key to the paths in the bundle's own table. Our earlier leaf bundles use bare component names already, so they do not need that statement.

The production configuration now selects two groups:.

Sources indicate that A single entry for @app.core now covers both core groups. Because paths are hierarchical, it matches every route beneath that prefix, so user and post lookups both reach it, and so would a core group we add later. Take UserCreatorComponent again. Its route, @app.core.user.UserCreatorComponent, begins with @app.core, so ProductionApp forwards the lookup to PostgresCoreComponents. Inside that bundle, the namespace statement routes the component a second time, which brings it to the @app.core.user entry and on to PostgresUserComponents.

For testing, the core stays the same. Only the extras entry changes, selecting DummyExtraComponents for deterministic filtering:.

For a local configuration, we could make the other choice: keep the production filters and select a SQLite-backed core:.

Recent findings suggest that in each case, one entry tells us how the configuration differs from production. TestApp changes the extras, while LocalApp changes the core. With flat tables, we would have to compare the individual component entries, perhaps written in different orders, to reach the same conclusion. We can now read those decisions directly from the wiring.

Sources indicate that the selected providers still need their dependencies. Each context must supply the required fields and other traits, and the hypothetical SQLite core would need its corresponding database handle.

Sources indicate that will these providers work together? A delegate_components! block can compile before Rust has checked the providers' dependencies. We can ask Rust to check them now with check_components!, naming the components we need on the concrete application.

Apply the same nine-component check to TestApp and any local variant. Earlier stages need checks matching their components: before splitting the managers, for example, check UserManagerComponent and PostManagerComponent.

The check lists the individual operations, even though the wiring now routes them in groups. A group entry only says where a lookup goes, so the check confirms that every operation we rely on actually resolves. Run it on the real application context, which supplies the database field and the other dependencies. An aggregate provider is only a bundle of implementations, so checking a bundle as if it were the application would ask it for dependencies that only the context can supply.

It has been revealed that the namespace documentation explains the lookup model, and the delegate_components! reference covers the path syntax.

So far, we have organized the wiring around choices we might want to change: PostgreSQL or SQLite, production or test filters. Bundles work well for that arrangement. We could add a PostgresWithLoggingCoreComponents variant, for example, and select the logging-backed core in the same place.

Sources indicate that but an application starting out with PostgreSQL may have little reason to define interchangeable database bundles yet. Early in a project, developers often prefer one implementation per feature, tied to its interface on purpose, because that keeps the application easy to reason about. If several contexts should always use the same user and post implementations, having each one select those bundles repeats a choice that never varies. We can instead record those choices once in a namespace and leave only the varying parts to each context. These are default implementations.

In a recent development, I see defaults as a way to adopt CGP gradually. Ordinary traits may already be enough for a single-crate application with one implementation of each operation. If that application later needs more modularity, it can move code into CGP components and record its initial provider choices as defaults. Bundles can follow when there are useful groups to swap.

Let's keep the routes we already registered in DefaultNamespace and define a configuration namespace that inherits them using the latest cgp_namespace! macro:.

Recent findings suggest that defaultAppComponents starts with the prefixes and any default bindings supplied by its parent. We can add our application-specific choices here without changing what other namespaces select. Every context that joins this configuration namespace will share those choices.

For a simple provider, we can place its binding beside its implementation. Add #[default_impl] to our earlier GetUserWithPostgres definition:.

According to recent reports, the implementation now declares that DefaultAppComponents uses it at @app.core.user.UserGetterComponent. If we prefer to collect the bindings in one place, we can write the same choice in the namespace body instead:.

These are alternative ways to register the same binding, so writing both would create a conflict. The namespace body looks like a delegate_components! table, but its choices apply to every context that joins the namespace. We bind the provider at the full path because the bare key is already taken. The route inherited from DefaultNamespace uses UserGetterComponent to send lookups on to @app.core.user.UserGetterComponent, so a second entry for the bare key would conflict with it.

According to recent reports, these defaults are fixed choices. Once the namespace binds a provider, a joining context or inheriting namespace cannot override it, even with a more specific entry. A context also cannot disable just one default while retaining the rest of that namespace. So a choice that should vary between contexts belongs on a path the namespace leaves open, as we will do with the filters below.

It has been revealed that there is also a constraint on where we write the registration. With a prefixed path, the binding must live in the crate that owns the namespace, here DefaultAppComponents. The path expands to CGP's PathCons type, and owning a component marker nested inside that type does not satisfy Rust's orphan rules. An unprefixed local component marker has different ownership rules, covered by the #[default_impl] reference.

FilterCensoredUsername is generic over its inner provider. For this configuration, we want to choose both the wrapper and its PostgreSQL implementation. We can assemble that complete provider choice directly in the namespace body:.

After we bind the remaining user and post providers in the same way, the application only needs to choose its filters. For this example, our production wiring then becomes:.

According to recent reports, every context that joins DefaultAppComponents gets its user and post providers from it. We left the filter path open so a test context can select DummyContentFilterComponents there instead.

Recent findings suggest that we kept the prefixes in DefaultNamespace and the provider choices in DefaultAppComponents for a reason. Another configuration, such as a SQLite one, can then inherit the same routes without also inheriting PostgreSQL choices it could not override. So the routes belong in a base namespace, and the fixed choices in a configuration namespace that inherits it.

In a recent development, if we later need to replace one of these fixed defaults, we choose a namespace that leaves its destination open. We could return to the base DefaultNamespace and supply the required bindings explicitly, as in the earlier bundle examples.

While the application lives in one crate, #[default_impl] conveniently keeps each binding beside its implementation. Once providers move into crates of their own, that attribute would sit in a crate that does not own the namespace, which the ownership rule above forbids. So we move the bindings into the configuration namespace's body instead, and the namespace's crate assembles the providers from there.

There is room to start with direct wiring, share fixed choices through defaults, and introduce interchangeable bundles as the application needs them. I would choose whichever arrangement makes the current decisions easiest to see, rather than build the full hierarchy in anticipation of future growth.

According to recent reports, namespaces are the largest change, but several smaller additions also make CGP easier to write, read, and use in more kinds of crates. You can use these without following the full application refactoring above:.

For the smaller changes, such as clearer errors from the handler macros and the restrictions this release lifts, see the v0.8.0 release notes.

Industry observers note that upgrading from v0.7.0 needs source changes. The largest is the removal of presets, which namespaces replace in this release, and most applications will also need explicit imports for items that used to come from the prelude. The v0.8.0 release notes list every change, with the upgrade steps in order.

According to recent reports, two projects built with CGP move to v0.8.0 at the same time. cgp-serde 0.3.0 can now serialize and deserialize enums, and Hypershell 0.2.0 assembles its language from a namespace instead of presets. If your code builds on either, the cgp-serde v0.3.0 and Hypershell v0.2.0 release notes give the upgrade steps.

In a recent development, the preset system described earlier is removed in v0.8.0. Its shared provider choices can become namespace bindings, while groups that need to remain interchangeable can become aggregate providers selected through paths.

Sources indicate that the following v0.7.0 example defines a preset and inherits it into a context. This is old syntax and does not compile with v0.8.0:.

According to recent reports, A configuration namespace can preserve the preset's fixed user-provider choices. Register the user components under @app.core.user in DefaultNamespace, using the #[prefix(... in DefaultNamespace)] attributes shown earlier. Then replace the preset with this namespace:.

The migrated context must also supply the censor required by its creation wrapper. Register UsernameCensor under @app.extra.content_filter in DefaultNamespace. With the user components and filter registered, replace the inheritance attribute with explicit delegation on the context:.

It has been revealed that the example above deliberately checks only the migrated user group and its filter. Add the post operations and any other dependencies your application uses.

Recent findings suggest that an aggregate provider keeps the user-provider group interchangeable. If configurations need that variation, retain PostgresUserComponents using delegate_components! { new PostgresUserComponents { ... } } and select it with @app.core.user: PostgresUserComponents, as in the main walkthrough. Choose between this configurable bundle arrangement and the fixed namespace bindings above according to what should vary.

The removed preset constructs and their replacements are:.

Industry observers note that cgp::prelude now exports only the names CGP code usually writes: the macros, the derives, PhantomData, and a few traits and providers such as HasErrorType, CanRaiseError, UseType, and DefaultNamespace. The code the macros generate reaches CGP's items through a separate cgp::macro_prelude, so the prelude no longer has to carry those items. If your code names one of the dropped items through the glob import, the compiler reports that it cannot find it, and you import it from its module:.

The dropped names come from these modules:.

Recent findings suggest that A derive does not need its trait imported, so #[derive(HasField)] still works through the prelude, while a HasField bound or a .get_field() call needs the import. A provider for a handler trait such as Computer imports its key, ComputerComponent, beside the trait, because the provider's header names the key, as Other improvements describes.

Raw compiler output changes slightly as a result. Where v0.7.0 printed a type such as cgp::prelude::Chars, the compiler can now print cgp::macro_prelude::Chars, as in the cargo check comparison above.

The type-level types also lose their Greek-letter names. v0.7.0 declared them as π, ε, σ, θ, ζ, ψ, δ, and ω, with Cons, Nil, Either, Void, Chars, Symbol, Index, and Field as aliases, and the prelude exported both spellings. Only the English names remain, so code that wrote a Greek name switches to the English one, imported from cgp::core::field::types. Raw compiler output changes with them, printing Cons<…> and Chars<…> where v0.7.0 printed π<…> and ζ<…>.

The default features of cgp are now empty, so the library builds without std or an allocator. In v0.7.0, the defaults turned on DebugError and DisplayError, the error providers that format an error into a String. If your wiring uses either, turn on the alloc feature:.

The associated-type separator in #[use_type] changes from :: to .:.

According to recent reports, equality imports use the new separator too. Write #[use_type(HasErrorType.{Error = AppError})]. An import from another context changes shape as well, with the context named after in: #[use_type(@Types::HasScalarType::Scalar)] becomes #[use_type(HasScalarType.Scalar in Types)]. The #[use_type] reference covers each form.

A component that generates a UseDelegate dispatcher moves the derive_delegate key of #[cgp_component] into an attribute of its own, one per dispatcher:.

A new component does not need either form, because the open statement from Other improvements dispatches it per type.

Recent findings suggest that the extra-feature macro crates are renamed from cgp-extra-macro and cgp-extra-macro-lib to cgp-macro-extra and cgp-macro-extra-lib. Upgrade direct dependencies on those crates. Imports through cgp::prelude keep their names.

In a recent development, self-contained handler-macro expansions may leave imports unused. Remove imports the compiler reports when they existed only for the old expansion.

In a recent development, #[cgp_auto_dispatch] rejects attribute arguments and typed receivers such as self: Box. It previously ignored the arguments or miscompiled those receivers.

Recent findings suggest that the upcoming Struct! and Enum! prelude exports can make a macro name ambiguous. Qualify the call if another glob import provides the same name.

DelegateComponent, IsProviderFor, HasField, and HasFieldMut no longer carry custom #[diagnostic::on_unimplemented] messages. Plain cargo check now reports an unmet bound on them in the compiler's own wording, and cargo cgp check rewrites those errors into its own summary. If a test compares compiler output, as a UI test does, revision the messages it expects.

cgp-error-eyre enables eyre's automatic default-handler installation and tracks the caller of raise_error and wrap_error.

cgp-error-std changes how wrapped errors are displayed. Ordinary Display prints only the outer detail, while alternate Display and Debug include the chain. This avoids duplicated sources when a reporter walks source() itself. Revision output assertions that depend on the old formatting.

Sources indicate that the minimum anyhow and eyre dependencies rise to 1.0.104 and 0.6.14 respectively. The backend READMEs in the CGP repository describe their use.

Sources indicate that we started with two manager choices and ended with applications that could share a core, change their filters, or use a different database. Namespaces let the top-level wiring express those choices even as we split the implementations into smaller pieces. I hope that makes similar refactorings easier to follow in your own projects, with cargo-cgp and the upcoming documentation there to help when something is unclear.

CGP still takes time to learn. Its ecosystem is small, and I still have work to do on the tooling and documentation. My suggestion is to try it on one problem you already have. If you already use CGP, try grouping one area of your wiring while keeping its component checks in place. If you are new to CGP, the Quickstart provides a smaller starting point.

In a recent development, I would appreciate hearing where you still struggle to trace an implementation, understand a diagnostic, or follow an explanation. Those examples will help me decide what to improve next. You can share them in GitHub Discussions. Thank you for reading and trying CGP.

I wrote the draft of this post, and an AI agent revised its prose and checked its code and claims against the CGP knowledge base. See How AI is used in this project.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Peter Farrelly's biopic "I Play Rocky" tells the story of a young Sylvester Stallone (Anthony Ippolito) as he rises through his early, sketchy acting career, eventually coming to write and star in 1976's "Rocky," itself one of the best sports movies ever made. The film doesn't sugarcoat Stallone's early struggles, including his run-down apartment, his inability to land good roles as a young actor going by the name of Mike (leading him to work on an adult feature), and the fact that, at one point, he had to sleep on the street.

Sources indicate that it also depicts the verbal abuse that he suffered at the hands of his domineering father, Frank Sr, who runs a barbershop and is hardly encouraging. When Stallone relates his acting dreams, Frank tells his son that he isn't handsome enough to be a movie star. Ouch, dad.

Sources indicate that frank is played by Matt Dillon, who exploded onto the cinematic scene in 1979 thanks to his role in Jonathan Kaplan's "Over the Edge," a film so beloved that it inspired both Richard Linklater and Kurt Cobain. Dillon rose to prominence shortly after that, appearing in movies like "Little Darlings," "Liar's Moon," and Francis Ford Coppola's S.E. Hinton adaptations "The Outsiders" and "Rumble Fish.".

It has been revealed that indeed, for a spell during the 1980s, Dillon was a teen heartthrob, and his intense performance style and tenacity dictated a steady stream of high-profile work as he got older. That includes his role in Gun Van Sant's 1989 picture "Drugstore Cowboy" (which caused quite a stir) and his turn in Cameron Crowe's 1992 movie "Singles" (one of the 1990s' defining films). From there, he collaborated with Van Sant again when he played a pushy husband in 1995's "To Die For" and had a key role in Frank Oz's mainstream 1997 queer comedy "In & Out.

Listing all of Matt Dillon's credits here would take up too much space. Just know that he has been a creative force in Hollywood for, gosh, almost 50 years, and has constantly teamed up with prominent directors, among them Garry Marshall, Arthur Penn, Allison Anders, Lars Von Trier, and Wes Anderson. His role as  Frank Stallone Sr. in "I Play Rocky" isn't even the first time Dillon has played a real person. In fact, he previously played Marlon Brando in the Maria Schneider biopic "Being Maria" and Henri Chinaski, Charles Bukowski's literary alter ego, in the 2005 film "Factotum.".

According to recent reports, "I Play Rocky" itself marks the second time Dillon has worked with Peter Farrelly, as he also appeared in the Farrelly Bros.' 1998 ultra-hit comedy "There's Something About Mary," playing the toothsome character of Pat. That same year, he played a sleazy, double-crossing teacher in the thriller "Wild Things" and thereafter worked on everything from Disney films ("Herbie: Fully Loaded") to the notorious Best Picture Oscar-winning "Crash," whose own director, Paul Haggis, later admitted didn't deserve to be crowned Best Picture. Nevertheless, Dillon is excellent in it.

It has been revealed that even now, Dillon reveals no signs of slowing down. And while he specializes in playing tough guys and aggressive heavies, he's quite capable of other things, with "Drugstore Cowboy" displaying his range with what, for my money, is his best performance. But then, there are so many to choose from. He does a good job as an oppressive father figure in the syrupy but highly watchable "I Play Rocky," too, embodying a hard-working barber who may love his son but doesn't think much of him. It's a solid, dark turn for a longtime, hardworking actor.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Grand Theft Auto 6's auto drive feature is perfect if you just want to see the sights of Leonida or avoid navigating through traffic. Not that GTA 6 goes out of its way to tell you there even is an auto drive feature. It's tucked away in a menu you have little cause to use early in the game, and you also need to make sure a specific setting is toggled on for it to work in some circumstances. It's best to still learn how to drive decently yourself, though, as auto drive isn't the best choice in hectic situations.

Below, we explain how to auto drive in GTA 6 and when you'd want to take the wheel yourself.

It has been revealed that autodrive is enabled automatically from the start, but only for safe scenarios. If you want to use it whenever, here's what to do.

The next time you're in a vehicle, do this to use auto drive:.

To turn auto drive off, you just need to hold down on the D-pad again.

Auto drive does what you'd expect. It handles the driving — or flying or sailing — for you, and it avoids accidents, road rage, manslaughter, crashed planes, and all the other problems you might get yourself into if you were driving manually. You don't have to set a destination for it to work, though if you do set one, it'll take you there.

The game enters cinematic mode and takes camera control from you, though you can still enter photo mode from the pause menu if you want to rotate the camera for a shot. You also still have control over the radio.

Just make sure you familiarize yourself with GTA 6's driving in between the bouts of cinematic vibes tourism. In unrestricted mode, you can use auto drive in "unsafe" scenarios like chase or escape missions, of which there are quite a few. You kind of don't want to, though. Knowledge of side streets, learning how to handle a sharp turn at speed, and a deft hand at avoiding collisions (or causing strategic ones) can make a significant difference in these sequences. Aut odrive also won't save you from damage or other issues you started before enabling it. It'll get you out of tight situations, like bad parking, but it might cause some damage to the surrounding area and your car in the process.

If you're just getting started in GTA 6, we have plenty of guides to help you live the high life in Leonida. There's a set of explainers for GTA 6's more open-ended side activities, like how to rob the Exotic Animal Front and where to find tree effigies for the Skunk Ape mission, and we've got all the GTA 6 cheat codes. You'll have to put in some effort before you can use those, though.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that "Slow Horses" is the best spy show on TV for many reasons, one of which is seeing veteran star and British national treasure Gary Oldman sharing scenes with relative newcomers, especially River Cartwright actor Jack Lowden. But while the Scottish star seemed to come out of nowhere when Apple TV's spy series debuted in 2020, he's actually been working since the early 2010s. By 2016, he'd landed a lead role in the BBCs "War & Peace" miniseries, which was a major step in his career. The following year, however, was arguably even more significant for Lowden as he not only played Morrissey in the unauthorized biopic "England is Mine," he had a significant part in Christopher Nolan's "Dunkirk.".

In a recent development, nolan made yet another great film with "Dunkirk." It depicts the evacuation of thousands of Allied troops from the titular French region during the six-week Battle of France in 1940. But in true Nolan style, we get a non-linear narrative and multiple perspectives on the legendary events that unfolded on the French coast. The writer/director follows two young soldiers on land named Tommy (Fionn Whitehead) and Gibson (Aneurin Barnard), civilian sailor Mr Dawson (Mark Rylance) and his son Peter Dawson (Tom Glynn-Carney), and two fighter pilots named Farrier (Tom Hardy) and Collins (Lowden).

Recent findings suggest that the various characters' harrowing journeys intersect as Nolan's retelling of the historic event goes on. Thankfully, Lowden isn't relegated to wearing an oxygen mask in a cockpit for the entire film, and is given quite a bit to do despite the expansive ensemble. One of his scenes in particular represents one of the film's most gripping moments. But Lowden is also able to showcase his talents in smaller moments as a shellshocked pilot left reeling from his experience in the skies over the English Channel.

Like all Christopher Nolan movies, most of the events in "Dunkirk" are captured in-camera using real props and vehicles. That lends the film an authenticity which adds so much to the experience. When Collins' plane goes down, for instance, you feel the thud as it hits the water. The following scene, wherein his cockpit fills with water, feels similarly visceral, bringing you into the experience and heightening the sense of panic. It's incredibly well done and beautifully shot by cinematographer and frequent Nolan collaborator Hoyte van Hoytema.

It has been revealed that but there's more to "Dunkirk" than visceral action sequences. Every aspect of the film comes together to create an unforgettable whole, and the performances are a substantial part of that. Nolan deliberately keeps dialogue to a minimum — a blessing for those who find his writing to be a tad overwrought at times — leaving the cast with the challenge of rendering the emotion through their reactions and expressions. Everyone, Jack Lowden included, delivers.

According to recent reports, not that that should be a surprise to "Slow Horses" fans. The actor, who's noted to be one of five finalists to become the upcoming James Bond, has been brilliant as River Cartwright, never allowing his humanistic portrayal of the frustrated sleuth to be overshadowed by his esteemed co-star's unforgettable performance as Jackson Lamb. Lowden fans, along with everyone else yet to see "Dunkirk," should definitely watch Nolan's war epic.
