Industry observers note that [Editor’s note: This review was originally published on January 23, 2026 during the 2026 Sundance Film Festival. Sumerian Pictures will release the film in limited theaters on Friday, November 20, with a wide release to follow on Friday, December 4.].

At this point, filmmaker Beth de Araújo is two for two. Not just in terms of the quality of her films — impeccably crafted fever dreams of very different stripes and horrifyingly similar themes — but in how these films make the viewer feel.

Industry observers note that more concisely: with her “Soft & Quiet” and “Josephine,” de Araújo remains undefeated when it comes to making stunning films that I will both heartily recommend and never, ever watch again. Related Stories Trump Renews Backing for Federal Film Tax Credit as Lawmakers Push for Year-End Passage ‘Disclosure Day’ Did Its Biggest Stunts Practically, So the VFX Team Worked Hard to Look Invisible — Watch.

The word that comes to mind when watching a de Araújo feature is heartsick. That applies to the feeling bestowed on both the audience and her characters (the good guys and the bad guys). While her first film, the unrelenting “Soft & Quiet,” was cleverly designed to appear as if it was shot in a single real-time take, her sophomore feature is more about the steady accumulation of dread. The heroines of “Soft & Quiet” recognize what they are dealing with almost immediately (the force of the evil that is bent on destroying them is what’s surprises most), but the star at the center of “Josephine” is not just wounded by the sickness that suddenly infiltrates her young life, but her complete lack of understanding about what is happening to her and why.

It has been revealed that in both films, it’s not just bad deeds that upends everyday lives, it’s real evil, actual monsters, perversions that don’t only show up in a movie screen. That’s true terror.

In a recent development, based loosely on an experience de Araújo, who both wrote and directed the film, experienced as a child, “Josephine” initially lulls us into a false sense of safety. It’s early morning in San Francisco, and fledgling soccer star Josephine (Mason Reeves, riveting in her first role) is getting ready for a run with her devoted dad Damien (Channing Tatum, bringing incredible girl-dad energy to the role). It’s something the pair do every Sunday morning: get up early to watch Premier League football, run through a woodsy neighboring park, and kick the ball around.

In a recent development, for her second film, de Araújo leans less on clever camera tricks, though she and cinematographer Greta Zozula occasionally put us in Josephine’s own perspective, shooting as if we are looking through the eight-year-old’s eyes. As with “Soft & Quiet,” the gimmick works, grounding us in Josephine’s world and immersing us, if briefly, in what the world looks like from her vantage. Jo-Jo, as her dad calls her, is plucky and fun and filled with energy, so when she briefly zips ahead of her dad while on their run through Golden Gate Park, it just seems like everyday high-jinks.

Industry observers note that but when the path forks (about as heavy-handed a metaphor as de Araújo will ever employ), Josephine goes to the left, while Damien goes to the right. What she finds there will forever alter the course of her life, and set “Josephine” off on a heart-wrenching journey with no easy answers. Curious and watchful, Josephine ducks behind a tree when she sees a woman (Syra McCarthy) running into a public bathroom at the bottom of a scrubby hill, and she sinks even further down when a young man (a bone-chilling Philip Ettinger) follows the unknown woman into the tiny building.

Sources indicate that de Araújo’s approach to portraying on-screen violence only furthers that heartsick feeling: straightforward, unsparing, and absolutely devoid of any possibility of being compared to “torture porn.” What we see, what Josephine sees, is something no person should ever witness or experience. And that’s the root of the film’s power: how do we talk about things that we should not have words for?

According to recent reports, when Damien arrives on the scene, it kicks off what will become one of Tatum’s best performances yet, a deep-feeling and heartbreaking exploration of layers of emotional unease. Damien does everything “right,” ensuring both Josephine and the woman are safe, chasing after the assailant, calling the cops, a neat little checklist of “how to handle an emergency.” And yet, the damage has already been done. There will be more to come.

Even when Josephine begins to seek out answers to what she’s seen (snatching her mom’s phone to search “raip,” reeling at what she discovers), it’s impossible to make sense of everything. There are things to fear she never even know existed, and the deep-seated powerlessness that overtakes her causes her to act out in chilling and increasingly volatile ways. Her parents’ reactions don’t help: her exceedingly calm mother Claire (Gemma Chan, thrilling as a character just barely holding it together) wants her to see a therapist now, her more action-oriented dad is eager to put her into self-defense classes. The mixed messages both give off (to say nothing of their own barely concealed terror) do little to help Josephine, who soon becomes someone almost entirely different than the care-free kid she just was.

She also picks up a upcoming friend: Ettinger begins to appear to her, a literal haunting figure, never saying a word, yet barging into nearly every moment of Josephine’s already upended life. It’s the sort of choice another filmmaker fight fill tricksy or silly, but that de Araújo delivers with the maximum of impact. And that we, like Josephine and only Josephine, can see him only furthers our immersion into her world. It almost goes beyond empathy.

In a recent development, josephine’s steadily unfolding breakdown is only compounded by the arrival of yet another situation no eight-year-old should ever have to encounter: handling the messy investigation of the crime itself. How she might help (or not) drives one more wedge between Josephine and her parents, who all have a different take on what the “right” thing to do is.

If these questions sound heady and heavy, they are, but de Araújo’s masterful ability to interrogate tension on every level keeps the film clipping along, each turn both a surprise and an inevitability. The monsters are here, they are real, and they’re coming.

“Josephine” premiered at the 2026 Sundance Film Festival.

Latest Update: 10 Best Directing Duos Of All Time, Ranked

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

In a recent development, most films treat the idea of the "director" with a dignified sense of reverence, especially since the end of the studio system. Where the producer's role was once seen as paramount in getting a film made and even in achieving a certain artistic vision, a film's achievements are now often attributed to the isolated decisions of the all-important director.

While we've talked plenty about the medium's great moviemakers — indeed, we already have a list of the 25 best directors of all time — it seemed appropriate to carve out space for the history's great directing partnerships. Though plenty of movies have two directors, the sustained union of two filmmakers over many years and/or films is rarer, and it warrants a closer look at the best of those recurring or long-lasting alliances. While the idea of the director usually implies one voice making the final decisions for the myriad creative components of a finished film, these directing duos prove that continuing that sense of collaboration into the chief position on a film set can bear rewarding fruit.

Here are the best directing duos of all time, ranked.

Jean-Pierre Jeunet and Marc Caro spent years honing their singular aesthetic in short films before making their feature debut with "Delicatessen," a pitch-black comedy set in a post-apocalyptic apartment building where a butcher-landlord keeps his tenants fed by turning unsuspecting newcomers into meat. Jeunet and Caro's penchant for grotesque faces and sickly yellow lighting helped make the film a sensation, earning it four César Awards, including Best First Film and Best Original or Adapted Screenplay.

Sources indicate that "The City of Lost Children" saw them double down on their peculiar sensibility: a fable set in a decaying port city, where a prematurely aging scientist steals children's dreams and a gentle circus strongman, played by Ron Perlman, searches for his kidnapped little brother. Its macabre, nightmarish storybook whimsy remains one of the most singular visions in French cinema — an underseen, visually stunning masterpiece.

Sources indicate that then the partnership abruptly ended. Jeunet was tapped to direct "Alien Resurrection", and his subsequent films, most famously the candy-colored "Amélie," have generally been warmer and more polished. Meanwhile, Caro's lone solo feature, the sci-fi film "Dante 01," never found the same audience. It makes for a fascinating what-if, as nobody has quite matched the blend of cruelty and tenderness the two cooked up together, and it's hard not to suspect that the grime and the heart needed each other.

John Musker and Ron Clements met at Disney while working on "The Fox and the Hound," and they went on to become one of the studio's most dependable directing teams during its biggest creative revival. They made their feature-directing debut alongside Burny Mattinson and David Michener on 1986's "The Great Mouse Detective," a Sherlock Holmes riff about a sleuthing rodent, before Clements pitched an adaptation of Hans Christian Andersen's "The Little Mermaid." Working with songwriters Howard Ashman and Alan Menken, they delivered a film that won Oscars for its score and for "Under the Sea" and helped kick off the Disney Renaissance.

In a recent development, "Aladdin" followed in 1992. The now-iconic musical was the highest-grossing film of its year and the highest-grossing animated film to that point, earning two more Oscars for Menken's score and "A Whole Newly introduced World." The duo kept working through shifting tastes, with "Hercules" in 1997 and the sci-fi swashbuckler "Treasure Planet" in 2002, which flopped but has since found its defenders. They returned to hand-drawn animation with "The Princess and the Frog" in 2009, then made their first fully computer-animated feature with "Moana," which earned an Oscar nomination for Best Animated Feature. It also spawned a widely criticized, remarkably premature live-action remake — part of a trend the pair described as "bemusing.".

Recent findings suggest that the pair has since retired, closing out a partnership that lasted more than three decades. Their films were defined by the fundamentals of Disney magic: musical numbers that developed the plot and emotions, and humor that never smothered the pathos underneath. Few directors have made so many movies that feel so effortlessly designed for all audiences.

Before they set box-office records, Joe and Anthony Russo were comedy filmmakers from Cleveland. After their micro-budget debut, "Pieces", Steven Soderbergh and George Clooney produced their second feature, "Welcome to Collinwood." The brothers broke through on television, winning an Emmy for directing the pilot of "Arrested Development," then directing the pilot of "Community" and many beloved episodes after it.

That sitcom background is key to the work that followed in the Marvel Cinematic Universe, where their instincts for staging a dozen characters trading blows and punchlines helped define the quippy, ensemble-driven sensibility of their "Avengers" movies. However, that style has become a grievance among certain viewers who wish the films could escape their unrelenting sense of brand management. The brothers have cited François Truffaut and the French Fresh Wave as major influences, but their biggest films operate within decidedly conventional blockbuster boundaries. Still, there's no denying the level of control needed to orchestrate some of the biggest hits of the 2010s.

According to recent reports, their post-Marvel streaming films, including "Cherry," "The Gray Man," and "The Electric State," have been considerably less successful creatively. But through their company AGBO, they also produced the far more inventive "Everything Everywhere All at Once." With "Avengers: Doomsday" scheduled for December 2026, the brothers are once again tasked with herding Hollywood's biggest cast into something halfway coherent — a feat they've proven capable of, against all odds.

Justin Benson and Aaron Moorhead work on the principle that a tiny budget and a big idea can take you a long way. They broke out with "Resolution," which premiered at Tribeca in 2012, a lo-fi two-hander about a man who holes up in a remote cabin with his drug-addicted friend while something strange lurks beyond the walls. "Spring" followed in 2014, a Lovecraftian romance set on the Italian coast that fuses monster spectacle with the heart of a character drama. Benson typically writes and Moorhead handles cinematography, but the two co-direct and often appear on screen.

According to recent reports, that approach led to "The Endless," in which they play brothers returning to the cult they escaped. The film explicitly connects to "Resolution", establishing a shared cosmic-horror mythology. "Synchronic," their 2019 time-bending drug thriller with Anthony Mackie and Jamie Dornan, contains looser connections to that world, while the pandemic-era "Something in the Dirt" finds them starring as neighbors chasing a supernatural mystery.

It has been revealed that marvel took notice. They directed episodes of "Moon Knight" and much of the second season of "Loki," then helped rework the first season of "Daredevil: Born Again" before returning for its second. You could have worse pairs acting as custodians for one of the entertainment industry's biggest brands. Even if their Marvel work lacks the more personal flourishes of their smaller projects, you can still feel their indie-horror sensibility breaking through.

Industry observers note that daniel Kwan and Daniel Scheinert met at Emerson College and built their reputation on music videos, most famously DJ Snake and Lil Jon's "Turn Down for What", before making their feature debut with "Swiss Army Man," an emotionally vulnerable absurdist comedy about Paul Dano befriending a flatulent corpse played by Daniel Radcliffe. The movie's surprisingly tender treatment of shame, loneliness, and the weird stuff that makes us human earned the duo the U.S. Dramatic Directing Award at Sundance in 2016.

In a recent development, that set the stage for their true breakout: "Everything Everywhere All at Once" cranked their style to maximalist levels in one of the decade's most unexpected hits. Michelle Yeoh's exhausted laundromat owner is dragged across the multiverse in a hyper-stylized, daffy yet sincere family drama about an immigrant mother and her daughter facing the potential end of the world. It was A24's highest-grossing release at the time — the studio's first film to reach $100 million worldwide — and won seven of its 11 Oscar nominations, including Best Picture, Best Director, and Best Original Screenplay, plus acting wins for Yeoh, Ke Huy Quan, and Jamie Lee Curtis.

According to recent reports, that made the Daniels only the third directing pair to win Best Director, after Robert Wise & Jerome Robbins and Joel & Ethan Coen. Though prone to hyperactivity, few other filmmakers could make a hot-dog-fingers gag and a mother-daughter reconciliation feel like parts of the same carefully calculated thematic throughline. Here's hoping their next film, with Matt Damon attached, sustains that momentum.

Recent findings suggest that phil Lord and Christopher Miller have built a career on finding inventiveness in projects that might have become franchise mediocrity under other filmmakers. The Dartmouth classmates started in television, co-creating the short-lived MTV cult satire "Clone High," before making their feature debut with "Cloudy with a Chance of Meatballs," a frantic, silly adaptation of a children's picture book filled with surprisingly clever gags and character detail.

The duo kept pace: "21 Jump Street," a seemingly ill-conceived reboot of a 1980s TV drama as a buddy-cop farce, became one of the 2010s' most successful and acclaimed comedies. "The LEGO Movie," seemingly a feature-length branding exercise, became an inventive parable about creativity and conformity, launching a franchise of other LEGO films while transforming a bad premise into a cinematic miracle.

Their commitment to a distinct filmmaking voice also caused friction within the franchise machine, leading to their firing from "Solo: A Star Wars Story" late in production, though they went on to find other successes. As producers of "Spider-Man: Into the Spider-Verse," they helped push the possibilities of mainstream animation forward. They also drew on their "Star Wars" experience in making 2026's "Project Hail Mary," a funny, meticulously crafted, heart-on-its-sleeve adaptation of Andy Weir's novel that has grossed roughly $685 million worldwide. The pair's irreverence remains central to their success: tongue-in-cheek self-awareness and a genuine love of subverting expectations have helped them turn unlikely premises into crowd-pleasers.

Industry observers note that lana and Lilly Wachowski came out of Chicago as comic-book obsessives, finding work as screenwriters before announcing themselves as directors with "Bound," a lean, sultry neo-noir starring Jennifer Tilly and Gina Gershon that highlighted off their formal command on a small budget. Then came "The Matrix," the iconic 1999 sci-fi smash that fused Hong Kong martial arts, anime, and heady cyberpunk philosophy into a defining text of 2000s action cinema. Its "bullet time" effects were imitated endlessly; it broke box-office records, and cinema was never quite the same.

But what really sets the sisters apart is how stubbornly they kept betting massive. "Speed Racer" may have flopped on release, but it has since gained recognition as a forward-thinking work of art. Similarly, "Cloud Atlas" and "Sense8," their Netflix series about psychically linked strangers, have attracted devoted defenders of the Wachowskis' uncompromising vision. Even "Jupiter Ascending" has its champions. Their work has also invited a deeper reading of "The Matrix" as a trans allegory, something Lilly has discussed directly.

It has been revealed that the sisters have pursued separate projects in recent years. Lana directed 2021's caustically self-referential "The Matrix Resurrections" on her own, while Lilly has been developing "The Hunted," a mid-sized thriller with an all-transgender cast. Even while working apart, both continue to follow the amplified, philosophical sensibilities that made their collaborations so distinctive.

Sources indicate that widely known as engineers of feature-length anxiety attacks, Josh and Benny Safdie were among the most exciting filmmakers working in New York before their broader breakthrough. They first drew attention with "Daddy Longlegs," a scrappy, semi-autobiographical portrait of a chaotic father that played Cannes' Directors' Fortnight in 2009. Then came "Heaven Knows What," a bruising drama about people struggling with heroin addiction, starring Arielle Holmes and drawn from her own experiences and writings. Their method of handheld close-ups, overlapping dialogue, and nonprofessionals cast alongside movie stars came together in "Good Time," in which Robert Pattinson plays a small-time crook losing control of one long night.

The apex was "Uncut Gems," in which Adam Sandler gave a career-defining performance as a gambling-addicted Diamond District jeweler hurtling through two hours of escalating bad decisions — a stress-riddled, darkly funny drama of street-level chaos and apprehension.

Sources indicate that the brothers have since pursued separate directing careers, and differences in their sensibilities emerged in their solo work. Benny's "The Smashing Machine," with Dwayne Johnson as MMA fighter Mark Kerr, struggled commercially but revealed a quieter, more observant side of his filmmaking. Josh's "Marty Supreme," with Timothée Chalamet as a force of chaos, continued the streak of relentless havoc. Both films still carry the fingerprints of what the two built together: textured environments, tightly observed characters, and an acute sense of the worlds they inhabit. But the partnership that produced "Uncut Gems" remains one of the most electrifying of its era.

In a recent development, few partnerships have been as productive or as generous to film history as Michael Powell and Emeric Pressburger. Although Powell generally handled on-set direction and Pressburger originated many of their stories, they famously shared writing, producing, and directing credit during their peak years as the Archers. Powell, an Englishman who learned his craft on British quota quickies, and Pressburger, a Hungarian screenwriter who fled Nazi Germany, first teamed up in 1939. Pressburger later won an Oscar for the original story of 1941's "49th Parallel," and in the early 1940s they formed their production manufacturer, the Archers, whose films opened with an arrow striking a target.

That led to one of the great runs in British cinema: the wartime satire "The Life and Death of Colonel Blimp," the pastoral "A Canterbury Tale," the romance "I Know Where I'm Going!," and "A Matter of Life and Death," a fantasy about a pilot who cheats death. "Black Narcissus" won Oscars for Jack Cardiff's cinematography and Alfred Junge's art direction, while "The Red Shoes" remains an utterly dazzling film about artistic obsession, with its nearly 17-minute ballet sequence nestled inside a classical yet fantastical melodrama.

Their main partnership ended after 1957's "Ill Met by Moonlight," though they collaborated again on smaller projects, including "They're a Weird Mob" and "The Boy Who Turned Yellow." Powell's solo thriller "Peeping Tom" was so reviled by British critics that it badly damaged his career, though it has since been rediscovered as a masterpiece, thanks in no small part to Martin Scorsese.

Industry observers note that joel and Ethan Coen have long worked like one filmmaker with two heads, though Directors Guild rules obscured that for two decades by crediting Joel as director and Ethan as producer. The two also shared editing duties under the pseudonym Roderick Jaynes, a nonexistent editor who nonetheless earned Oscar nominations for "Fargo" and "No Country for Old Men." They finally received joint directing credit with 2004's "The Ladykillers." By then, the work had long spoken for itself: "Blood Simple" and "Raising Arizona" declared a pair of formalists with a wicked sense of humor, and "Barton Fink" swept Cannes in 1991.

It has been revealed that working frequently with cinematographer Roger Deakins, they moved between screwball comedy ("Raising Arizona," "Burn After Reading"), gangster pictures ("Miller's Crossing"), and Westerns ("True Grit") with unmatched formal and tonal precision. Few filmmakers could make movies as equally iconic as "The Big Lebowski" and "No Country for Old Men," works at opposite ends of the tonal spectrum that still feel unmistakably of a piece with the brothers' sardonic, philosophical sensibility.

After 2018's "The Ballad of Buster Scruggs," the brothers pursued solo directing projects, with Joel making "The Tragedy of Macbeth" and Ethan making "Drive-Away Dolls" and "Honey Don't!" But in October 2026, while receiving the Lumière Prize in Lyon, they noted they planned to direct another film together. Joel's upcoming "Jack of Spades," which Ethan co-wrote and Netflix plans to release theatrically in fall 2027, is still a solo directing project, but their reunion comments suggest another collaboration may be ahead. Hopefully they'll add another movie to a remarkable joint filmography, which we've ranked in full.

'Ghost Accounts' Are Putting Your Security at Risk, but You Can Protect Yourself

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (481 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that these so-called "ghost accounts"—all the old, forgotten logins that are still active but not in use—could expose your data in the event of a breach, increasing the risk of your information being used in malicious ways.
  • As McAfee describes, ghost accounts may retain lots of sensitive data, such as your contact details (phone numbers, emails, and addresses), purchase histories, payment details, and passwords.
  • In a recent development, you're less likely to be keeping tabs on activity in older accounts, which may also have weak or reused passwords that haven't been updated in years.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that these so-called "ghost accounts"—all the old, forgotten logins that are still active but not in use—could expose your data in the event of a breach, increasing the risk of your information being used in malicious ways. That's why it's important to go through the effort to find and delete dormant accounts. Here's how to get started.

As McAfee describes, ghost accounts may retain lots of sensitive data, such as your contact details (phone numbers, emails, and addresses), purchase histories, payment details, and passwords. While this doesn't mean your information is sure to be compromised, the more places it lives, the more opportunities there are for bad actors to get ahold of it.

In a recent development, you're less likely to be keeping tabs on activity in older accounts, which may also have weak or reused passwords that haven't been updated in years. If that firm or service experiences a data breach, not only is your stored data there exposed, but that information (including your password) can be used to access other accounts using tactics like credential stuffing and phishing. This also increases the risk of identity theft, as threat actors can use your name, birth date, and other information to open fraudulent accounts.

Unfortunately, finding and removing forgotten accounts can be tedious. If you have a password manager, the easiest way to start is to audit older items as well as look at security reports that identify weak or reused passwords, as well as data breaches that have impacted your accounts. If you've saved credentials in your browser keychain, go through the same process to find dormant accounts.

According to recent reports, next, audit accounts you've created using single sign-on, such as Google, Apple, or Facebook. For Google, this is under Account Settings > Linked apps. For Apple, go to System Settings > [Your Name] > Sign in with Apple on your Mac (or the same path in the Settings app on iOS). On Facebook, this is under Settings & privacy > Apps and websites. Disconnecting these accounts won't automatically delete them, but you can add them to the list to take action. Finally, you can search your email(s) on HaveIBeenPwned and username(s) on IDCrawl or WhatsMyName to find dormant accounts.

Once you've found accounts you no longer use, the next step is to deactivate or delete them, which you may be able to do through the settings or by reaching out to customer support. At the very least, remove all identifying information and change the password, and if possible, upgrade the address to a burner using your browser's or password manager's hide-my-email feature. If you no longer have access to an old account, that doesn't mean it's been deactivated and your information removed, so you may need to reach out to customer support to find out how to access and delete it.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

James Bond is back at the forefront of pop culture, thanks to the announcement that Robert Pattinson will portray the super-spy in Denis Villeneuve's upcoming Bond movie. While opinions on Pattinson's casting are mixed, it signals that Amazon MGM Studios is swinging for the fences with Bond. Now, a new report hints that Amazon is planning another project that could radically reshape how people see James Bond. The Sun recently ran a piece claiming Prime Video is looking to develop a television series focused on Bond's early years before he joins MI6.

Industry observers note that the reasoning for such a project is twofold. First isthe success of Young Sherlock, another prequel seriescentered on a literary icon. Young Sherlock quickly rocketed up Prime Video's streaming charts, thanks to Guy Ritchie's involvement and its exploration of a young Sherlock Holmes' evolution into a master detective. Second is the Young James Bond novels by Charlie Higson, which chronicle Bond's education at Eton College. The Sun also reports that Amazon has been considering some form of a Bond spin-off for quite some time:.

"There was no way that Amazon were going to pass up on the opportunity to make more spin-off versions of the Bond franchise, and some sort of prequel is a natural choice.".

According to recent reports, while a series focused on Bond's younger years sounds appealing, it could be a step too far for the franchise. Going through with the project could also cement a fear most movie fans have held since Amazon took the reins of the Bond franchise.

The dangers of a James Bond prequel run parallel to those of any prequel: approaching questions fans have wondered about could lead to disappointing answers. Take the Star Wars prequels. The idea that the Force is fueled by microscopic bacteria or that Emperor Palpatine's first name is "Sheev" stripped away much of the original trilogy's mystique. A young James Bond prequel could do the same thing, especially since most of the character's backstory was already explored during Daniel Craig's tenure. Learning that Bond was an orphan explains his life choices and why he joins MI6, and you don't really need to go deeper than that.

If Prime Video eventually goes through with a young Bond series, it raises a question: Will more Bond spin-offs follow? One could imagine a series being centered on Bond's CIA ally and close friend Felix Leiter, or the formation of the terrorist organization SPECTRE. But that approach could dilute the Bond franchise. It could also reduce the impact of the James Bond movies themselves, which is something Amazon doesn't want. James Bond is a character built for the big screen, and trying to spread out his adventures is a death sentence for the franchise.

While Prime Video might be eyeing a young James Bond series, a great story focusing on the super-spy's younger days already exists, and it was released earlier this year. That story is 007: First Light, the video game in which a 26-year-old Bond works to achieve his "00" status. First Light quickly gained critical acclaim due to its story, the gameplay that features Bond doing what he does best (aka killing bad guys and romancing beautiful women), and the game design feeling cinematic enough to be its own Bond movie. Trying to top First Light would be foolish.

According to recent reports, another elephant in the room is Casino Royale, the first movie in Daniel Craig's Bond era and a "de facto" secret origin in the vein of Batman Begins. In its opening sequence, the audience will see Bond earn his "00" status in a brutal fight, the origins of his playboy persona as he loses Vesper Lynd (Eva Green), the one person he truly cares for, and his full slide into the more polished secret agent fans know and love. Again, a bar has been set, and rather than trying to clear it, Amazon should focus on ensuring Robert Pattinson has a strong first outing as Bond.

Stay tuned to Collider for future James Bond updates.

Bolt's Scooters Are Becoming Accessibility Sensors

📅 28 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1878 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Geoawesome

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that bolt has demonstrated that a shared scooter can be more than a vehicle.
  • During its Wheels4Wheels pilot in Tallinn, Estonia, the tech giant used sensors already installed in its scooters to assess pavement conditions, curb transitions and other features affecting wheelchair consumers and people with reduced mobility.
  • Recent findings suggest that bolt says the project covered approximately 550 kilometres across all eight Tallinn districts, producing 40.5 million accelerometer readings and more than 66,000 surface-quality assessments.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that bolt has demonstrated that a shared scooter can be more than a vehicle. It can also be a mobile geospatial sensor.

During its Wheels4Wheels pilot in Tallinn, Estonia, the tech giant used sensors already installed in its scooters to assess pavement conditions, curb transitions and other features affecting wheelchair consumers and people with reduced mobility.

Recent findings suggest that bolt says the project covered approximately 550 kilometres across all eight Tallinn districts, producing 40.5 million accelerometer readings and more than 66,000 surface-quality assessments. The resulting information was contributed to OpenStreetMap, according to Bolt’s accessibility programme page.

Sources indicate that publishing the results as open data makes the project more significant than a conventional corporate mapping exercise. Municipalities, routing applications and accessibility services could all potentially use the observations.

Industry observers note that the larger opportunity is the conversion of commercial vehicle fleets into continuously operating urban-observation networks. Thousands of scooters already traverse city streets during everyday operations, potentially detecting damaged surfaces and deteriorating infrastructure without requiring a dedicated municipal survey.

Recent findings suggest that according to Geo Week News, Bolt combined GPS with accelerometers, gyroscopes and cameras. The company reports that the pilot increased available surface-quality data in Tallinn by 26%. These figures have not been independently audited.

Industry observers note that the difficult step is converting motion signals into reliable accessibility information. A vibration could represent broken pavement, cobblestones, a drainage channel or an abrupt rider manoeuvre. Results may also vary with speed, tyre pressure, weather and scooter model.

Coverage presents another limitation. Scooters primarily travel where their use is permitted and commercially viable. They may miss residential streets, pedestrian paths and disconnected sections that create the greatest problems for wheelchair owners.

Each observation therefore needs provenance, a confidence level and an effective validation method. The most notable validators should include wheelchair and mobility-aid owners, who can determine whether a detected anomaly represents a genuine barrier.

Sources indicate that wheels4Wheels complements rather than replaces existing accessibility platforms. Wheelmap maps the accessibility of public places, while Project Sidewalk combines crowdsourcing, machine learning and street imagery to identify curb ramps and obstacles. Bolt adds passive, recurring fleet sensing.

A future workflow could use scooter telemetry to flag anomalies, imagery to classify them and local contributors to confirm their significance before the information enters OpenStreetMap.

Public discussion of the project has also highlighted a contradiction: poorly parked scooters can themselves block sidewalks and curb ramps. Bolt’s accessibility strategy must therefore address parking and obstruction management alongside data collection.

Industry observers note that if the organization can demonstrate reliable classification, transparent data handling and meaningful participation by accessibility users, Wheels4Wheels could evolve into more than a mapping experiment. The sensing capacity already exists. The next challenge is turning it into trustworthy, routable and genuinely inclusive geospatial infrastructure.

For decades, “more bands” in Earth observation meant one of two things: you either work with multispectral sensors; four to ten broad bands, cheap, fast and familiar or else transition to the hyperspectral domain, which has hundreds of narrow, contiguous bands, costly and enormous data volumes. However, this gap is closing not by making hyperspectral high-resolution accessible, but by rethinking what “enough bands” actually means. A category is quietly establishing itself between the two: Superspectral, a curated set of roughly a dozen to a few dozen discrete bands, placed purposely at specific wavelengths that correspond to something physically meaningful, rather than being sampled continuously across the electromagnetic spectrum.

Multispectral sensors were built around a simple idea: a handful of broad bands such as blue, green, red, red-edge, near-infrared are enough to compute NDVI & NDRE, delineate landcover, and monitor vegetation vigour at scale. Many of these systems also carry a panchromatic band: a single high-resolution spectral channel spanning across the visible spectrum (400-800 nm), used purely to sharpen spatial detail rather than to add spectral information. That’s the multispectral-era trade-off at minimal where spatial resolution and spectral resolution were treated as two separate problems, solved by two different types of bands. It works and it still works, for a huge share of remote sensing applications.

However, broad bands average out the very features that distinguish stressed vegetation from healthy vegetation, one water body from another, or one mineral from the next. A 100-120 nm wide band cannot resolve a narrow absorption or reflectance feature within it. Indices tied to specific physiological or physical processes such as pigment ratios, early-stage stress signatures and water turbidity, often require reflectance captured at precise, narrow wavelengths which a standard four or five-band setup was never designed to capture.

Why Hyperspectral isn’t the Universal Answer.

Hyperspectral imaging solves the problem by capturing contiguous and narrow bands. A 20-band sensor covering 500-700 nm at 10 nm interval is hyperspectral by this definition, while a sensor with 20 discrete, non-adjacent bands spanning the visible through infrared is still, technically a multispectral. That distinction matters because hyperspectral sensors carry real expense; complex optics, strict calibration requirements, and data volumes that stretch onboard storage, downlink bandwidth, and downstream ML pipelines. For most applied problems, that’s more data than the underlying problem statement actually needs.

The Middle Category: Superspectral.

Sources indicate that superspectral fits between the two. Rather than sampling the electromagnetic spectrum continuously, it samples it selectively – a dozen-plus discrete, narrow bands chosen because they align with known absorption or reflectance features, not because they happen to be adjacent on a continuum. It’s a knowledge-first approach to sensor design: instead of asking “how much of the spectrum can we cover continuously,” it asks “which specific wavelengths actually carry the signal we care about.”.

Industry observers note that this only works if the band selection is grounded in the underlying physics or biology of the target. Which is exactly where the reasoning gets interesting — because the “right” dozen bands look completely different depending on what you’re trying to measure.

Building the Case: Three Domains, Three Different Superspectral Stacks.

Water swiftly absorbs longer wavelengths, which is exactly why coastal and bathymetric applications require the shorter wavelength of the visible spectrum. In clear, deep water 400-450 nm wavelength penetrates furthest, making it the band of choice for shallow-water bathymetry and seafloor mapping. In turbid or CDOM-rich coastal water the picture inverts: suspended sediment and dissolved organic matter absorb and scatter strongly in the blue, and the transmission peak migrates toward green. On sediment loaded reef sites it has been observed shifting by around 100 nm into the green-yellow, peaking near 575 nm. A standard multispectral blue band, which is broadly tuned for atmospheric correction and land applications, is not optimized for this; a narrow, purpose-placed coastal-blue bands are. This is a case where one extra, carefully positioned band is more beneficial for the application than several additional generic ones.

According to recent reports, extending the vegetation logic straight into urban environments using Red-edge and NIR bands, but the physics doesn’t transfer as cleanly. Red-edge and NIR bands are diagnostic of chlorophyll and canopy structure, which makes them excellent for mapping urban vegetation fraction: street trees, park canopy, green-roof coverage, and green-space stress, all of which are legitimate and useful urban indicators, especially as proxies for urban surface extent and heat island risk. But Red-edge and NIR bands are not, a strong basis for classifying built materials themselves — asphalt, concrete, and rooftops don’t have a red-edge-style feature the way vegetation does. The spectral region that most cleanly separates impervious surfaces from vegetation and bare soil sits further out, in the shortwave infrared, where built materials and natural surfaces diverge most sharply. A Red-edge/NIR-only superspectral stack can tell you a great deal about a city’s green infrastructure; it can’t, tell you what the non-green parts of the city are made of. Getting that requires extending the band selection into SWIR — which is a fair, extension of the same superspectral principle: add exactly the band the physics calls for, nothing more.

Superspectral Sensors Exists: Drones to Satellites.

Recent findings suggest that micasense Drone payload: RedEdge-P Triple. A stacked triple narrowband camera bodies on one drone platform, each contributing a handful of 15 discrete, narrow, non-contiguous bands, pan-sharpened to 4 centimetres per pixel, enough to compute pigment and stress-sensitive indices that a standard five-band multispectral sensor can’t generate. This is the smallest-scale, most accessible end of the superspectral sensor; no continuous spectral coverage, just a deliberately chosen set of narrow bands.

Commercial VHR satellite: WorldView-3. Rolled out in 2014, WorldView-3 is explicitly described in the remote sensing literature and by its operators as a “Superspectral” sensor, a term used specifically to distinguish it from hyperspectral. Its imager collects 8 discrete VNIR bands (coastal, blue, green, yellow, red, red-edge, and two NIR bands), 8 discrete SWIR bands, and a separate 12-band CAVIS instrument for atmospheric correction (clouds, aerosols, water vapor, ice, and snow) 29 bands in total, but none of them contiguous in the way a hyperspectral band are. That distinction matters: WorldView-3 has been used for tasks like hydrocarbon and mineral detection that’s the domain of hyperspectral, precisely because its SWIR bands were placed at known diagnostic absorption features rather than spread evenly across the spectrum.

Industry observers note that research microsatellite: VENμS. A joint French–Israeli mission (CNES and the Israel Space Agency, rolled out 2017), was purpose-built VENμS Super-Spectral Camera (VSSC) with exactly 12 narrow bands between 415–910 nm, at 5.3 m resolution with a 2-day revisit. The band placement was designed specifically around vegetation status and the chlorophyll red-edge, plus atmospheric correction. It’s one of the cleanest real-world matches to the “12-18 narrow, targeted bands” definition of superspectral, since it was purpose-built as a science mission rather than adapted from a broader commercial sensor.

It has been revealed that next-generation Landsat constellation: Landsat Next. Planned for launch in late 2030/early 2031, the USGS and NASA’s Landsat Next mission is explicitly presented as “26-band Superspectral”, more than double the 11 bands on Landsat 8 and 9. It combines refined versions of Landsat’s legacy bands, ten newly introduced bands targeting applications like harmful algal blooms and snow hydrology, and five thermal infrared bands. When, a government agency formally classifies its flagship imaging mission as “superspectral” rather than multispectral or hyperspectral, that’s a strong indication the category has moved from marketing language to an accepted technical classification.

Why This Matters for GeoAI Pipelines.

The pattern across all three domains is the same, and it’s the real reason for superspectral as a category:.

Sources indicate that the multispectral or hyperspectral is a simple binary choice. Superspectral won’t replace either, broadband multispectral remains the workhorse for large-scale, low-cost monitoring, and hyperspectral remains necessary where continuous spectral coverage matters, like detailed mineral mapping or ore detection. But for the growing set of problems that need specific physical or biological signals – water quality, vegetation stress, urban green infrastructure and many more; without the overhead of a full hyperspectral sensor system, superspectral is becoming the realistic answer. It’s less “how much of the spectrum can we see” and more “how much do we actually need to see, and where.”.

According to recent reports, superspectral systems, by design, only see what they were told to look for. That’s a real trade-off, not a compromise to gloss over, it’s the whole point of this technology.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The flexibility of the K-drama medium continues to be eagerly studied by its devoted fan base across its multiple beloved genres. Plenty of viewers justifiably flock to its excellent romance offerings, with no small amount of love for its other niches like legal or fantasy K-dramas. But there's something special and raw about the indicates coming out of South Korea boasting exceptional action, combat choreography, and more than likely, at least one favorite series starring Ji Chang-wook.

In a recent development, the beauty of action-packed K-dramas is that they can focus on different time periods, settings, and entire genres, including horror and more run-of-the-mill action manhwa adaptations, while still having more left in the well to draw from. Action K-dramas are as popular as they are well-received, as shown below.

The star-crossed lovers Yoo Si-jin (Song Joong-ki) and Kang Mo-yeon (Song Hye-kyo) find themselves constantly torn apart because of Yoo Si-jin's active role in the military and Kang Mo-yeon's busy professional life as a doctor. Moments of war and conflict are punctuated with a genuine love story between the pair, which elevates both aspects of the narrative.

There's something for both ends of the K-drama audience spectrum in this series. Audiences who are less interested in romance have great action scenes, but there are plenty of soft and sensual moments between the central couple for romance fans as well. However, Descendants of the Sun should not be overlooked as an action series just because of its love story. For the international audience, it provides an interesting look into the South Korean military.

The series has become an international hit as well, sold for distribution to 32 different countries. It was also broadcast in China and South Korea simultaneously after a Chinese network paid nearly 40% of the production costs for the show to have the broadcast rights. That was the first time for a K-drama to get that treatment.

Healer takes down corrupt media outlets and solves murders through the lens of Seo Jung-hoo (Ji Chang-wook), a man known by the moniker Healer, who has a reputation for getting things done. Even though he starts the series thinking only of himself, he soon builds a connection with Chae Young-shin (K-drama romance darling Park Min-young). The two of them quickly get caught up in a case Chae Young-shin is reporting on, and the secrets from her past start resurfacing.

This intrigue is paired well with the excellent fighting skills Seo Jung-hoo indicates off and the high-stakes of freedom of the press. The action scenes here are actually more like some of the traditional action scenes in modern-day thrillers, like rooftop chase sequences or hand-to-hand combat in close quarters. Fans of the fight scenes in the Bourne movies will likely love this one.

According to recent reports, after her father is killed, Yoon Ji-woo (Han So-hee) aligns herself with a mob boss in the criminal underworld to catch her father’s murderer. Han So-hee is known for some of the best K-dramas, and My Name might be the greatest of all of her indicates because of how lightning-fast the pacing is and how much material she has in portraying Yoon Ji-woo.

It has been revealed that it's made all the more encouraging that she'll portray one of the most iconic action manhwa heroines in recent years, Cha Hae-in, in Netflix's upcoming Solo Leveling live-action series, too. She grows into a fearsome warrior and trains herself to be a weapon in her single-minded quest. Things heat up beyond belief when she goes undercover within the police force to root out corruption as an agent for her criminal organization.

The show was incredibly well-received when it premiered in South Korea, but also around the world. It was nominated for several awards, with Han So-hee in particular racking up nominations, though she, unfortunately, didn't take home any wins. Newly introduced Musical Express out of the UK named the series one of the best Korean dramas of the year.

It has been revealed that in Bloodhounds, the bonds of friendship are on full display between Kim Geon-woo (Woo Do-hwan) and Hong Woo-jin (Lee Sang-yi), who use their talents as boxers to help those in need. Money lending is the root of the conflict in the series as the men work to topple a man who uses his power as a loan shark to prey on those without money or resources. The bulk of the action takes place in the guise of boxing.

It has been revealed that even though the boxing is brutal, and the men don't pull any punches, the show is surprisingly nuanced and takes care to represent the issues of class and financial difficulties with empathy. As much as the series basks in action, it's also a crime drama and provides plenty of social commentary.

Recent findings suggest that though the series didn't see a lot of award show love in South Korea, Lee Sang-yi was awarded the Actor's Excellence Award at the Korea Drama Awards for his work in the show. Time also named it as one of the best Korean Dramas of 2023. It even returned in 2026 for a second season, earning acclaim and swiftly garnering comments from its studio about a Bloodhounds season 3 return beyond that.

Sources indicate that vincenzo is one of the best revenge K-dramas because it weaves a complex web of lies and betrayal. There are so many twists that they must be seen to be believed. Vincenzo Cassano, AKA Park Joo-hyung (Song Joong-ki), is adopted by an Italian family with ties to the mob.

Sources indicate that however, when his brother tries to have him killed, Vincenzo escapes back to South Korea to get his vengeance and start building his empire. Each character is brutal and exacting in their ruthless climb to the top and desire for money and power, but no one is who they say they are.

Recent findings suggest that the series combines elements of a crime thriller with those of an action series, legal drama, and even a romance. The show manages to weave elements of all of these genres into an intense and entertaining narrative. It is also creative with its fight scenes, even using tape in one.

Just before the turn of the nineteenth century, Mr. Sunshine unpacks the experience of Eugene Choi (Lee Byung-hun), a young man who returns to Korea after living in the United States for many years. He falls in love with a woman in the upper class, but their love has a lot more to overcome than economic differences. Much of the conflict in Mr. Sunshine stems from the tensions between Korea, Japan, and the United States during this period.

According to recent reports, hand-to-hand combat and samurai skills are showcased throughout the show. Fans might have loved the drama and the fight scenes, making it one of the highest-rated shows in South Korea at the time, but historical inaccuracy and using the trope of an American savior didn't sit well with many. While some parts of the show are polarizing, there's no question that the strong characters and well-choreographed action make it worth watching.

Thrillers are known for their slow-burn narratives that uphold a commitment to suspense over too many overtly violent scenes. However, that means that in demonstrates like The Worst of Evil, when the tension spills over, the payoff of a fight sequence is all the more satisfying.

Sources indicate that the series is a 1990s period piece that follows two detectives attempting to disrupt a drug trafficking ring, leading one of them to go undercover. It soon becomes clear that the criminals aren't the only dangerous ones, and most of the characters will do whatever it takes to get ahead.

Recent findings suggest that weapons in the series range from fists to buckets of water, making for some interesting variety in the more action-packed scenes. The series was well-received the year of its debut, earning three nominations at the Baeksang Awards and winning one for Best Director for Han Dong-wook.

There will simply never be enough thrilling K-dramas to go around featuring the talented Ji Chang-wook, and in the case of The Manipulated, his character, Park Tae-jung, goes to some truly dark places to expose the rot at the heart of high society. Falsely accused and rapidly crucified in the courtroom due to evidence stacked against even his originally ironclad case, Tae-jung finds himself swept into prison and forced to endure horrific abuse and violence while serving a crime he didn't commit.

The worst part? It's all part of a vast conspiracy to cover up the crimes of the ultra-wealthy, with Tae-jung far from the first or last victim. The Manipulated takes exactly as much time as it needs across its 12-episode run to flesh out the original story of the 2017 Fabricated City film it adapts (also starring Ji), in which he finds comfort in a kindred spirit while in prison.

But as the truth begins to expose itself again as Tae-jung successfully draws in those who set him up before, Tae-jung soon finds himself in an array of deadly encounters, including a memorable Death Race-like scenario, in which he meets the real operation's ringleader.

The Manipulated possesses everything there is to enjoy about revenge K-dramas, but with Ji at the center and plenty of character development and good supporting cast, he's still thoroughly human even as he takes down everyone along his way to exposing the truth. It subsequently makes Ji easier to root for in the series, as viewers hold out hope that he can return to the charming, idyllic life that was so viciously upended in the premiere.

High school is already filled to the brim with violence, drama, and intrigue, but combining that with zombies makes it impossible to turn away from All of Us Are Dead. In a compelling twist, it's a human teacher who creates the zombie virus and effectively ends the world, and the kids are the ones who decide to join together and survive. Now with season 2 on the way, it'll be interesting to see its world expand as it builds on these concepts further.

Recent findings suggest that though the outbreak starts in the confines of the school, the outside world doesn't have to wait long to fall victim to the virus. All of Us Are Dead is at its best in how it builds tension throughout its episodes and punctuates the action sequences with the complex development and organization of social groups.

According to recent reports, the themes of the apocalypse are played out on the small scale of one school, which raises the stakes and increases the pacing of the action. Each character has a unique skill set and range of abilities, and watching the students learn to fight keeps the audience on the edge of their seats.

Sweet Home has garnered enormous popularity through Netflix and around the world, and with season 3 over, this horror K-drama has left a strong and lasting impression, even if its visual effects differed drastically from the beginning. The series’ premise revolves around a post-apocalyptic world where humans start turning into monsters, and the show's heroes are trapped inside an apartment building, trying to fight their way out and survive.

What makes the show so successful is how well it uses the environment and circumstances to its advantage. This limited setting gives the audience the sense of being trapped alongside the characters and increases the likelihood that every encounter with a monster will be violent.

It has been revealed that not only is the action, gore, and violence top-notch, but the series builds character development and relationships, making the quiet moments just as compelling as the high-octane fights. Blending horror, interpersonal drama, and the best of the action genre, Sweet Home stands out among its K-Drama competitors.

#62833. Every Version of 'A Christmas Carol,' Ranked (and Where to Stream Them)

Every Version of 'A Christmas Carol,' Ranked (and Where to Stream Them)

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2047 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that charles Dickens’ A Christmas Carol is the greatest story about Christmas ever written—even better than the one with Mary and Joseph and the manger.
  • I've carefully considered every major theatrical and TV adaptation of A Christmas Carol and rated each in terms of holiday spirit, Dickensian whimsy, and Scrooge-osity to arrive at the definite, no-argument-possible best-to-worst list of Christmas Carols.
  • It has been revealed that to rank Christmas Carols, you have to decide what A Christmas Carol is to you.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that charles Dickens’ A Christmas Carol is the greatest story about Christmas ever written—even better than the one with Mary and Joseph and the manger. The 1843 tale of a miser browbeaten by self-righteous ghosts is (probably) the most filmed story of all time. Dozens of cinematic adaptations of A Christmas Carol have been released in theaters and on TV since Scrooge; or Marley's Ghost came out in 1901. Hundreds or thousands if you count re-imaginings and very special episodes of sitcoms. But which version is the very best?

I've carefully considered every major theatrical and TV adaptation of A Christmas Carol and rated each in terms of holiday spirit, Dickensian whimsy, and Scrooge-osity to arrive at the definite, no-argument-possible best-to-worst list of Christmas Carols.

It has been revealed that to rank Christmas Carols, you have to decide what A Christmas Carol is to you. My criteria for inclusion: It has to be full-length (at least around an hour long); it has to have been released widely, either in theaters, on network television, or through a larger streaming service, and it has to be fairly close to a direct adaptation—modernizations, re-imaginings, sequels, and that episode of The Six Million Dollar Man don’t count (sorry, Scrooged fans). Using those criteria, I’ve winnowed the Carols down to the 17 you see below, ranked from best to worst, along with where you can stream each one.

Sources indicate that it's tough to pick a single adaptation of A Christmas Carol as the absolute best of all time, but the 1984 TV movie version starring George C. Scott is unassailable. Other versions do some things better, but this one does everything right—no mistakes. It stays close to the original text; it's perfectly produced; and it has a consistency of tone and vision that makes it the most balanced of all versions of the story. A Christmas Carol might not have the best Scrooge of all time, but George C. Scott's performance is a solid nine out of ten, and this version features the most adorable and pitiable Tiny Tim of all and the best Ghost of Christmas Present, played by Edward Woodward, who played the policeman in The Wicker Man.

Where to stream it: Roku, Tubi, Pluto TV.

Sources indicate that shot in the midst of the Great Depression, the first sound version of A Christmas Carol digs deeper into the despair and horror of the story than any other adaptation. It’s a bleak, German expressionist Christmas flick, and Seymour Hicks’ sickly, haunted portrayal of Ebenezer Scrooge fits the tone perfectly. Instead of delighting in his own crapulence, Hicks plays Scrooge like Satan in The Divine Comedy—he's not the ruler of Hell; he's its most tormented prisoner. Scrooge's miserliness is played as pathology. He wears dirty, torn clothing and shivers miserably while eating gruel because he can’t bring himself to burn a single scrap of coal. Even when he converts, it seems like a manic episode instead of Christmas spirit, suggesting this could be a story about an old man going mad.

Where to stream: Sadly, the version on free streaming services like Tubi and Plex is colorized, but you can watch it on YouTube in glorious black and white.

This big-budget musical take on the Yuletide classic turns Dickens up to 11. Scrooge is huge, a raucous, crowd-pleasing musical with hundreds of extras, elaborate sets, and a scenery-chewing central performance from Albert Finney to hold it all together. But Finney and company also manage to keep the emotional core of the story intact. The music is great, with memorable tunes like “I Hate People,” a song that Finney snarls instead of sings. Scrooge has the best ghosts of any version of A Christmas Carol, too—you can't beat the cheesy awesomeness of big-money 1970s special effects.

Where to stream it: Tubi, Pluto TV, Plex.

Before Hallmark devoted its corporate life to forgettable holiday-themed romantic comedies, it co-produced one of the best versions of A Christmas Carol ever made. This entire movie belongs to Patrick Stewart, whose nuanced, layered portrayal of Scrooge is the best that has ever been done. His "conversion" scene is so visceral and honest, it brought a tear to my eyes, even though I've seen the exact scene performed in at least 40 other movies, stage plays, and episodes of 1980s sitcoms. Sadly, the paucity of basic cable budgets in the 1990s results in some chintzy-looking sets and laughable special effects that mar an otherwise top-notch production.

Where to stream it: Digital rental only.

According to recent reports, horror director Ti West's Carol adaptation muddies the moral clarity of Dickens' tale and suggests there's something deeply troubling beneath all the Victorian holiday catharsis. With a few exceptions, Ebenezer hits the familiar beats of A Christmas Carol: It delivers the crowd-pleasing rich-jerk-turns-good story moviegoers expect, but West layers in subtle hints along the way that suggest the floorboards are rotten, and if you dance with Christmas joy too hard, you'll fall into the dark basement below. Ebenezer seems to whisper to audiences, "How much does the conversion of one miserly wretch matter in the face of systemic injustice? And isn't he going to snap out of it when the fright wears off anyway?" Bonus: As you'd probably expect from a Ti West movie, the ghosts are genuinely scary.

Where to watch it: In theaters now.

Industry observers note that I'm sticking A Muppet Christmas Carol randomly here on the list because you can't reasonably compare it to other versions of the story. The Muppet version is a thing unto itself. Like the Ol' Dirty Bastard, its style has no father. A Muppet Christmas Carol is absolutely delightful from start to finish, for children, grown-ups, cats, dogs, space aliens, and anything else you got. It shouldn't even work to set Michael Caine's serious portrayal of Ebenezer Scrooge against a supporting cast of puppets, but somehow it all seems natural.

Alastair Sim takes Ebenezer Scrooge on a real journey in this movie. In the first act, he plays Scrooge like Capitalism personified, an uncaring, amoral monument to pure acquisition. He seems like a Scrooge who'd scare away ghosts, but when Marley shows up dragging his trademark chains, Sim is instantly reduced to pop-eyed fear, like the single chink in his armor is the supernatural. Scrooge then regresses to a childlike, bashful figure as ghosts lead him to different visions, finally emerging from his symbolic death to his rebirth as a Christmas-obsessed guy who lives to serve others. This movie might be among the best of the genre, but an unnecessary subplot about Scrooge's business sandbags the movie through part of the second act.

Sources indicate that mr. Magoo's Christmas Carol was the first animated version of A Christmas Carol and the first animated holiday special ever shown on American TV. The main character, Mr. Magoo, was the star of a one-joke, limited-animation cartoon popular in the early 1960s about an old man who couldn’t see very well, so it’s surprising how carefully crafted and effective this version of A Christmas Carol is. It's weirdly meta too: Jim Backus voices Mr. Magoo, who is a (blind) actor performing as Scrooge in A Christmas Carol on Broadway, so the play is bookended with "this guy can't see!" bits. The songs are strange, memorable and funny (listen to "Razzleberry Dressing" above once and you'll never forget it), but the emotional core of the story remains surprisingly powerful. Jim Backus is amazing.

Where to stream it: Peacock, Roku, Tubi.

I'm breaking my own rule about not including shortened versions of the story because this animated Carol is that great. Its evocative, graceful, hand-drawn look belongs to animation legend Richard Williams and was inspired by the illustrations from the original version of A Christmas Carol. It's a cartoon, but it's not a kiddie cartoon, so the darkness of the ghosts isn't glossed over. Plus, Scrooge is voiced by Alastair Sim, reprising his role from 1951's Scrooge.

According to recent reports, there's nothing wrong with this brightly lit, by-the-numbers take on A Christmas Carol, but it seems designed to appeal to as broad an audience as possible, so the rough edges of the story have been sanded off. The ghosts aren’t that scary. Scrooge isn’t that miserly, etc. It’s fine for a Christmas movie to be lighthearted fun, but the lowered stakes ultimately blunt the emotional resonance of the climax, leading to a mediocre Christmas Carol.

In a recent development, I'm including this version of A Christmas Carol because it's Lifehacker editor Meghan Walbert's favorite. Sorry, Meghan, but this flimsy 1970s TV movie adaptation hasn't aged well. Henry Winkler does a good job as Scrooge, and it's cool to see Burgess Meredith and other old-timey stars, but overall, this is a schmaltzy, plodding film that unwisely replaces a lot of Dickens' best writing with the work of 1970s TV hacks.

Where to stream it: Pluto, Tubi, Amazon Prime.

Recent findings suggest that I really wanted to like Disney’s A Christmas Carol. Robert Zemeckis is a great director and Jim Carrey is a force of nature, but I couldn't get through it. There might be a lot to recommend this version of the story, but using 2009’s technology to create realistic-looking characters was such a puzzling choice. The whole movie looks like a video game cutscene from a PS3 game, and I kept wanting to hit “A” to skip ahead to the gameplay.

Sources indicate that it doesn't seem like the producers of this obscure 2012 straight-to-streaming feature had much money to work with, which is too bad. If they had, they might have been able to better realize some of the intriguing ideas behind this movie. It's a straight-up horror take on the tale, but it just isn't scary. Sadly, you can't carry a feature film on good intentions. Overall, a swing and a miss.

Where to stream it: Tubi, Amazon Prime.

Sources indicate that the animation in this 1997 musical cartoon version of A Christmas Carol is dated, pedestrian, and ugly. The songs are forgettable, and Scrooge has a pet bulldog for some reason. (The one good joke is that he named his dog "Debit.") It’s just not good, which is a shame, because the cast is overflowing with talent, including Tim Curry as Scrooge, Ed Asner, and Whoopi Goldberg.

Where to stream it: Roku, Pluto TV, Xumo.

Industry observers note that this BBC drama goes for a philosophical, moody version of Scrooge, but it doesn’t come together. It’s dark, grim, and so ponderously self-serious that it collapses under its own weight. In an effort to present aspects of A Christmas Carol that haven't been seen before (like "How Marley got his chains"), A Christmas Carol rewrites the original text from the ground up, but it comes across like Dickens' first draft with a bad case of Surf Dracula.

Where to stream it: Hulu, Disney+.

Recent findings suggest that the current state of Dickens adaptation is not good. Netflix's uninspired, sappy, CGI version of A Christmas Carol tries to tart the story up with slapstick, songs, and jokes, but it’s all cynical, lowest-common-denominator horseshit. The dialogue has been dumbed down and joked up. Scrooge has a silly dog for comic relief. They added scatological humor. Think about this: The minds behind Scrooge: A Christmas Carol read Dickens and concluded, “This story would be better with a wacky dog and fart jokes.”.

A Christmas Carol is such a solid story, even a grade-school production of it can be fun to watch. But a cynical production of it is extra terrible, given the message of the story. This terrible ego project is a bottom-of-the-barrel Christmas Carol because it feels like a money grab. Kelsey Grammer sucks as Scrooge, mugging his way through a lightweight performance. Jason Alexander sucks as Marley. Jennifer Love Hewitt is, well, actually pretty good as Scrooge’s Christmas-past romantic interest. She is a rare bright spot in this dreary movie, however. Everything else is mid to terrible. It’s shot and lit like a TV show; the sets are bland and the songs forgettable. Overall, it has the cynical feeling of assembly-line, “let’s get this shit over with” TV production.

Where to stream it: Tubi, Pluto TV, Plex.

  • It has been revealed that ebert subsequently wrote that the action of "The Two Towers" "would no doubt startle the gentle medievalist J.R.R.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that roger Ebert wasn't as effusive about Peter Jackson's "The Lord of the Rings" films as many other critics. For reference, Ebert gave "Fellowship of the Ring" and "The Two Towers" three stars (out of four) and then "Return of the King" three and a half.

Recent findings suggest that "A true visualization of [J.R.R.] Tolkien's Middle-earth it is not," wrote Ebert of Jackson's "Fellowship," arguing it "adds up to more of a sword and sorcery epic" that loses the "innocence" of the books. Though, Ebert conceded in that review that "That 'Fellowship of the Ring' doesn't match my imaginary vision of Middle-earth is my problem, not yours.".

It has been revealed that ebert subsequently wrote that the action of "The Two Towers" "would no doubt startle the gentle medievalist J.R.R. Tolkien." However, he praised "Return of the King" as a strong conclusion which solidified the trilogy as "a work of bold ambition at a time of cinematic timidity," even if he felt the film and trilogy fell "a little shy of greatness.".

Recent findings suggest that but you know what fantasy movie Ebert did love? 2007's "The Golden Compass," adapted from Philip Pullman's "His Dark Materials" novels. It's set in an alternate world where a piece of every person's soul exists in the form of an animal, called a dæmon. British orphan Lyra Belacqua (Dakota Blue Richards) embarks on a quest to rescue a friend and stumbles onto a much more cosmic struggle. Ebert gave it four stars, writing:.

"'The Golden Compass' is a darker, deeper fantasy epic than the 'Rings' trilogy, 'The Chronicles of Narnia' or the 'Potter' films. It springs from the same British world of quasi-philosophical magic, but creates more complex villains and poses more intriguing questions.".

While most would disagree with Ebert's quality assessment, he's onto something, as "Golden Compass" invites "Lord of the Rings" comparisons.

"The Golden Compass" was produced by Upcoming Line Cinema, the same production firm behind "The Lord of the Rings," and it's clear the studio was hoping to repeat its previous success. "The Golden Compass" even features two important "Rings" alums: Ian McKellen (Gandalf) as the voice of polar bear king Iorek Byrnison, and Christopher Lee (the corrupted wizard Saruman) as a leader of the Magisterium, the Church of Lyra's world. It was reported in 2007 both actors were cast at New Line's behest.

It has been revealed that but quite the contrary, "The Golden Compass" under-performed ($372 million in theaters against a $180 million budget), and sequels were never made. "The Golden Compass" even contributed to the end of Latest Line as an independent studio, as it was folded into Warner Bros. in 2008. Not helping the movie's financials was a religious backlash. The Magisterium allegorically represents all authoritarian religions but especially the Catholic Church, and "The Golden Compass" was in turn condemned by the Vatican.

"The Golden Compass" didn't win over fans of its source novel, either, due to abundant changes. The movie cuts out the book's entire ending, which directly sets up the sequel, "The Subtle Knife." But the attacks on religion? Those are taken right from the book. Philip Pullman is an atheist, and "His Dark Materials" is his rebuttal to the Christian-themed British fantasies of J.R.R. Tolkien and "Chronicles of Narnia" author C.S. Lewis, particularly the latter as both stories are about children traveling to different worlds. (Though Tolkien, for what it's worth, is noted to have disliked "Narnia.").

It has been revealed that "I cordially dislike allegory," Tolkien once famously claimed, believing it robs readers the freedom to interpret a work. For decades, stated readers have since read into the influence of Tolkien's Catholic faith on his Middle-earth stories.

Sauron and his ring are a Luciferian conception of evil: A fallen angel who rules a fiery, molten realm and whose darkness spreads as temptation. J. R. R. Tolkien's villain is the Devil, Philip Pullman's is the Church.

Frodo carrying the ring echoes Christ carrying his own cross to Golgotha and, in turn, the metaphorical crosses that all of Christ's followers carry. "The Chronicles of Narnia," meanwhile, features talking lion Aslan as a direct allegory for the Christian God, Christ-like sacrifice and resurrection included.

In a recent development, in "His Dark Materials," the Magisterium worships "the Authority," a name suggesting an "authority" is all that organized religion is. The Authority is also a liar: He is not the creator of the universe, merely the first "angel" who came into being. The weak and withered "god" eventually crumbles into dust, as if humanity has no more use for him. The very last dialogue of the trilogy is Lyra endeavoring to build a "Republic of Heaven" on Earth.

Yet, circling back to Roger Ebert, he disputed the anti-religious reading of the "Golden Compass" movie, arguing it reworks the Magisterium into a more purely political villain, "a Soviet dictatorship or Big Brother." He specifically praised the film's themes as "murky," compared to Pullman's blatant allegory for the death of God, and affirmed that "the controversy surrounding ['The Golden Compass'] obscures its function as a splendid entertainment.".

Amusingly, Ebert championed the movie for the same reasons many "His Dark Materials" fans rejected it. Toning down the anti-religion elements did not spare the movie the Church's wrath, either. One can only wonder what Ebert would have thought of the eventual "His Dark Materials" TV series that adapted Pullman's story to book fans' delight.

Audiences don’t know how to quit Panem.

It has been revealed that ““The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping” earned $21 million in Thursday previews and early screenings on Wednesday and is expected to dominate the box office this weekend. Analysts believe it will earn north of $100 million. The preview figures are the second-best of 2026, behind “Spider-Man: Brand New Day’s” massive $72 million haul. It’s also the second-best for the “Hunger Games” franchise, just behind the $25.5 million that “Catching Fire” earned in 2013. It’s a big improvement on the last “Hunger Games” prequel, “The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes,” which made $5.75 million in previews and kicked off with $44 million. That film would gross over $166 million domestically and nearly $364 million globally, figures that “Sunrise on the Reaping” is on pace to easily eclipse.

“Sunrise on the Reaping” is based on Suzanne Collins’ bestselling novel of the same name. It tells the origin story of Haymitch Abernathy, the alcoholic former Hunger Games victor played by Woody Harrelson in the films. The sequel checks in with him at 16 as he’s forced to compete in gladiatorial combat. “East of Eden” breakout Joseph Zada plays Haymitch. He’s surrounded by an all-star cast that includes Jesse Plemons, Ralph Fiennes, Glenn Close, Kieran Culkin, Elle Fanning, Mckenna Grace, and Maya Hawke. Francis Lawrence, who helmed most of the series’ films, returns as director. Lionsgate, which is having a strong year at the box office thanks to “Michael,” is backing the “Hunger Games” sequel as it has the previous films.

The biggest competition for “Sunrise on the Reaping” this weekend isn’t another major movie, but the release of “Grand Theft Auto 6,” which is expected to be a phenomenon.
