📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

[Editor’s note: This review was originally published on October 2, 2026 during the 2026 Upcoming York Film Festival. Janus Film will release the film in limited theaters on Friday, November 20.].

Paul Thomas Anderson‘s eye for vivifying music onscreen dates back to the late 1990s when, after “Boogie Nights,” he made Technicolor mini-masterpiece music videos with his ex-girlfriend Fiona Apple — or made a San Fernando Valley-sized shrine to Aimee Mann with his third feature, “Magnolia.” Since then, he’s kicked around with HAIM while turning one third of its Los Angelino triumvirate, Alana Haim, into a screen actress. He’s shot for Radiohead and made a regular collaboration with band member Jonny Greenwood to create some of the 21st century’s most memorable scores. Many young cinephiles now associate the mischievously lilty notes of “Phantom Thread” with the poison promise of newly introduced love and obsessive creation. Related Stories Trump Renews Backing for Federal Film Tax Credit as Lawmakers Push for Year-End Passage ‘Disclosure Day’ Did Its Biggest Stunts Practically, So the VFX Team Worked Hard to Look Invisible — Watch.

Last December, PTA teamed up with Geese frontman Cameron Winter to film, while operating his own Panavision camera, his solo stage performance at Carnegie Hall, running through sparse piano arrangements of tracks off his solo album, “Heavy Metal.” The result, a 72-minute film now being distributed roadshow-style by Janus Films before inevitably living on the Criterion Collection, is a stunning arrangement of its own: a deeply achey, sincere but never cloyingly earnest concert movie that’s tender to the point of frailty. (Benny Safdie counts as a co-producer, and the film’s scratchy Upcoming York quality and setting can’t help but have his imprint.).

Industry observers note that the matted-hair, lithe Winter can seem a bit uncomfortable in his own skin in the public eye, as he did onstage ahead of “Cameron Winter at Carnegie” at its Fresh York Film Festival world premiere at Alice Tully Hall. But on the piano, laser-beamed into his songcraft, he’s quietly electrified, at seemingly at peace as his tenorous vocal glissando and nimble fingerwork on the piano produce shiveringly tender folk ballads that echo Harry Nilsson and Van Morrison. (The usual comparisons to Tom Waits and Rufus Wainright are right, too, but Winter is his own strange thing.) If you weren’t previously sold on the wily Winter antic rock chaos of Geese — rapidly becoming one of the most popular contemporary art rock bands of these times — you’re about to. Paul Thomas Anderson has created a rhapsodic shrine to the man that is nonetheless ballad-sized in its emotional scale.

Winter, in December, played and sang to a sold-out crowd of more than 2,700 at the stately cultural temple that is Carnegie Hall, and this film can at times feel like a religious experience, an incantation, a lonely vigil. The singer/songwriter was 23 at the time of the performance, one year older than Bob Dylan when he headlined Carnegie Hall, and similarly at the precipice of major fame. Fixed on a mobile rig that will at times careen and whoosh across the stage when not otherwise holding on Winter, Anderson’s camera catches the expressionism and chiaroscuro of stage lights illuminating and fading off the singer’s face.

The result is hynoptic, a concert film up there with “Stop Making Sense” but for introverts. Songs like the popular single “$0” acquire an even more wrenchingly somber quality as a lovelorn protagonist rues being exploited by a relationship (“You’re making me feel like a dollar in your hand / You’re making me feel like I’m a zero dollar man”). Stripped of production, his indie hit “Love Takes Miles” plays even better. While many of the songs sort of hover in the same key and bleed into one another, that makes for an all the more transfixing experience. The lack of an interstitial anything save for a sweet prologue and moving coda make for experience also that’s immersive, deep, and the kind whose truth you can feel somewhere in your body even if you can’t quite articulate it.

It has been revealed that “Cameron Winter at Carnegie Hall premiered at the Upcoming York Film Festival. Janus Films will release it in theaters starting November 20.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, if you're tired of a mass culture that pumps out Harry Potter reboot series and Chris Pratt films so bad even AI couldn't generate them, why not revisit one of the great films of the 20th Century. Ingmar Bergman's "Persona" is right now available to watch on HBO Max, and offers a wonderfully confounding, disturbing yet lyrical experience that any film fan should see at least once. You're not going to have much of a clue about what's going on, but that's sort of the point.

Recent findings suggest that the 1966 psychological drama was made following a bout of severe illness for Bergman, during which he was struck by a vision of two women slowly merging into one identity. "Persona" was the realization of that vision. It stars Liv Ullmann as an actress named Elisabet who during a stage performance suddenly stops speaking and moving. Her doctor advises she be taken to a remote seaside cottage to be nursed back to health. That job falls to nurse, Alma (Bibi Andersson) who in her frequent one-sided conversations with her mute patient reveals candid details of her own past. As their time together goes on, Alma and Elisabet begin to assume each other's identities.

Industry observers note that aside from urging viewers to feel rather than understand "Persona," Ingmar Bergman explained the film as a sonata for the instruments that were Bibi Andersson and Liv Ullmann. Andersson had worked with Bergman regularly since their first collaboration on "Smiles of a Summer Night" in 1955. "Persona" was, however, Norwegian actress Liv Ullmann's first Bergman film. Given the director's view of it as a "sonata" for the pair, it would seem the filmmaker was interested in his actors more than anything else.

Recent findings suggest that but "Persona" is full of fascinating symbolism and is thematically rich enough that it's spawned endless critical analysis interpreting the film as everything from a modernist horror movie to an interrogation of acting itself as an art form. It's also been interpreted as an exploration of the distinction between our true selves and the masks we wear in social settings — which, considering the film's title, clearly has some relevance.

Industry observers note that but even Roger Ebert admitted to not understanding the movie upon his initial viewing in 1967. When the critic revisited "Persona" in 2001, he still seemed somewhat perplexed, even while writing, "I know most of what I am ever likely to know about films, and I think I understand that the best approach to 'Persona' is a literal one." The ending of "Persona" certainly offers no answers, but it's not supposed to. Susan Sontag wrote that "Persona" is "bound to trouble, perplex and frustrate most filmgoers," and it does — but in the most beautiful, mesmeric, and disturbing way possible. The film is streaming on HBO Max at the time of writing, but can also be found on the usual digital platforms as well as on archive.org for free.

While fans who followed the marketing will already be very familiar with characters like Brian and Cal before encountering them in-game, others, like Vicki, might be more surprising.

The character has a distinctive in-game appearance, rocking bangs, space buns, and plenty of tattoos, but it might be her voice that rings a bell. Vicki is portrayed by the actress Taryn Manning, and there's a reasonable chance you've seen her in some live-action work in the past.

Taryn Manning has several big credits to her name, but the most notable might be Orange is the Newly introduced Black, as she had a major role in the hit streaming series. Manning played Tiffany "Pennsatucky" Doggett across 87 episodes of the show, ultimately appearing in all but four episodes. While her character there could easily fit into the world of GTA 6, it's very different than Vicki, with Tiffany initially taking on an antagonistic and highly judgmental role.

Manning also appeared in the FX show Sons of Anarchy, portraying Rita "Cherry" Zambell across seven episodes, and the CBS reboot of the procedural drama Hawaii Five-0, playing Mary Ann McGarrett in nine episodes.

In a recent development, television isn't Manning's only claim to fame. She's appeared in plenty of films over the years, with several mid-2000s works stand out as major career highlights. Manning had a central role in Hustle & Flow as Nola and revealed up in 8 Mile as Janeane. Fans of Britney Spears might also recognize Manning from Crossroads, a 2002 road trip movie where her character, Mimi, is at the center of a surprisingly heavy plotline.

GTA 6 is an impressive addition to that repertoire, with the game shattering day-one sales records and receiving glowing critical acclaim (despite a more contentious audience reception). While plenty of fans may not have gotten to Vicki quite yet, as Chapter One alone takes quite a few hours to complete, she steals the show in the early stages of Chapter Two. Along with the potential to casually encounter her after the initial meeting in "Just Moved In" and excursion in "Girls Trip," she also highlights back up for another mission later in the chapter.

White Oleander, Cold Mountain, and A Lot like Love are several more notable films that Manning has starred in over the years.

At the time of this article's publication, Manning hasn't yet spoken publicly about her role in Grand Theft Auto 6, but she'll doubtless have plenty of opportunities to do so in the future. Thanks to the massive cultural footprint of the game, millions of players will be meeting Vicki for years to come, making it the kind of role that will be remembered for a lifetime.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that there are so many great war movies that are more than watchable. If you really need a few classics listed off, uh, take a gander at Lawrence of Arabia, The Great Escape, and The Longest Day. Those three are huge as well, so they’ll take you about 10 hours to get through all up, but that’s 10 hours well spent. And then by the end, you might realize they all came out in the first half of the 1960s. You’ve seen some GOATs, sure, but you’ve barely scratched the surface if you want to understand and fully appreciate the whole history of this particular genre.

Recent findings suggest that on the opposite end of things, and if you're simply straight up not in the mood for quality, maybe you'd like to take a look at some of the following films. These are all among the most unwatchable war movies of all time, and indeed some of the very worst, going back almost 100 years in one instance, and then addressing some other painful movies of a slightly more recent nature. And then a fair bit of stuff in between. Don’t watch these, unless you're really curious for whatever reason. Actually, even then… like, be careful.

Industry observers note that the ever noteworthy and memeable Nicolas Cage has appeared in a surprisingly high number of war movies that aren’t particularly good, and so you're going to have a few of them mentioned here, as a warning. First up is 2001’s Captain Corelli’s Mandolin, which is a love triangle kind of movie with a woman at the center, and said triangle exists because her husband goes off to fight in World War II,.

It’s got a memorably silly title, and there is some amusement to be found in how all-over-the-place all the accents are, yet that’s about it.

In a recent development, that leads to her falling in love with another man stationed nearby: the titular Captain Corelli, played by Cage. And sure, Cage isn't a half-bad love interest in the right movie (see Moonstruck and maybe Raising Arizona, if the latter counts), but Captain Corelli’s Mandolin is not the right movie. It’s got a memorably silly title, and there is some amusement to be found in how all-over-the-place all the accents are, yet that’s about it. Most of Captain Corelli’s Mandolin is sluggish and tedious, so it’s honestly probably best avoided.

In a recent development, sure, Cavalcade won an Academy Award for Best Picture, but nowadays, it feels like an absolute slog to get through, and it’s a shame it even won said award, because Cavalcade goes some way toward diminishing that award’s significance and prestige. There are plenty of movies from the 1930s that hold up a whole lot better, including the even older All Quiet on the Western Front, which was also a Best Picture winner (and a far more deserving one at that).

Cavalcade is something of an epic, since it’s a movie that takes place over several decades, starting at the very end of the 19th century and ending in the early 1930s. There are various characters involved with different historical events, and the Second Boer War and World War I taking place during this period is what makes the film technically a war movie, at least in parts. Just a really boring war/drama movie. Even if you're a fan of early talkies, Cavalcade will still likely prove difficult to get through and endure.

If only Midway was actually “mid.” Midway wishes it was mid. Midway is in fact about as boring and disappointing as a technically epic war film can be. It’s such an odd viewing experience, since it’s about the Battle of Midway, and that should feel grand, and then it also has a rather obscenely star-studded cast, with the likes of Charlton Heston, Henry Fonda, James Coburn, Robert Mitchum, Toshirō Mifune, Robert Wagner, Pat Morita, and Tom Selleck (among others) all showing up here.

It’s a shame everyone is wasted in such a lifeless film, and also a bit of a bummer that some of these actors are given very little to do, all the while not having much screen time. Midway feels like a cinematic scam, with all the money thrown into getting numerous legendary actors to appear, giving the impression that it’s a prestigious film, but then about $5 was spent on the rest of the movie, and all the actors look/sound bored anyway. It’s woeful and honestly kind of embarrassing stuff, sorry.

Look, First Blood is pretty awesome, if you're looking at the overall Rambo series. That’s hard to classify as a full-on action movie, since it feels pretty focused on survival and there’s a surprisingly low kill count overall, and then while it involves a main character who had his life altered by taking part in war, it’s not really a traditional war movie, and more of a post-war film about trauma and the difficulties of recovering.

Recent findings suggest that the first sequel amps up the action, and then the second sequel, Rambo III, pushes things way too far. It is technically more of a conventional action/war movie, but man is it a silly film. It’s also pretty lazily done and eventually tedious, even if there are so many guns fired and things blown up. Rarely is action so tiring, and also not really tiring in a clever way, nor a way that feels intentional. One gets the sense that Rambo III is supposed to be entertaining and spectacular, but it really ain't either of those things, sadly.

Though Missing in Action might almost succeed as a brainless Chuck Norris action movie, it doesn’t fare nearly as well when judged as a war movie. Also, even with its action, it might not exactly satisfy the majority of people just after mindless combat, since such people will inevitably have to overlook moments of tedium and filmmaking/technical shakiness throughout. It’s like a Rambo sequel but worse than even the just-mentioned Rambo III, at least by a little.

Sources indicate that throughout Missing in Action, there are a good number of explosions, guns fired, and other acts of destruction committed, but it’s all captured pretty lifelessly and eventually feels repetitive. Even some fun character actors showing up (M. Emmet Walsh and James Hong) can only do so much in giving Missing in Action more of a pulse. The whole thing ends up being shockingly boring for something that’s technically so action-packed, and even big Chuck Norris fans might want to give Missing in Action a miss.

It has been revealed that there are things about Ambush at Cimarron Pass that might make it look like something of a curiosity or oddity, at first glance, but actually sitting through the darn thing is such a slog. That’s really saying something, considering the film is just 73 minutes long, and stands out for being one of Clint Eastwood’s earliest starring roles… these are those potentially intriguing or enticing elements, yet you shouldn’t be swayed.

According to recent reports, like, Ambush at Cimarron Pass is a bland blending of the war and Western genres, narratively being about soldiers banding together to fight against numerous Native American warriors in Old West times or whatever. It’s way too old-fashioned, and probably felt so back when it first came out. There are countless better war and Western movies Eastwood ended up being involved with making years/decades later, so just watch (or rewatch) those rather than wasting 73 minutes of your finite life on Ambush at Cimarron Pass. Even if you end up living for as many years as Eastwood has (96 and a half and counting, at the time of writing), it's still not worth spending any of that time on this movie.

According to recent reports, somehow, Captain Corelli’s Mandolin is not the only time Nicolas Cage has played an Italian soldier in a movie, as he did the same thing 12 years earlier in an even worse movie called Time to Kill. This is real bottom-of-the-barrel stuff, made with the most shoestring-y of shoestring budgets and having uncomfortable scene after uncomfortable scene, making it hard to recommend, even to people who might otherwise like to see Cage being weird on screen.

According to recent reports, you’ve got so many other strange Nicolas Cage movies you should watch before ever trying to tackle this one, truth be told. Here, he plays a soldier who unravels psychologically while having to find his way to a hospital after being hurt and separated from his fellow soldiers. That involves him yelling, screaming, and committing heinous acts for basically the whole movie. Time to Kill almost feels like an exploitation film, but not a good, engaging, or clever one, and would probably be completely forgotten, had it not featured a young Cage in a starring role.

Industry observers note that so if you want a trilogy of bad Nicolas Cage war movies, you’ve got one in the form of Time to Kill, Captain Corelli’s Mandolin, and then, finally, USS Indianapolis: Men of Courage. The last of those is the most recent, and also perhaps the worst of the bunch, so you can finish your cursed triple feature on a real low, if you feel so inclined to tackle such a ridiculous marathon in the first place.

Industry observers note that this one’s a World War II movie that ends up being more about surviving against shark attacks, because early on, the titular vessel is destroyed, and its crew members find themselves stranded at sea. USS Indianapolis: Men of Courage is confounding and very silly at times, retelling a true story and making it schlocky in a way that feels more than a bit disrespectful. There was probably a way to do this right, but whatever was done here was not it, to put it mildly.

Industry observers note that there is a very good movie about Pearl Harbor called Tora! Tora! Tora! It came out well over half a century ago, but it still holds up. There’s a real immensity to its scale and ambition, and then even without the spectacle, it’s still pretty compelling as a historical drama. Sure, Pearl Harbor is going for a slightly different thing, even if it’s broadly about the same chapter of World War II, but you should still avoid it at all costs.

In a recent development, basically, Pearl Harbor feels like it’s unashamedly trying to scratch the same itch as Titanic, which was also an epic-length movie that balanced high-intensity action/disaster sequences with romance, but did so in a far smoother manner. Pearl Harbor isn’t really worth anyone’s time, even if some of the technical qualities are impressive and Hans Zimmer delivers a pretty solid score, especially when it takes so much time to watch. Even those who are willing to defend most of what Michael Bay’s made might well find themselves struggling with this one.

According to recent reports, truly one of the worst – and least exciting – war movies ever made, Sniper: Special Ops should be avoided at all costs, if you're someone after good action or tense war-related sequences. It is only allegedly a war/action movie, starring Steven Seagal, who’s of course best known for his action films. Unfortunately, he infamously spends most of Sniper: Special Ops sitting down, mumbling, and occasionally shooting people.

Recent findings suggest that it’s kind of funny, but also a little sad that he gives what would have to be one of the most disinterested and static lead performances in cinema history. Outside some occasional laughs, Sniper: Special Ops is pretty tedious and woefully bare-bones as far as production values go, making a story about rescuing an American congressman from the Taliban feel remarkably boring and entirely lacking in energy. It’s the sort of film that’s so still and boring that it kind of has to be seen to be believed, and it might be hilarious with the right frame of mind, but like, enter with caution, you know?

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that tom Cruise‘s performance in Alejandro González Iñárritu‘s “Digger” is one of the boldest and most entertaining of the actor’s career, as he suppresses not only his usual movie star charisma but his entire way of walking and talking to play paunchy, aging oil tycoon Digger Rockwell. Cruise is barely recognizable in the role, which is about as far from heroic characters like Pete “Maverick” Mitchell and Ethan Hunt as Cruise’s Ron Kovic in “Born on the Fourth of July” was from race car driver Cole Trickle almost 40 years ago.

It has been revealed that to aid in his complete transformation, Cruise called on one of the best prosthetic designers in the business, Kazu Hiro. Hiro has turned Gary Oldman into Winston Churchill (“The Darkest Hour”), Charlize Theron into Megyn Kelly (“Bombshell”), and Dwayne Johnson into “Smashing Machine” Mark Kerr, but transforming Cruise into Texas oilman Digger Rockwell was a whole fresh task — one made even more challenging by Iñárritu and Cruise’s persistent striving for perfectionism, and constant eagerness to try new approaches. Related Stories Trump Renews Backing for Federal Film Tax Credit as Lawmakers Push for Year-End Passage ‘Disclosure Day’ Did Its Biggest Stunts Practically, So the VFX Team Worked Hard to Look Invisible — Watch.

“Alejandro is an amazing director, and he has lots of ideas,” Hiro told IndieWire. “Every day he comes in with a new idea, and we have to come up with an answer for how to achieve it. And Tom is really professional, and expects everybody else to be at that same level, ready for any situation. After the first day of testing, I learned that I had to stay flexible to respond to whatever they wanted.”.

It has been revealed that to that end, Hiro created modular prosthetics whose parts could easily be swapped out and moved around, so that Cruise and Iñárritu could constantly try new looks. “Sometimes with heavy makeup, you can’t change it,” Hiro noted. “I created prosthetics that could be mixed, so we could make new designs on the spot — try this forehead with these cheeks and this nose, then change it.” Creating Cruise’s look was a constantly evolving process throughout the long prep period. “We didn’t have a clear answer until the end of rehearsal.”.

In a recent development, hiro’s mandate at the beginning was a bit open-ended, which gave him room for artistic exploration but also made it difficult to zero in on a precise look. “Alejandro mentioned the character was 76 years old and an oil tycoon,” Hiro said. “He also said he didn’t want the character to look like Tom, but he still wanted to see Tom in the character.” To try to find a concrete image for Digger Rockwell, Hiro immersed himself in research.

Recent findings suggest that “I researched real oil tycoons and how they aged and what kinds of lifestyles they had,” Hiro noted. “Those lifestyles affect how they age.” As Hiro did more and more research, however, he realized that there was no one look that defined the entire profession he was trying to represent. “Everybody looked so different, so in the end I relied more on the storyline and how this particular character behaved.” The idea, in keeping with the slightly heightened style of the film as a whole, was to exaggerate Cruise’s features but keep the character realistic.

Hiro began with a 3D scan and life cast of Cruise, which he used to sculpt his designs. His paramount concern was allowing the actor to be as expressive as possible under the makeup. “The key part is to make the prosthetic very soft so he can move,” Hiro stated, noting that three weeks before shooting, Iñárritu called with a significant change. “He decided that Digger should be 65, not 76, so I quickly made a fresh design. Tom is around that age, but he looks much younger than a normal 65. Under his eye was exposed and the rest of the face was covered, but I made it thin to give him freedom.”.

In addition to Digger’s face, Hiro was also tasked with creating an upper body for an early scene in which Cruise would be seen stripped down to his pajama pants. The body prosthetic was intended only for that one scene, with a lighter bodysuit created for the rest of the movie. “We made a light version of the padding for under the costume, because we don’t need to see the skin after that first scene,” Hiro mentioned. “For the first scene we made a silicone prosthetic that was a lot heavier — the body padding was around 10 pounds, but the silicone was 40 or 50.”.

Sources indicate that during one of Cruise’s costume fittings, he told Hiro he wanted to feel the weight of the silicone throughout production. “He tried the body prosthetic on and remarked, ‘I like this, I want to wear it every day,'” Hiro said. “I told him it would be really heavy and hot, but he said he was training and would be fine.” Since gluing the body prosthetic on every day would be extremely time-consuming, Hiro created a strong spandex foundation and glued the prosthetic to it so Cruise could slip it on each day.

Sources indicate that “He wore that for the whole film,” Hiro said. “One time he said, ‘This is so heavy, it’s really hard on my back.’ I thought, ‘Okay, you asked for it,’ but he went through with it and finished the film, so that was amazing.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the best part about any Grand Theft Auto game is the cheats, and Grand Theft Auto 6 delivers on that front. Rockstar's latest includes a whole mess of password-protected secrets that will really let you have some fun in Vice City. You'll have to work for them, though. GTA 6's cheats are deeply hidden, and will require you to jump through a few hoops to start using them.

Here's everything you need to know about cheats in GTA 6, from how to unlock them, to the list itself.

[Ed. note: We're still working to hunt down every cheat code, but until we find them all, this will give you an idea of what you'll need to do to unlock them all.].

Update (Nov. 21): We've updated this guide with inputs for three cheat codes.

It has been revealed that if you're looking for a way to enter cheat codes the moment you start GTA 6, you're going to be disappointed. You won't be able to use them until you have fully cleared the story. Once you finish the game and return to your save file, you'll find a new Cheat tab. Open your Map, tab over to Progression, and scroll to the end to find the Cheats menu.

You won't get the actual cheat codes immediately. Each one is locked behind a requirement. That can be as simple as finding a specific car to earn the ability to summon it, or as demanding as having Jason and Lucia hold hands for four hours. Once you clear a condition, a pop-up message will tell you that you've unlocked a new Cheat code, and the unlock requirement in the Cheats menu will be replaced with the code.

Notably, your progress throughout the game, even before beating it, does contribute to these requirements. By the time you roll credits and unlock the Cheats menu, you'll likely already have a few of them unlocked.

According to recent reports, to activate a cheat code, first pull out your phone by pressing Up on your D-Pad. Then hold down L1 and R1 on the home screen. (We have only been able to test the PS5 version of the game so far, but our assumption is that you'll need to hold LB and RB on Xbox Series X.) While holding those buttons, you'll have to enter the unlocked code with the D-Pad. Based on our testing, you won't be able to activate a code until you've actually beaten the game and unlocked the Cheats menu.

Sources indicate that note that activating a cheat code will disable saving for the rest of your play session. You also won't be able to earn achievements while cheats are on. Always remember to save before activating a cheat so you don't lose any progress.

GTA 6's cheats are broken out into five categories:.

Below, we've listed every cheat along with their effect, unlock condition, and code.

Make $250,000 from fenced goods.

Up, Right, Down, Left, Up, Left, Down, Right.

Instantly makes you and your partner drunk.

Up, Left, Right, Up, Up, Left, Right, Up, Left, Right.

Raises your level of heat across the map.

Left, Down, Right, Down, Up, Down Up.

Lose a 3-star wanted level 50 times.

Down, Up, Up, Down, Up, Down, Up, Down Up, Right.

#62819. Breaking: Why Do AI Posters All Look Like That?

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1283 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Lifehacker ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Why Do AI Posters All Look Like That?

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1283 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Every poster for a business or event has pictures of uncanny-looking people, buildings that don’t look right, and always that one font.
  • It has been revealed that at this point, gone are the days of chatbots like ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini simply generating text immediately in response to a prompt.
  • In a recent development, to borrow a classic and implausible example, if you were to give an AI chatbot the instruction “Make a peanut butter and jelly sandwich,” it would start by generating step-by-step instructions on how to make the sandwich before trying to make one (if it could).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

You know “the look” by now. Every poster for a business or event has pictures of uncanny-looking people, buildings that don’t look right, and always that one font. But why? If generative AI is supposedly able to “think” and be “creative,” why do so many of its results come out looking exactly the same? The answer is complicated, and it has to do with what chatbots define as “thinking.”.

It has been revealed that at this point, gone are the days of chatbots like ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini simply generating text immediately in response to a prompt. Some very fast models do, but most employ what’s known as “thinking models”, which are a bit of a misnomer. The “thinking” really just consists of generating a set of sub-prompts before executing the main one. And it’s in that hidden, generated text that most of the “choices” (to the extent that we can call the statistical output of an AI model a “choice”) occur that determine how a design looks.

In a recent development, to borrow a classic and implausible example, if you were to give an AI chatbot the instruction “Make a peanut butter and jelly sandwich,” it would start by generating step-by-step instructions on how to make the sandwich before trying to make one (if it could). Most of this happens invisibly in the background, and many proprietary chatbots won’t show you their in-process “thinking” prompts even if you ask.

In the case of an AI poster, it might break down “make a poster” into smaller steps such as “create a design brief for a poster.” To demonstrate this while doing some testing for this piece, I added additional prompts for ChatGPT to explain the “design briefs” it generated, which included details like layout, colors, and typography.

The problem is those instructions are still subject to the same flaws as any other AI-generated text. They can’t properly fact-check; they can’t walk into the real world and see the thing they’re describing; and they can hallucinate or fall back on stale formats that become easy to notice after a while.

Industry observers note that for example, while testing, I had ChatGPT generate a poster for a Lifehacker-themed nightclub. In every case, the underlying brief it generated outlined some basic details, but occasionally it added things I hadn’t asked for. This included additional text, iconography, and in one case it even added the “design brief” explanation I had requested as the bottom half of the poster.

Sources indicate that those mistakes filter into the final product, when the brief is then fed into the image generator that ultimately makes the poster. In my case, ChatGPT demonstrated me the underlying explanations for its reasoning (though even that could be different from what was actually sent to the image generator), but most people who use a chatbot for this task won’t see these factors before getting the final result.

While most chatbots won’t show you exactly what underlying “thinking” they use, most can be coaxed into describing the vague outlines of how they reached certain outcomes. And those descriptions provide some insight into why certain chatbots keep outputting similar results over and over. It doesn’t take long for some patterns to emerge. For example, any prompt to generate a poster for a nightclub almost invariably generated a brief that had specifications for a color palette including “electric purple,” “electric yellow,” and “electric pink.”.

The reason for this should be pretty obvious: When the statistical model underlying LLMs needs to come up with an example for “colors for a nightclub poster,” the most obvious answers are neon, high-energy colors. Unless you know something about the specific club’s vibe (and write that out and feed it to the chatbot), the AI will have to fill in the gaps with something. And that something will be based on the same statistics it uses to predict any word.

This pattern of repetition was everywhere in all the design rationale ChatGPT gave me. Across multiple attempts to generate a Club Lifehacker poster, the generated design brief added an overarching “concept” that described the fictional club’s atmosphere as “high-energy” and “futuristic.” Every bot mentioned using images with the “silhouette” of either the DJ or a dancing crowd (often both). All the text had to be “bold” and “futuristic.".

According to recent reports, if there's one dead giveaway that a poster was made with AI, it's that one brush-stroke font that they all seem to use. Now, this is a bit more speculative, but I have a theory on where that specific design comes from. And it’s worth noting upfront that this seems to only apply to posters generated by ChatGPT specifically.

One of the most common factors I found in my design brief testing was the use of phrases like “brush lettering” or “brush script.” Brush lettering is a design term that refers to using any number of methods like markers, paint brushes, or brush pens to write text. In digital design, that can take the form of fonts that are designed to emulate the look of fancy, handwritten text.

In every test poster I created, however, ChatGPT seemed to take the phrase “brush lettering” rather literally. Every instance I encountered of a design brief that mentioned any kind of “brush” text generated an image with letters that looked as though they were created with a broad paint brush. A human designer would understand “brush lettering” to mean “something that looks handwritten," but ChatGPT didn’t seem capable of understanding the phrase as anything other than using an actual paint brush.

It has been revealed that the generated posters aren’t even using a “font,” strictly speaking. (Often, letters that should be identical had slight variations.) The image generator part of the chatbot is still a diffusion model, so it can’t employ a vector-based font, per se. But the brush-style font is so common that its look surfaces in any statistical model.

This is an odd quirk of ChatGPT specifically, and it’s possible that it could change in the future. Especially if OpenAI intentionally tries to train this behavior out of its chatbot. However, it’s helpful to illustrate the underlying mechanism. The only way a chatbot can conceptualize design elements in a visual medium is to generate more specific text to feed to the image generator. And that text is just as prone to mistakes and blandness as any other AI model.

I’ve been examining this with a focus on the kinds of posters ChatGPT generates because they’re very common, but posters (or any AI-generated content) from other models might look different. Every model has its own tendencies. For example, a lot of vibecoded websites are made with Anthropic’s Claude, and you can often tell by the tiny text, buttons with rounded corners, and tile-based layouts.

Recent findings suggest that to a certain extent, this is inevitable. While AI models are very different from humans and do not make “choices” in the same way people do, design elements still have to come from somewhere, and whether human or AI, it’s impossible to make these decisions in a vacuum. Humans will have preferences based on the things they like or emotionally resonate with, and AI models will have tendencies based on what their statistical model determines is the most appropriate output.

That means that an AI model’s “style” is naturally going to change over time. Even if a model improves or makes fewer mistakes, it’s impossible to ever change the fact that all ChatGPT images are made by ChatGPT. Whatever you generate with any particular model will have a lot in common with what everyone else who uses the same tool generates.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The legacy-quel is alive and well, and it only makes sense that a sequel/reboot/reimagining would eventually come for “Home Alone,” Chris Columbus’ 1990 holiday classic starring Macaulay Culkin.

There was buzz that Culkin over the summer pitched an idea to Disney as to where a grown Kevin McAllister would be today after enduring two child abandonments and harassment and attempted murder from bumbling bandits (our interpretation, not necessarily his read on Kevin’s childhood shenanigans and trauma). Disney now seems to have warmed to the idea like a cup of hot cocoa, especially thanks to the two additional names who are working with Culkin on the project: Seth Rogen and Evan Goldberg. Related Stories Trump Renews Backing for Federal Film Tax Credit as Lawmakers Push for Year-End Passage ‘Disclosure Day’ Did Its Biggest Stunts Practically, So the VFX Team Worked Hard to Look Invisible — Watch.

Disney’s 20th Century Studios is in early development on a sequel to “Home Alone” that would star Culkin reprising his original role and in which Rogen and Goldberg on behalf of their Point Grey banner would write and produce the film, working with Culkin on his idea, IndieWire has learned.

Things are very, very early days, and any plot details are being kept under wraps for now, and no director is attached at the moment.

Chris Columbus directed the original “Home Alone” and its nearly-as-loved sequel “Home Alone 2: Lost in Latest York,” and both written by the late great John Hughes. If you can believe it, there have been six “Home Alone” movies in all, with the third one at least released in theaters and doing respectable box office numbers. The others are all TV movies or in the case of the most recent 2021 film “Home Sweet Home Alone,” a Disney+ streaming movie.

The original two films though grossed $477 million and $358 million worldwide, respectively, and the original still gets tons of cable play and finds its way into the Nielsen streaming charts. It makes sense that a more serious sequel with Culkin back in the fold would be welcomed by audiences.

Sadly, “Home Alone” has been back on the minds of audiences of late after the recent passing of Catherine O’Hara, who played Kevin’s mom, and also Tim Curry, who had a small role as a hotel clerk in “Home Alone 2.” Joe Pesci and Daniel Stern as the Wet Bandits are still around, though Pesci has been mostly retired outside of his return in Scorsese’s “The Irishman” back in 2019 and his role in the Pete Davidson Peacock series “Bupkis” in 2023.

Culkin too has had a bit of a resurgence, making a cameo in the most recent season of “Fallout” and doing a voice in Disney’s “Zootopia 2.”.

Star Trek's George Takei Played A Villain In A Beloved Batman Series

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, throughout its 60-year history, the "Star Trek" franchise has been the home to some truly fantastic voices.
  • Needless to say, those signature dulcet tones make him easy to pick out when you hear him showing up somewhere other than the bridge of the USS Enterprise, even when the character he's playing could not look any more different than the man himself.
  • According to recent reports, "Batman Beyond" debuted in 1999 when creators Bruce Timm, Paul Dini, and Alan Burnett came up with a desperate pitch to satisfy the studio's demand for a new Batman show: a slightly sci-fi, near-future take on the Dark Knight.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, throughout its 60-year history, the "Star Trek" franchise has been the home to some truly fantastic voices. The dramatic, over-the-top delivery of William Shatner as Captain Kirk, the sonorous tones of Avery Brooks as Captain Sisko, and the cat-like vocal fry of Kate Mulgrew as Captain Janeway are, in their own way, as iconic as the ships they helmed. You don't need to go all the way to the captain's chair to find those voices, though. George Takei, who played Lieutenant Hikaru Sulu on the original "Trek," had a voice so recognizable that he was able to turn something as simple as "oh my" into a full-on catchphrase.

Needless to say, those signature dulcet tones make him easy to pick out when you hear him showing up somewhere other than the bridge of the USS Enterprise, even when the character he's playing could not look any more different than the man himself. So if you were catching up on one of the best Batman shows ever made, you were not having an audio hallucination. That was in fact George Takei as Mr. Fixx in the two-part pilot of "Batman Beyond.".

According to recent reports, "Batman Beyond" debuted in 1999 when creators Bruce Timm, Paul Dini, and Alan Burnett came up with a desperate pitch to satisfy the studio's demand for a new Batman show: a slightly sci-fi, near-future take on the Dark Knight. Set decades after the events of "Batman: The Animated Series," the series followed high school student Terry McGinnis (Will Friedle) as he took over the role of Batman from a retired Bruce Wayne, played by legendary "BTAS" voice actor Kevin Conroy. Terry's youth, struggles balancing his Batman identity with life as a cool teen, and wisecracking demeanor gave the character a vibe that was equal parts Batman and Spider-Man. That may have turned off a few viewers at the time who thought a teenage Batman was a ripoff, but the end result speaks for itself.

Industry observers note that while he only appeared in the first two episodes, Takei's character was arguably the most important villain in the entire series. Derek Powers, who would go on to become the supervillain Blight, might've been the mastermind who ordered the hit, but it was Mr. Fixx who actually killed Terry's father and set him on the path of vengeance that would lead to him becoming Batman. The casting was an interesting one, too. Fixx had the design of a hulking brute with a scarred eye, but even a few words in Takei's rich voice gave him a depth that subverted looks and hinted at a much deeper character. Unfortunately, that character wound up at the bottom of the ocean off the coast of Gotham City before we could really get into his hopes and dreams, but that's the life of an evil henchman for you.

Takei wasn't the only notable celebrity on "Batman Beyond." Hardcore rocker Henry Rollins had a recurring role as D-list supervillain Mad Stan, former James Bond actor George Lazenby indicated up as King, the leader of the Royal Flush Gang, and "Terminator" star Linda Hamilton made an appearance as a scientist who built a fresh body for a cryogenically preserved Mr. Freeze, among others. Cary Elwes, Tim Curry, Michael McKean, Ice-T ... the list goes on, and it's full of compelling performances that helped to make the show the beloved classic that it is.

Industry observers note that if you've got a good ear, "Batman Beyond" is worth watching just for spotting celebrity voices. And if you don't, well, it's worth watching because it's a great take on Batman with some phenomenal episodes and a great design sense. Just don't be surprised if you find yourself thinking some of those supervillains sound awfully familiar.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that as soon as the first clips from DreamWorks’ latest animated film, “Forgotten Island,” started popping up online, there was one specific shot that caught on fire online — the lip pointing.
  • Industry observers note that “That moment had been in the script since the first draft, because we wanted to put in as much as we can from our personal experience with Filipino culture,” director Joel Crawford told IndieWire.
  • In a recent development, the lip pointing may not happen in a pivotal scene, or be vital for a character, but it became a sort of symbol for the film’s approach to representation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that as soon as the first clips from DreamWorks’ latest animated film, “Forgotten Island,” started popping up online, there was one specific shot that caught on fire online — the lip pointing. It happens at a goodbye party for Raissa Molina (Liza Soberano), who is heading to Caltech. Her best friend Jo (H.E.R.) is late to the party and asks around to see where Raissa is, when an older woman points with her lips in the right direction. It’s a small moment, a visual gag that can easily go over the audience’s heads amidst all the other jokes in the sequence. But audiences familiar with Filipino culture immediately caught on to it, as did Latino fans and many others who recognize that gesture as the most potent and accurate way to point at something. Related Stories Trump Renews Backing for Federal Film Tax Credit as Lawmakers Push for Year-End Passage ‘Disclosure Day’ Did Its Biggest Stunts Practically, So the VFX Team Worked Hard to Look Invisible — Watch.

Industry observers note that “That moment had been in the script since the first draft, because we wanted to put in as much as we can from our personal experience with Filipino culture,” director Joel Crawford told IndieWire. “Growing up around Filipinos, the lip point was something that was so specific and unique to me, so it’s beautiful that it transcends into other cultures. Adding that felt like a celebration of it, but also something that makes characters feel real. And in adding that specificity about the culture, it ends up being the most universal aspect of the movie because it invites everyone in.”.

In a recent development, the lip pointing may not happen in a pivotal scene, or be vital for a character, but it became a sort of symbol for the film’s approach to representation. Later in the film, Jo does the lip pointing because an animator thought it would be a good idea to reprise it, after learning about its place in the culture. Indeed, in addition to having an authentically Filipino cast and a cultural consultant to really capture Filipino culture, the animation team found their own ways of homaging or capturing aspects of Filipino culture to bring to the movie.

When creating the character of Jo, the animation team based a lot of her hand expressions on Filipino skater Margie Didal and her own hand gestures, while the villainous Manananggal’s movements were created by the animation team watching choreography done by Filipino-American dancer Phil Tayag, who brought a pop locking influence to the vampire-like creature.

In a recent development, “When we first approached DreamWorks and Universal with this story, it was notable to everybody that we got every detail of this story and this culture right,” director Januel Mercado said. “.

After challenging what was thought possible with DreamWorks animated films in “Puss in Boots: The Last Wish,” Crawford and Mercado push the studio’s visuals forward with “Forgotten Island.” With most of the story taking place on the island of Nakali, which is populated by all sorts of mythical creatures, to really capture the fantastical possibilities of this world, the movie’s visuals go wild, taking inspiration from 1990s Filipino art as well as anime from that time period.

In a recent development, for Crawford, the big lesson learned from “The Last Wish” was that you could take big swings in the animation style and the visuals, but you could also do specific things in the story with those visuals. Indeed, when it came to “Forgotten Island,” the idea of memories and friendship became not only central to the story of Jo and Raissa, but also to the eclectic visual styles represented in the movie.

“The idea became that we could push the animation styles to represent the different ways people recall memories,” Crawford explained. “We didn’t need to be limited by Western CG-style animation, but actually bring in some of our own nostalgia into it and make sure it fit the characters. When Raww tries to explain what happened when he met Jo and Raissa, he sees himself as way cooler than he is, so he sees himself as Goku or Guile from ‘Street Fighter,’ the animation going 2D in an action-heavy tone. But when we meet Mermahn, he is very shallow and narcissistic, and we felt his glamorous point of view fit the aesthetic of ‘Sailor Moon’ with the silly kind of heart-shaped lens flare.”.

In a recent development, still, just because you can go Super Saiyan doesn’t mean you let go of reality. Instead, the directors worked with the head of cinematography, Scott Cullen, to make sure the film had a live-action look to it. The idea was to capture the nostalgia of growing up, while being able to feel the camera in the space the action takes place in, as if it was a physical set.

It has been revealed that “Joel and I really wanted to make sure you feel like live-action, you feel the cameras there, and the way the light interacts with the lens is reminiscent of tangible photos we grew up taking, where you don’t know how they’ll develop,” Mercado stated. “ We wanted to add imperfections, and to have interaction of weather on the camera, like condensation of rain and droplets on the camera.”.

In a recent development, this all added to making “Forgotten Island” look like a part of the evolution of DreamWorks Animation, while standing out as something entirely fresh and unique. As Crawford said, the studio doesn’t really have a specific house style like other big studios. “Every movie requires innovation and pushing boundaries and finding solutions,” he added.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This week's column is bleak. First, there's the looksmaxxing trend where teenagers are taking dangerous chemicals to correct perceived physical shortcomings. Then there are the AI job interviewers. Depressing, but at least some young people are having a little fun with their dystopian hellscape.

You can judge a generation by the illegal drugs it pioneers. In the 1960s, hippies smoked weed and dropped acid to expand their consciousness; the yuppies of the go-go '80s fueled their drive to acquire with Colombian cocaine; but kids today don’t want to go deeper or work harder. They have a smaller, sadder goal: They take drugs to look better. The substance of choice for a growing number of teenage boys are steroids, peptides, and other exotic chemicals designed to enhance appearance.

Industry observers note that would-be muscle-men have been injecting themselves with black market ‘rhoids since the Eisenhower administration, but that was a small cult of adult weirdos with a specific goal. In 2026, kids are into it, and they aren’t using steroids to win a $500 prize in the Mr. Topeka contest; they’re using unapproved research chemicals to looksmaxx. Looksmaxxing is an online movement of young men trying to maximize their physical appearance. Teenagers are taking the normal desire to look their best to dangerous, pathological levels. Driven by a combination of undiagnosed body dysmorphia and relentless social media algorithms that turn amoral “red pill” kooks into gurus, teenage boys are ingesting a panoply of exotic and dangerous compounds in a quest to fix the angle of their jawlines, change their skin tone, lose weight, grow taller, and otherwise “correct” perceived physical problems.

Sources indicate that in the "good old days" of steroid abuse, people generally stuck to abusing anabolic-androgenic steroids that had at least been tested for decades. Teens today are buying SARMs (Selective Androgen Receptor Modulators) and synthetic peptides marked "not for human consumption" from shady laboratories online. Steroids primarily affect the muscles, but many of these newer substances target different biological systems. A recent Rolling Stone article reports that kids are “heightmaxxing” by swallowing erdafitinib, a drug that treats advanced urothelial cancer, because the drug is known to trigger growth spurts (that can result in a curvature of the spine and other nasty side effects). They’re also trying MK-677 to get taller, an experimental growth hormone secretagogue that carries the risk of insulin resistance, water retention, and high blood pressure. Others are injecting Melanotan II, a synthetic peptide that forces a long-lasting deep tan, with side effects of extreme nausea and the sudden, aggressive darkening of moles. (And they're doing steroids too.).

Recent findings suggest that in the looksmaxxing community, softmaxxing is doing generally-considered-acceptable things to look better, like getting enough sleep, exercising regularly, and eating a balanced diet. Hardmaxxing is taking more extreme measures like plastic surgery, smashing your face with a hammer, or taking experimental drugs.

In the bodybuilding and looksmaxxing community, “natty” refers to a natural, non-steroid-enhanced physique.

Sources indicate that here's something more lighthearted than the growing popularity of illicit self-esteem chemicals: the bicep heart and waist heart trends. The Bicep heart came first. Thirst trap videos started appearing on Instagram and TikTok in October in which dudes make a heart with their hand and bicep. Then people started posting variations where they frame the shot with someone they love inside the heart. The bicep heart rapidly led to women posting the waist heart.

Industry observers note that okay. So maybe it's not that lighthearted of a trend. While there are some videos of dudes with skinny arms doing the bicep heart, it's mostly jacked dudes. And the waist heart doesn't seem like it would work at all unless you are a specific shape, as this video illustrates. So maybe this isn't a silly meme but an illustration of how young people are inundated with content that can trigger feelings of physical unworthiness, even if they're just looking for silly memes.

Recent findings suggest that as if searching for a job wasn't alienating and horrible enough, some companies have begun using AI agents to conduct interviews. Begging a robot to let you work in a cubicle farm is as dystopian as anything Phillip K. Dick ever imagined, but don't count humanity out yet. Young people are sticking a finger in the eye of the machine by creating comedy videos that focus on trolling these AI job interviewers. They're hilarious because AI is the ultimate straight person in a comedy team, and the raw compute costs to run these interviews means corporate money is burning with each second of wasted time. Here are some of the top creators in the genre.

Bo Bongo: This YouTuber indicates up to AI interviews shirtless but insists he's wearing a "corporate tube top," then focuses on daring the interviewer to notice he's doing things like smoking a cigarette or eating a rotisserie chicken.

Cam Whitt likes to wind up AI by arguing, interrupting, telling outrageous lies, and asking the dumbest questions imaginable, like, "When does the interview actually start?" and "How do I figure out what my name is?".

Grahamn Raabe: Among this YouTuber's schticks is speaking only in nonsense, like describing his professional background as "freight cadence, walnut, a little bit of Richard, spruce wood—six years of spruce wood.".

Industry observers note that nick Reid: Is so obnoxious, he seems to make the AI furious at him, even though it's a computer without emotions. Two thumbs up!

Latest Update: 5 Greatest Fantasy Book Series of All Time, Ranked

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1404 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Collider

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that what elevates a fantasy novel from great to exceptional?
  • Industry observers note that given fantasy's vast history, it's impossible to give every noteworthy title its due.
  • Robert Jordan allegedly envisioned his career-defining The Wheel of Time as a smaller undertaking.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that what elevates a fantasy novel from great to exceptional? Although there are certain structural expectations to meet, the genre defines itself by its boundless capacity for creative flexibility and evolution. The real magic happens when all the imagination-captivating trappings we associate with comforting escapism fuse with intimately relatable and resonant metaphors; in short, works by authors who are unafraid to grapple with humanity's best and bleakest aspects, demand justice, and underscore what most matters. That is the genre's guiding light.

Industry observers note that given fantasy's vast history, it's impossible to give every noteworthy title its due. The following five series were selected according to their cultural impact and longevity, whether they achieved their ambitious aims, and the crucial ways in which their writers' perspectives deconstruct and revitalize well-worn tropes into infinitely more authentic products — as only the most transformative, timeless stories can.

Robert Jordan allegedly envisioned his career-defining The Wheel of Time as a smaller undertaking. His lore proceeded to explode into 14 installments and a cumulative word count that might make prospective readers faint from intimidation. The payoff, however — a comprehensive magic system, history, culture, religion, and political intrigue, with themes surrounding external and internal imbalance, dichotomy, and division — is worth relishing. Jordan's initial set-up pulls from numerous philosophical and mythological influences and also unabashedly homages the mechanics of old-fashioned tales. This enthusiastic lack of cynicism contributes to the series' appeal. An equally key component to Jordan's success is his deft ability to twist expectations from the beginning, planting subversions and nourishing their seeds until they blossom into a polished, awe-inspiring behemoth of a world.

The characters whirled around by the stormy clash between their cosmic destinies and personal autonomy aren't effortlessly flawless heroes or automatically irredeemable villains; they either grow into or surpass their archetypical origins. And despite sometimes succumbing to unfortunate stereotypes, The Wheel of Time's gender dynamics remain astonishingly progressive for the '90s fantasy landscape. The Dragon Reborn might be male, but an abundant ensemble of formidable women drives the plot forward. Few other authors demonstrate such a consistent track record with epic endings, either — every battle is a feverish home run that catapults readers' hearts into their throats.

The late and dearly missed Terry Pratchett is one of those beloved figures who, in terms of mainstream awareness, still feels like an underappreciated genius. Playfully satirizing fantasy's fundamentals doesn't invalidate Discworld's ingenuity, nor Pratchett's unrivaled mastery over prose and plotting. His life's work comprises 41 breezily paced books, all of which take place on the titular planet — which just so happens to be carried by four giant elephants riding atop an even larger turtle. (Because, why not?).

While interconnected, Pratchett divides Discworld into multiple sub-series. These shenanigan-filled misadventures feature different stylistic flourishes and lead characters, like a gritty film noir-esque detective, a hapless and cowardly wizard, a resourceful witch-in-training and her keen, stereotype-defying elderly mentors (plus some exuberant fairies), and a version of Death who speaks in all-caps but negates most of his intimidation factor once he names his requisite pale horse "Binky." Such versatility means there's a corner of Discworld to suit everyone's preference. Yet no matter which protagonist or genre takes center stage, each installment retains astute insights on society, class, prejudice, and the universal insecurities and uncertainties that plague humanity. Pratchett sheathes his dagger-piercing reflections inside a vibrantly witty heart. The results nourish the mind and the soul.

Sources indicate that one of her generation's most strikingly effective and inventive fantasy voices, Robin Hobb hit the ground running in 1995 with Assassin's Apprentice and hasn't let her foot off the gas since. Instead of crafting one massive sequential series, a la The Wheel of Time, The Realm of the Elderlings' 16 novels span four trilogies and one quartet, three of which (Farseer, The Tawny Man, and The Fitz and the Fool) follow the trials and tribulations of FitzChivalry Farseer, an expert assassin with an illegitimate aristocratic heritage. The Liveship Traders and The Rain Wild Chronicles explore beyond Fitz's homeland of the Six Duchies; the former trilogy's seafaring saga of multi-generational female determination and liberation includes sentient ships, whereas Rain Wild upsets the medieval-inspired realm's power hierarchy by re-introducing dragons.

Sources indicate that hobb, arguably, can't be compared against anyone except herself. In terms of sheer breadth and depth, the only thing that matches her superb premises is her psychologically rich work. Human complexity is the proverbial tool of her trade, and she refuses to either sugarcoat our repellent facets or descend into outright nihilism. It's a pleasure to witness her creations — all prone to moral ambiguity, immaturity, and mistakes, but earning empathy — mature over the decades. Their dimensionality and gravitas ignite her world. In turn, the world's machinations shape their wounds, which Hobb exposes one affecting layer at a time by examining patriarchal violence from survivors' perspectives, bigotry, queer sexuality, gender fluidity, ecology, enslavement, the intersection of colonialism and Machiavellian regimes, and religious propaganda. As a woman in a space long overpopulated by the white male perspective, she's a trendsetter worthy of that designation.

Recent findings suggest that the Broken Earth, N. K. Jemisin's follow-up series to her acclaimed The Inheritance Trilogy, enshrined her status in the history books. She became the first author to win the Hugo Award for Best Novel for every book in a trilogy and the first to win the same award three years in a row (from 2015 to 2017). The Broken Earth's fantasy-meets-sci-fi premise unfolds on the Stillness, a single-continent planet routinely wrecked by environmental devastation. This instability reflects the Stillness' civilization; humanity has reshaped their daily lives around apocalyptic threats, but the prevailing power structure dooms itself by perpetuating systemic oppression, discrimination, and dehumanizing exploitation. Orogenes, the only people who can magically temper the planet's geological calamities, are vital to the Stillness' survival, yet reviled and persecuted. Meanwhile, non-orogene individuals are sorted into strict caste systems predicated upon whatever predetermined resources they can contribute to society.

Partially inspired by "the protests in Ferguson, Missouri, over the killing of unarmed Black teenager Michael Brown," Jemisin's staggering sophomore achievement serves as both a mirror and a warning. The futuristic Stillness is terrifyingly easy to visualize; ancient sins continue to rule and ruin, and these forces are as fundamentally destructive and merciless as climate change. The Broken Earth's themes, realized through three women's entwined journeys, concern the haunting effects of cumulative trauma on identity and autonomy as well as everything it actually requires to interrogate, shatter, and remake a corrupt world. It's a seismic feat from an extraordinary creator, intricate and urgent and acutely unforgettable — a work of art as relevant and limitless as fantasy should be.

Is this the most obvious choice under the sun? Of course. Does The Lord of the Rings wield an incalculable level of pop culture influence that's usually reserved for Greek myths and Bible tales? Undoubtedly. Fantasy as we know it rests largely upon J. R. R. Tolkien's shoulders. But let's set aside the author's tremendous footprint long enough to acknowledge a more impressive fact: The Lord of the Rings still feels as fresh as the day it was published. Countless direct and indirect adaptations have either revisited or channeled every corner of Middle-earth, yet the saga remains an irreplaceably distinct and immersive magnum opus. Heavily informed by Tolkien's horrifying time as a combat soldier during World War I, his poignant ode to gentleness, compassion, community, altruistic sacrifice, and "the smallest person" triumphing against insurmountable evil dazzles with all the sharpness of a fresh-cut diamond in direct sunlight.

Even when hope dawns anew, however, Tolkien tempers his fictional victory with the bittersweet ache that accompanies acknowledging humankind's vulnerabilities, fears, and tragedies — which war's life-altering scars compound beyond measure. Resilience and integrity demand a high cost. Tapping into the emotional intimacies we universally share is why the Fellowship's journey, especially Frodo Baggins' unfathomable burden as an unlikely and haunted hero, has provided catharsis to generations of fans. The Lord of the Rings embodies fantasy's enduring importance, not to mention the reasons why we gravitate toward storytelling throughout our lifetimes like it's oxygen. After 72 years, world-shifting feature films, and at least one more movie and two seasons of Prime Video's The Rings of Power on the way, it's safe to say that Tolkien's legacy indicates no signs of ever diminishing.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the "Hunger Games" universe is full of wild, larger-than-life characters, especially when we're talking about denizens of the ultra-wealthy and super-powerful Capitol that controls Panem. Every year, during the annual Hunger Games that cull (or "reap") children from each of Panem's tightly controlled and impoverished 12 districts, Capitol citizens help beautify those kids before sending most of them to their deaths, and many Capitol higher-ups pursue plastic surgery and extreme fashion for high-concept looks.

Industry observers note that one of those people in the latest "Hunger Games" book and movie, "Sunrise on the Reaping," is the erratic and unreliable District 12 stylist Magno Stift, who's legally married to the surgically-enhanced District 12 chaperone Drusilla Sickle (an unrecognizable Glenn Close in the film) and who's played on screen by Billy Porter. In the novel, our protagonist Haymitch Abernathy — a young version of the District 12 victor played by Woody Harrelson in the previous "Hunger Games" films and Joseph Zada in this new prequel — notes that nobody speaks highly of Magno, and "he's every bit as bad as they say." He continues, "While the other stylists do new costumes each year for the parade and interviews that happen before the Games, he seems to have a limitless supply of the same crappy coal miner overalls in an array of sizes.".

According to recent reports, when Magno finally shows up, we see him through Haymitch's eyes: "Magno Stift's sun-leathered skin has been tattooed with a snakeskin pattern. He wears a long shirt made of metal diamonds and no visible pants. His sandals lace all the way up to his pelvis, and from each of his ears dangle tiny, living garter snakes that twist and turn in misery." Eventually, he stops showing up to work when one of his wearable reptiles poisons him. So, why does Magno look familiar in the movie?

You've definitely seen Magno Stift actor Billy Porter in at least one of his recent high-profile projects, so let me walk you through some of them. After earning fame and acclaim for his role as Lola in the Broadway stage musical version of "Kinky Boots," which won him a Tony and a Grammy, Porter's massive-screen career slowly began to take off. Though he did, to be totally fair, appear as a singer in the 1996 classic "The First Wives Club," Porter's newfound name recognition in the 2010s earned him roles in films like "The Humbling" alongside Greta Gerwig and Al Pacino, the 2020 comedy "Like a Boss" with Tiffany Haddish, and 2021's "Cinderella," which gave Porter one of his biggest roles yet as the fairy godparent Fab G.

Recent findings suggest that during a 2021 interview with People Magazine, Porter talked about gender-flipping the role played by none other than Whitney Houston in the much-loved 1997 TV film adaptation of the stage musical "Rodgers & Hammerstein's Cinderella" starring Brandy. "When I was 14, my dream was to be the male Whitney Houston," the actor quipped before adding, ""Magic has no gender. That is the most crucial for me.".

After starring in "Cinderella" with Camilla Cabello and James Corden, Porter directed the coming-of-age film "Anything's Possible," popped up in the senior comedy "80 for Brady," and got dramatic in "Our Son" with Luke Evans and Andrew Rannells. So, what about Porter's small-screen career? It's booming, too.

Billy Porter's early years on TV include credits on "So You Think You Can Dance" as a performer and stalwart procedurals like "Law & Order," as well as its massively successful spin-off "Law & Order: Special Victims Unit" — but after winning that Tony and Emmy and hosting an eight-episode 2013 special called "Land of Lola: Backstage at Kinky Boots," Porter was finally on the map. Aside from "American Horror Story: Apocalypse" and other recurring and guest arcs on highlights like the 2021 "Gossip Girl" reboot, Porter's most recognizable role is as Prayerful "Pray" Tell, an emcee in the Newly introduced York ballroom scene, on Ryan Murphy's series "Pose." Not only did Porter get the chance to play a character who shares his HIV diagnosis (something the actor revealed in his own life in 2021), he won an Emmy for playing Pray Tell and became the first-ever gay Black man to win in any lead Emmy category. As Porter told People Magazine in 2021, it was also an crucial role for him for other reasons:.

It has been revealed that "'Pose' and Pray Tell have been a proxy for my healing. The trauma was so difficult. The grief was so heavy. The antiretroviral drugs [for HIV] came, and everybody moved on. There's a whole generation of us that really never got a chance to process having lived through the AIDS crisis [and] having lived through an epidemic.".

You can see Billy Porter (briefly) play Magno Stift in "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping," which is currently playing in theaters.

Curry Barker Would Have Completely Reshot ‘Obsession’ If He Could
