💡 Key Takeaways
  • It’s been quite a year for Curry Barker.
  • Which is why it’s interesting that Hollywood’s hottest new director took time out from editing (he’s cutting “Ghosts” himself) and writing (“I have my next thing that I’m working on — I’m really excited about it, and nobody knows anything about it, which is super exciting”), and an unexpected Oscar campaign (“Obsession” is a legit contender for Best Picture, Actress, and Original Screenplay nominations), to make a 5-minute short film, “Mama Bear.” On this week’s episode of the Filmmaker Toolkit Podcast, Barker talked about how the success of “Obsession” interrupted his established flow of churning out short-form content for his popular YouTube channel.
  • It has been revealed that “I have two or three short films where I’m like, ‘Oh man, this all took off really promptly, and I have this short film idea I’ve been dying to do,” said Barker on Toolkit.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It’s been quite a year for Curry Barker. In September 2025, he brought his $700,000 horror film to the Toronto International Film Festival, where it sparked a bidding war that Focus Features won for $17 million. That hefty price tag turned into the deal of the century, as “Obsession” went on to become a half-billion-dollar box-office sensation, with audiences growing week to week. It was clear the then 26-year-old “YouTuber” (a moniker Barker rightfully dismisses) was something special. This was not just a flash in the pan, but a real talent with a seemingly boundless number of ideas and movies he wanted to make. His next film, “Anything but Ghosts,” was already in the can by the “Obsession” premiere, a yet-to-be-revealed third film is in the works, while potential franchises (“Texas Chainsaw Massacre” and “Obsession,” Barker sees the One Wish Willow story device having “Knives Out” anthology-like potential) linger in the background. Related Stories Director Brian Duffield Had to Find a Latest Form of Visual Storytelling for ‘Whalefall’ How ‘Paper Tiger’ Evolved When Jeremy Strong and Anne Hathaway Couldn’t Reprise Their ‘Armageddon Time’ Roles.

Which is why it’s interesting that Hollywood’s hottest new director took time out from editing (he’s cutting “Ghosts” himself) and writing (“I have my next thing that I’m working on — I’m really excited about it, and nobody knows anything about it, which is super exciting”), and an unexpected Oscar campaign (“Obsession” is a legit contender for Best Picture, Actress, and Original Screenplay nominations), to make a 5-minute short film, “Mama Bear.” On this week’s episode of the Filmmaker Toolkit Podcast, Barker talked about how the success of “Obsession” interrupted his established flow of churning out short-form content for his popular YouTube channel.

It has been revealed that “I have two or three short films where I’m like, ‘Oh man, this all took off really promptly, and I have this short film idea I’ve been dying to do,” said Barker on Toolkit. “I actually have no time to do those short films, and then justifying if it be would be worth my time to do them when I need to be writing this, I need to be editing this, and I need to be doing press for this.”.

It’s less about Barker’s desire to scratch the itch of the shorts he never got to make, but more about a hesitancy to step away completely from the iterative process by which he learned his craft — justifying the brief time he took off to make “Mama Bear” because he felt the need to sketch.

Recent findings suggest that “It’s fun to have that playground because the features are bigger stakes,” said Barker. “We were like, ‘Okay, this is a short film: We can do weird stuff. Let’s come up with crazy rules that don’t make sense, and experiment.’”.

Recent findings suggest that barker and his “Mama Bear” cinematographer — his young brother Riley, who worked on the “Obsession” camera department — created different rules for the camera, as Curry is still trying to hone his discipline for storytelling within longer takes. Not only would they shoot a narrow 4:3 aspect ratio, but the Barker brothers denied themselves the ability to move the camera left, right, up, down, or dolly in.

“I do have a lot to learn,” noted Barker of making “Mama Bear.” “It’s so funny because I was having dinner and I told someone, ‘Oh, I’d love to shadow on Ari Aster’s set.’ And someone was like, ‘Well, you’re Curry Barker, what are you going to shadow for?’”.

His 2026 meteoric rise has allowed Barker to collect a group of more experienced peers he views as mentors — including Aster, Bill Hader, Zach Cregger, and Rian Johnson — and successful producers, like Jason Blum, investing in his career, but he believes there’s a misconception of what comes along with “making it.”.

“People think that once you’re in this club, you’re in the club, and everyone talks to everyone. But no — you’re in a bubble, and I want to know how Zach Cregger writes his outline. I want to watch him do it,” stated Barker. “You’re all alone. Your process is your own, and you figure this stuff out on your own. Once you get into this league, there’s no one telling you, ‘Well, actually you do it like this, this, and this.’ It’s whatever you learned all along your journey; that’s your process.”.

It has been revealed that one of the most impressive things about the self-taught Barker’s journey is how rapidly he turned himself into a successful actor/writer/director/editor. In 2018, when Barker left Alabama to come to Los Angeles to pursue a career in movies, he saw himself as an actor. Despite all the story scenarios dancing around his head, the idea that he would become a screenwriter was laughable.

“I never would’ve thought I was a screenwriter. I didn’t make great grades. I made Cs and Ds, and I wasn’t the best in English class,” noted Barker, who naively assumed professional writers were the kids who won spelling bees: “I just thought to be respected as a writer you have to be that.” Barker credits taking screenwriter Aaron Sorkin’s MasterClass as what opened his eyes. “It was the first time I thought, ‘I can do this, too.’ It’s really just about being creative and cracking a story, and there are rules, there’s structure.”.

In a recent development, directing organically grew out of Barker pulling together collaborators to shoot sketches and shorts for him to act in. Barker, half-joking, likes to say he realized one day that what he was doing was directing, and that he both enjoyed “telling people what to do” and had a knack for it.

What Barker accomplishes in a single shot — establishing a tonal balance that teeters between horror and comedy, combining blocking and camera movement to edit within the frame — is remarkably sophisticated. But Barker, who studies and strives for what masters like Kiyoshi Kurosawa can accomplish, quickly indicates he fell short in “Obsession.”.

Industry observers note that “Things that you might think we pulled off [with longer takes in ‘Obsession’], we reshot,” said Barker, who on the podcast described in detail a key early scene between Bear (Michael Johnston) and Nikki (Inde Navarrette) in the bedroom that had to be reshot because the action took too long to unfold. “I think Ari [Aster] said once that if you realize you needed to give this information in four seconds, but then it took 25 seconds, you’re stuck with 25 seconds.”.

Curry Barker, the editor, is Curry Barker, the director’s harshest critic, giving him a bird’s-eye view of what he believes is the director’s inability to envision the required pacing of how a scene will play on screen, even if it might feel unnaturally fast on set.

In a recent development, “Every single oner that I’ve shot in my career has been a problem in the edit,” said Barker. “I think there’s two ways to fail at something. You can either fail, realize that it didn’t work, get scared of it, and then be like, ‘Well, in my last film I did a bunch of oners and then it killed me in the edit, so I’m not going to do that anymore.’ Or you can fail, realize how you did it wrong, and try to get better at that for the next time.”.

As Barker discussed at the Future of Filmmaking Summit last month, that iterative process is key to how he got where he is, and it’s a mindset he clearly hasn’t given up. When asked how “Obsession” would have been different if he had more money, Barker doesn’t talk about locations, sets, special or visual effects, or scenes he envisioned that he couldn’t pull off — in terms of scale, he likes both writing and directing within set limitations.

In a recent development, “I would’ve reshot everything,” Barker answered without hesitation. “If I was finishing the edit before we got into TIFF, and you were like, ‘Dude, this is really good, we really love this movie, we think it has potential, but we want to give you $10 million to reshoot the whole thing, I would be like, ‘Deal.’ I would take it.”.

“I think it’s so funny to look back and think about that now,” Barker catches himself, knowing he’s talking about a film that broke the box office and catapulted his career. “Now I wouldn’t change anything because I would be too scared to touch it.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that known as being one of Spider-Man's most notorious enemies, the Green Goblin has been a formidable foe for our favorite web-slinger since he first debuted in The Amazing Spider-Man #14. As the alias of many super villains, he has been mostly incarnated as Norman Osbourn, and over the years, the iconic character has been portrayed by the likes of Willem Dafoe, James Franco, Chris Cooper and Dane DeHaan, to name but a few.

According to recent reports, more recently, the character of Norman Osbourn has played an crucial role in 2023's Marvel's Spider-Man 2, and it was clear to see that the storyline was setting him up to become the next Green Goblin. If you have not caught up with the Insomniac saga so far, you had better click off, but in the final moments of Marvel's Spider-Man 2, Harry Osborn falls into a coma following the defeat of Venom. As such, his father, Norman, demands that his assistants create the "G-Serum", which we can safely assume will lead to his transformation into the Green Goblin.

So, at the time of writing, fans have not yet seen Insomniac Games' interpretation of the Green Goblin, with many believing that the transformation will finally take place in Marvel's Spider-Man 3. However, despite rumors suggesting that a third installment is currently in development, it has not been confirmed by neither Insomniac nor Sony.

One such rumor that suggests Marvel's Spider-Man 3 is in development is uncovered concept art for none other than the Green Goblin himself, which was discovered over three years ago and shared to r/GamingLeaksAndRumors.

It is here that we can see concept art that was highlighted in what many believed to be an Insomniac Games' leak. It depicts the Green Goblin, looking quite fashionable in a black hooded jacket complete with purple accents. His green face and arms can be seen, with the latter being quite muscular, and he has various contraptions strapped to his fitted ensemble. Finishing off with a menacing grin, this Green Goblin looks a lot more fashionable than previous depictions, but no less terrifying.

According to recent reports, not only that, but the leaked screenshot reads, "Marvel's Spider-Man, the best-selling superhero game of all time, continues in Marvel's Spider-Man 3 with an explosive confrontation with a villain whose story spans all three games." Of course, it is worth taking this leak with a pinch of salt, and nothing has come of it in over three years. However, it did not stop fans from heading to the comments to share their thoughts.

"It's been interesting they've been building Norman up as the significant bad of the whole trilogy," one user commented. "I kind of wish him and Peter had a closer relationship because it's clear it's so one-sided (e.g, Norman indicates s*it about him being like a son to him, but it's clear Peter hates Norman with good reason, of course). Not sure if that'll be a good payoff. Also, I hope he still has the power of Oscorp behind him as the Goblin." Another shared, "I love Venom, but Green Goblin is my favorite of Spider-Man's Rogues Gallery, so, I'm down for this finally, especially this style too.".

For now, we can only hope that the rumors are true and Marvel's Spider-Man 3 is in development behind-the-scenes. If so, we may finally see another epic showdown between Spider-Man and the Green Goblin once more.

Tech Report: How World-Class Filmmaker Andrey Zvyagintsev Came Back to Life for ‘Minotaur’

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1294 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Indiewire

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • [Editor’s note: This interview was originally published during the 2026 Cannes Film Festival.
  • In a recent development, world-class Russian filmmaker Andrey Zvyagintsev (“Leviathan”) returned to the Croisette this year in Cannes competition with “Minotaur,” having recovered from a near-fatal illness.
  • When he left the hospital in Germany in 2022, as he told me while at Cannes this year, he was in a wheelchair.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

[Editor’s note: This interview was originally published during the 2026 Cannes Film Festival. MUBI will release “Minotaur” in theaters on Friday, November 20.].

In a recent development, world-class Russian filmmaker Andrey Zvyagintsev (“Leviathan”) returned to the Croisette this year in Cannes competition with “Minotaur,” having recovered from a near-fatal illness. After contracting a severe case of COVID in 2021, he reacted badly to the Sputnik vaccine and was put into a medically induced coma for 14 days. When he came out of it, his arms and legs were paralyzed due to Guillain-Barré Syndrome. He lay flat on his back for a year.

When he left the hospital in Germany in 2022, as he told me while at Cannes this year, he was in a wheelchair. While he indicates he hasn’t watched TV for 20 years now, “I watched a lot of films online,” he said through an interpreter on the roof of the Palais. “I read some things. I did not know if I would ever be able to walk again, to live again as a normal person. I have still now some consequences. I’m not at my best. I have regained completely the motion of my hands, but I have still a bit of a difficulty walking.” Related Stories Trump Renews Backing for Federal Film Tax Credit as Lawmakers Push for Year-End Passage ‘Disclosure Day’ Did Its Biggest Stunts Practically, So the VFX Team Worked Hard to Look Invisible — Watch.

But he did manage to shoot his sixth feature film last year, but not in Russia. After nine months of waiting, in the spring of 2023, he let go of one expensive project (“Jupiter”) for which he couldn’t seem to raise funding. “I said, ‘Let’s put it on ice, we’ll come back to it later. I don’t want to sit and wait for years and years for you to find the money. I want to make a film now.'”.

Sources indicate that so instead the filmmaker focused on a parallel project he had also been developing, an adaptation of Claude Chabrol’s 1969 thriller “The Unfaithful Wife,” starring Stéphane Audran as a well-heeled wife cheating on her husband, which was later remade as “Unfaithful” with Richard Gere and Diane Lane. The result, “Minotaur,” is the “Leviathan” Oscar nominee’s first film in nearly a decade, since 2017’s “Loveless.”.

It has been revealed that at the same time that the filmmaker was coping with his illness, four years ago, at the start of the Ukraine war, he made the decision to leave Russia and move to Paris. Going home would mean the risk of being considered a traitor or an enemy of the state in Russia. “It might result in us becoming what is called foreign agents; it’s a hard thing,” he said. “Maybe this will happen, maybe not. Let’s not be too pessimistic, but mostly all independent journalists are saying that their oppressions are going to get even harsher, and that I think we have decades ahead of us before things get better.”.

Recent findings suggest that his 16-year-old had been studying at a French high school in Moscow before the war. “His French was pretty good,” remarked Zvyagintsev. “So it was an obvious choice. And also, my wife [has been] in love with France for a long time, she has been learning French for many years. So it was a choice, also for both of them, and for their future.”.

Sources indicate that how’s his French? “Zero,” he noted. “The other reason for me was that France is the homeland to cinema; that’s where cinema was born, and also there are so many cinephiles among spectators. Also here in France, directors have the final cut. In the states, it’s much harder to get in a position where you are not censored; it’s not a producer or someone who decides instead of you.”.

The filmmaker set about creating believable Russian locations in Riga, Latvia, which still resembles its neighbor country. “The dormitory suburbs around Riga look exactly like Russian dormitory suburbs,” said Zvyagintsev. “A Russian eye would not be able to distinguish between Russia and Latvia in this instance. As for interiors, Anton’s flat was constructed as a set, so it’s a constructed set, and the villa where the main characters live is a contemporary building, a very modern one, and you could find something exactly like this anywhere.”.

Industry observers note that when it came to finding his cast, the casting director put out a call for Russian characters of a certain age. “Every actor from anywhere who is interested in working with you, they will send you a video presentation,” mentioned Zvyagintsev. “They can be from Argentina, London, Moscow, Paris, wherever. You send them a scene they have to play, and they make a self-tape for you on their iPhone. Before, I despised self-tapes, but it’s convenient, because now with everybody scattered around the world, it’s the only way for us to work. We could not possibly pay for all the people I wanted to check to come to Riga to make a real-life casting. There were people also from Riga who do speak Russian.”.

One serious issue for Russian actors still living in Russia was the possible repercussions of participating in a Zvyagintsev project. “I would talk to them about the script and show them parts of the script, so that they know what they’re getting involved in, because, of course, they were at risk of getting blacklisted,” he said. “Most of them, with heartache, refused to take part in the film, but there was one who accepted, and I’m still completely amazed at his courage. It’s the main part, the main character, [actor] Dmitriy Mazurov. I said to him, ‘Are you sure you want to film with me?’ And he said, ‘If I’m not doing this part, I don’t know what I’m doing in acting.'”.

Industry observers note that of course, the filmmaker took a different approach to the Chabrol story. “In the first minute, the story is completely revealed,” he said. “We understand that she is being unfaithful, so then all the film is about observing him, observing her, trying to understand, hesitating, and trying to guess what is going on, and while he observes, the spectator starts doing it along with him. And after the murder, actually, he goes back to this position where he’s mostly observing her reaction to the disappearance of a lover, yeah, and she knows what’s going on, and again it’s about observation.”.

It has been revealed that the filmmaker loved one bravura sequence that is 20 minutes long without any dialogue at all. “The sequence after the murder, it’s 20 minutes, even a little bit more, with not one subtitle, so you only observe his actions, and there are no words: it’s extremely cinematic in its essence.”.

And Zvyagintsev added many telling details from the real world, from corruption to the war. “The Chabrol film is much more classical,” he remarked. “It follows a pattern: he killed, then he’s discovered, and then he will be punished. And I wanted to break up this classical structure and to invent something different based on our Russian realities.”.

Was shooting the movie a physical challenge? “When you are full of inspiration, when you are searching constantly for solutions, the light, the sets, the performance of the actors, you don’t feel fatigued in the same way,” he remarked. “There is such a joy in making the film that is, in your head, real. I think it’s the best drug there is.”.

Next up, he will try and resuscitate “Jupiter.” ” I have met some producers who are interested in it,” he mentioned, “so hopefully we will be able to get it moving again.”.

Industry observers note that even six decades into his Hollywood career, Steven Spielberg is still synonymous with a brand of movie magic and spectacle that very few can rival. And when he decides to direct a fresh popcorn blockbuster like “Disclosure Day,” you know you’re in for a few dazzling sequences.

One of the most exciting moments in the film comes when a train collides into a car with stars Josh O’Connor and Emily Blunt close at hand. The sequence tested every department, from camera and production design to visual effects. And during IndieWire’s recent Craft Roundtables, VFX Supervisor Matthew Butler explained the unique challenge of incorporating subtle VFX work into a scene where so much happens in camera. Related Stories Trump Renews Backing for Federal Film Tax Credit as Lawmakers Push for Year-End Passage How World-Class Filmmaker Andrey Zvyagintsev Came Back to Life for ‘Minotaur’.

“With Steven, he wants everything to be as practical as it can be,” Butler mentioned. “We had a real train. A real train, a real car attached to that train, it was being dragged on a real track. That actually did happen.”.

But while Spielberg’s preferences were clear, Butler clarified that blockbusters on this scale rarely come down to a binary choice between practical effects and VFX. The biggest scenes often contain elements of both, as the pairing between in-camera human acting and cutting edge post-production is what leads to movie magic.

Recent findings suggest that “When you combine some of the live action blue screen work, clearly that’s your lead actor and actress there, and your stunt work where it’s like ‘Oh my God, that looks really real’ and the stuff that you just can’t do that’s just too dangerous … that’s where visual effects came in,” he mentioned. “But I wouldn’t say it was a visual effects sequence. It was a sequence that contained all of those, and it came together in the right way.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It feels like every time you look at your phone lately, another company is having an outage.
  • That pattern, in turn, has begun to fuel anxiety among the general public.
  • Recent findings suggest that but to skeptics of the U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It feels like every time you look at your phone lately, another company is having an outage. Last week, there was Microsoft, whose outage took down services from Outlook to Teams. Then, the FAA grounded all flights across the U.S. following "communication complications." This week, a number of banks experienced outages, as did Apple. Even the NSA's internal communications network went dark. Some of the biggest corporations and organizations in the world can't seem to keep their services running, leading to widespread disruptions and confusion. When it's a one-off, it's an annoyance; when it's outage after outage, it starts to feel like a pattern.

That pattern, in turn, has begun to fuel anxiety among the general public. What could possibly be causing Apple, Microsoft, JP Morgan Chase, and the NSA alike to go dark at roughly the same time? Is it a coordinated cyberattack? An AI revolt? Is the end finally nigh? To an outside observer, it certainly appears like something coordinated and nefarious is happening here. Secretary of State Marco Rubio is insistent that there is "zero evidence" that hackers or bad actors caused any of these outages, and President Trump is particularly unconcerned by the whole ordeal, saying, "It's life," and "Things like that happen.".

Recent findings suggest that but to skeptics of the U.S. government, these trickles of information aren't necessarily reassuring. While I agree with calls for someone from the government (perhaps the president himself) to make an official announcement explaining the situation, the root cause does appear to be clear at this time: The short answer? AI is at fault here, but not in the way you think.

Love it or hate it, AI is a force to be reckoned with. While you might know that AI can generate hyper-realistic videos and manage your emails on your behalf, certain models are adept at discovering fresh security vulnerabilities in software. These models aren't just helpful tools; they far surpass the abilities of human researchers. You might remember Anthropic initially pulled the brakes on its breakthrough model, Claude Mythos, when it found that the model could root out security vulnerabilities in just about anything.

Mythos, and models like it, are a double-edged sword. On the one hand, they can be major assets for developers and researchers to find fresh security vulnerabilities that humans otherwise wouldn't have discovered, and patch them accordingly. Unfortunately, the same can be remarked for bad actors, who can use these models to learn about new security flaws and attempt to exploit them before researchers have a chance to find them. As such, software developers across the spectrum, from small-time devs to major corporations, have been racing to patch as many security vulnerabilities as they can find—and they're finding a lot.

You might notice your PC's security updates, for example, are shipping with more patches than usual—historic levels, even. Microsoft keeps breaking its own records with its Patch Tuesday updates, including over 1,400 fixes with its October upgrade. The company's October 2025 Patch Tuesday update, by comparison, included fewer than 180 fixes.

Industry observers note that it's important to understand that just about every company that develops software is furiously working to patch its systems before hackers or AI agents exploit vulnerabilities first. And while there are successes (Microsoft is now protecting its customers from thousands of flaws each month), this speed is also inadvertently breaking things along the way. That's not just speculation: According to The Washington Sun, both Wall Street executives and the NSA explained to members of Congress that patching security flaws discovered by AI models caused this week's widespread outages.

Barring some campaign to cover up a coordinated attack on systems and services, it does seem like these outages are simply the result of companies breaking their own products in an attempt to stop AI-assisted hackers from exploiting undiscovered flaws. But that's not all that reassuring, either. AI models are only going to keep getting better at finding vulnerabilities; likewise, AI agents are only improving at hacking into systems autonomously. Companies will need to ramp up their efforts to patch their software before both hackers and AI agents discover those flaws first, and so the cycle will continue. Unless something changes, we may see routine outages as companies try to fix things as rapidly as possible.

In a recent development, the implications aren't specific to any one manufacturer, either. Our world increasingly relies on fewer companies to keep us all connected. We saw that last year, when cloud hosting providers like AWS and Cloudflare each experienced outages. When these services go down, so do all of the networks that rely on them. If AWS or Cloudflare break something while trying to patch their systems, whole parts of the internet go dark.

According to recent reports, of course, it'll only be more difficult for the general public—if not the developers themselves—to recognize when outages are the result of maintenance or a cyberattack. Just because recent outages don't appear to be nefarious in nature, that doesn't mean future outages will be so innocent. For the time being, however, it seems we can worry less about an active cybersecurity incident, and more about how AI is disrupting modern life in ways few of us saw coming.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the news that there is yet another Taylor Sheridan show on the way might not sound surprising, but the Tulsa King spinoff’s unexpected genre shift certainly is a shock. There is a specter haunting TV networks and streaming services, and its name is Taylor Sheridan. The prolific writer/director first rose to prominence thanks to his screenplays for the hit movies Sicario, Hell or High Water, and Wind River.

Recent findings suggest that however, Sheridan truly came into his own with the success of his Neo-Western TV franchise Yellowstone. The saga of the Dutton family and their beloved eponymous ranch lasted five seasons and spawned as many spinoffs, between the prequels 1883 and 1923, the sequels Dutton Ranch and Marshals, and the upcoming third prequel 1944. Viewers can debate whether Marshals or Dutton Ranch is Yellowstone’s true successor, but one thing is beyond debate.

Between this franchise, the five-season crime drama Mayor of Kingstown, the three-season spy series Lioness, the family drama The Madison, the oil business saga Landman, and the crime comedy Tulsa King, Sheridan is one of TV’s biggest creators right now. He is also a writer/director with a recognizable style and a reliable set of recurring themes, something that has only been marginally altered by Tulsa King, but now seems set to be thoroughly rearranged by its spinoff, Frisco King.

It has been revealed that there is no shortage of killer mob reveals on streaming right now, and, even within this genre, there is no shortage of mob shows specifically focusing on aging gangsters trying to secure their legacies without getting themselves killed. This basic plot is shared by the BBC’s grim two-season hit This City Is Ours, Guy Ritchie’s glossier and more operatic, but no less brutal MobLand, and even Sheridan’s own three-season hit Tulsa King.

Debuting in 2022, Tulsa King follows Sylvester Stallone’s New York career criminal Dwight "The General" Manfredi as he is exiled to Tulsa by the mob. Manfredi’s former mafia colleagues make up an excuse about him setting up a crime syndicate in the sleepy city to cover up what is clearly intended to be a retirement post, only for Stallone’s indefatigable antihero to end up building an unlikely empire in Tulsa.

While Ethan Hawke’s neo-noir The Lowdown is the stronger Tulsa-based crime comedy, this is mostly due to Tulsa King’s uneven tone. Tulsa King is, as many critics have noted over the years, a weird blend of surprisingly straightforward dark crime thrills and playful, goofy midlife crisis dramedy. Tulsa King’s tone, as a result, feels like the comedy of Analyze This blended with the sudden bloody brutality of The Departed.

It has been revealed that luckily, Frisco King has already proven that the show empathically will not be repeating this mistake. After years of fun thrillers like The Hitman’s Bodyguard, The Kill Room, and Just Play Dead, Jackson’s latest show keeps this trend going strong with a trailer that is far more action comedy than crime drama. Viewers expecting something akin to the glum melodrama of Sheridan’s Mayor of Kingstown will need to look elsewhere.

This genre shift might be a surprise, but it is a thoroughly welcome one. After Jackson’s mafia hitman, Russell Lee Washington Jr, opted not to fulfill his contract to kill Stallone’s antihero and instead went into business with him, the character was always going to need to flee his native Fresh York. However, arriving in the sunny suburbs of Frisco, Texas puts Jackson’s career criminal in a comically unfamiliar setting.

When they’re not taking themselves painfully seriously, Sheridan’s indicates can be funny in a dark, deadpan manner. However, the first trailer for Frisco King promises a more broadly comedic, openly playful and farcical series with a winking sense of humor and plenty of outrageous gags, and this could be a welcome change of pace after the unclear tone of Tulsa King’s lengthy run.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Looks like Hollywood could be heading into the new year with relief on a national level. The push to pass a federal film and television tax credit by the end of 2026 picked up momentum on Friday at a White House press conference, where President Trump mentioned his administration was actively negotiating the measure and predicted it would pass.

In a recent development, “It’s running its way through Congress, and it has unbelievable support,” Trump said. He singled out Senator Adam Schiff, the California Democrat who introduced the bill with Republican Senator Tim Scott of South Carolina back in September, and said, “I tell you what, Adam Schiff said, ‘Wow, we love that bill.’ Adam Schiff said that.” Related Stories ‘Disclosure Day’ Did Its Biggest Stunts Practically, So the VFX Team Worked Hard to Look Invisible — Watch How World-Class Filmmaker Andrey Zvyagintsev Came Back to Life for ‘Minotaur’.

According to recent reports, trump mentioned Georgia and Latest Jersey by name as states with good tax credits for film and TV production, but argued that those incentives alone would not bring enough production work back from overseas. With a federal credit, he mentioned, “Hollywood would open again.”.

Trump remarked his administration was also negotiating whether to extend the measure to benefit movie theaters, but said the matter was unsettled. He first publicly called for a federal production incentive in August after meeting with actor Jon Voight: one of three industry “special ambassadors” he appointed early last year.

The bill’s sponsors unveiled more than 60 latest House cosponsors and four new Senate cosponsors on Thursday morning — with lawmakers from both parties signing on in both chambers. The following day, Trump himself brought up the Motion Picture, Television, and Entertainment Revitalization Act in response to a question about whether he could work with Democrats. Calling the bill “very bipartisan,” he mentioned, “I can tell you right now it’s going to happen.”.

Trump gave no timetable, though earlier this week, Representative Linda Sánchez, one of the bill’s House sponsors from California, called for Congress to pass it before 2027 so productions could qualify for benefits on the first of the year.

“Members of both parties have watched jobs in their districts move overseas,” she mentioned in a release from Schiff’s office sent to the press. “Momentum is on our side, and we need to strike while the iron is hot by passing this bill before the end of the year.”.

A floor vote has yet to be confirmed, but multiple sources told IndieWire the measure would move faster if attached to a stopgap government funding bill. If passed and approved, the federal initiative would give qualifying film and TV productions a 20 percent credit on labor expenses for American workers. The credit could reach 30 percent for productions that qualify for bonuses.

For crews accustomed to watching projects follow tax breaks to Canada or the U.K., the proposal would give producers a clear financial incentive to keep that work here for them in the U.S. The bill’s new Senate cosponsors include Republicans Katie Britt of Alabama and Thom Tillis of North Carolina — as well as Democrats Chris Coons of Delaware and Dick Durbin of Illinois.

The AFL-CIO and the American Hotel & Lodging Association also endorsed the bill, joining a coalition that already included IATSE, SAG-AFTRA, the Directors Guild of America, and the Motion Picture Association.

“Given the support from Republicans and Democrats in both chambers and the president, we can get this legislation across the finish line,” Schiff mentioned.

According to recent reports, marvel establishes its latest psychic powerhouse as the one X-Men character who could render Emma Frost obsolete. Overshadowing Emma Frost is no easy task, as the White Queen ranks among the most skilled and powerful telepaths on Earth, an Omega-level mental force capable of matching Charles Xavier and Jean Grey in sheer potential, and also benefiting from a secondary mutation that shields her body from physical injury and her mind from psychic attacks. Emma Frost has also cemented herself as one of mutantkind's best leaders, having gone from one of their many enemies to a permanent guide to the X-Men and other mutant squads.

Alongside psychic heavyweights like Professor X, Jean Grey, Psylocke, Kwannon, Rachel Summers, Cable, Nate Grey, Quentin Quire, Legion, and Dani Moonstar, Emma Frost belongs to one of the most common mutant mutant archetypes in the Marvel Universe, which overflows with powerful telepaths and telekinetics. Naturally, mutantkind’s rogues' gallery mirrors the heroes' psychic abundance with telepaths of their own, from ancient astral parasites like the Shadow King and Cassandra Nova to the Mastermind family, Mesmero, Exodus, Selene, Stryfe, Madelyne Pryor, Gamesmaster, and the psychic entity Onslaught.

As if this quantity of psychic X-Men characters weren't enough, Marvel has also introduced mutants with the overpowered ability to copy superpowers, which naturally entail the replication of Professor X, Jean Grey, and Emma Frost's signature abilities.

In the pages of X-Men United, Justina LaGuardia aka Superior steps out of the shadows to confront Emma Frost threaten her status as mutantkind's foremost psychic. Justina’s unique mutant gift lets her replicate and immediately surpass any mutant power she encounters, which means that merely standing near the White Queen automatically elevates Justina’s telepathy far above Emma’s own Omega-level power. As flashbacks in X-Men United #9 reveal, Justina actually psychically overpowered Emma in the 1990s, secretly implanting the mental suggestion that drove Emma to host the fateful Hellfire Club truce dinner where the original Hellions were slaughtered.

The main cover for X-Men United #9 is an homage to Astonishing X-Men #2, where Emma places her hands over Cyclops' naked eyes.

Now targeting Emma Frost’s newly introduced Graymatter Lane school, Justina LaGuardia intends to tear down the White Queen’s authority and expose how easily mutantkind’s proudest telepath can be outclassed. Justina stayed hidden for decades after she rejected Charles Xavier’s original invitation to become a founding X-Man because she despised Xavier’s naive idealism and saw superheroes as reckless vigilantes. After decades of amassing wealth and secret influence, Justina’s antagonistic initiative is to assemble a private arsenal and army to wage a war against mutantkind and tear the X-Men apart.

Recent findings suggest that justina LaGuardia's ability to replicate and surpass any mutant power is so broken that Marvel will probably need to introduce a clear limitation to keep future X-Men battles dramatic. In that regard, Justina runs straight into the same narrative roadblock as Isca the Unbeaten, whose Omega-level mutant gift literally prevents her from ever losing. Since an automatic-victory power removes all tension from a fight, Marvel had to sideline Isca on Arakko and exploit her compulsion to switch sides whenever victory probability changes, thus preventing one of the most effective mutant fighters from becoming a regular fixture.

It has been revealed that without a similar weakness, Justina’s "Superior" mutation inevitably flattens every confrontation, not only with psychic mutants like Emma Frost, but also with all mutantkind as a whole. Marvel can resolve this problem by establishing strict rules for her power, such as forcing her to endure overwhelming mental feedback when copying multiple Omega-level minds, limiting her to one mirrored ability at a time, or leaving her completely vulnerable to non-mutant threats like human technology, magic, and baseline fighters whose skills fall outside mutant genetics. Emma Frost herself once got a weakness to balance her power, with her diamond form preventing her from using her psychic skills.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Jensen Huang’s resignation as Nvidia CEO shook up the AI market and US economy last week, but now via The Wall Street Journal Huang has spoken out publicly for the first time since stepping down, and he signals he’s ready to return as CEO if asked.

Today Robbie Whelan at The Wall Street Journal published Jensen Huang’s first public statement since departing Nvidia last week.

It has been revealed that “Since my departure, I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from Nvidia’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO,” Huang said in a short statement. “If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.”.

To be clear, I’m also willing to step in as CEO of Nvidia if asked. I’ve owned several generations of their graphics cards, so I have plenty of experience with their products. More importantly, this is probably my best chance of finally having enough cash to afford a Mac with 32GB of RAM.

The timing is likely no coincidence, as Nvidia is set to report its quarterly earnings later today.

Even though Huang technically resigned as CEO rather than being fired, it was clear that his ouster wasn’t exactly his choice. Thus, today’s statement is the former CEO formally putting it out into the world that he’s ready to return if asked.

According to recent reports, since Huang stepped down, President Trump publicly called on Apple’s Tim Cook to step in as Nvidia CEO. But it’s expected that a new CEO—assuming it’s not Huang—will take much longer for the organization to find and Cook is unlikely to want the job.

What do you make of Huang’s remarks today? Let us know in the comments.

Sources indicate that I've been using the XGIMI MoGo 3 Pro since it came out in 2024 and have been recommending it to friends and family every chance I get. It promptly became my favorite portable projector, and two years later, it's still my go-to for a spontaneous projector session. If you're on the lookout for a good deal on a portable projector, I recommend considering the following XGIMI deals.

According to recent reports, if you're looking for the most affordable option, the Vibe One projector is just $179 (originally $299) after a 40% discount. This is a 1080p resolution and 1500:1 contrast portable projector for casual watching at night with 250 ISO lumens of brightness, and the price reflects that. It already comes with Google TV, which is my favorite OS, so you can download and stream any app you want. It's battery-powered, which means you can take it anywhere with you (as long as you have wifi). The battery lasts up to 1.2 hours for projecting video (in Eco Mode), and up to four hours as a speaker (it has built-in dual 3W JBL speakers). The auto keystone from XGIMI is one of the best ones I've experienced among all of the projectors I've tested, and it will adjust to practically any surface you cast it on, which can, with the 160° adjustable built-in stand, even be the ceiling. The current bundle brings an 80-inch screen included in the price.

In a recent development, if you have a bit more money to splurge, the MoGo 4 is the same concept as the Vibe One but takes its specs to the next level, and it's available starting at $359 (originally $499). It's still small and compact with 1080p resolution, but it nearly doubles the brightness, with 450 ISO lumens. The battery life more than doubles to two and a half hours in Eco Mode, while still keeping the projector under three pounds. It also has Google TV as its OS, but the projection is 360° with its adjustable built-in stand. You also have the option of getting the bundle with the PowerBase Stand, which extends the battery to five hours. Like the Vibe One, it has a built-in speaker, but this one uses dual 6W Harman Kardon speakers with Dolby Audio.The MoGo 4 Laser is a slightly upgraded version that uses triple laser technology for a better picture. It still supports 1080p resolution, but it's brighter with 550 ISO lumens and a 1000:1 contrast. The battery life, OS system, stand, speakers, and auto keystone technology are the same—but the bundles are different, so they're worth considering if they fit your needs.

If you're looking for a premium portable projector, the Horizon 30 Pro is a great option that competes with the best options on the market. It supports 4K resolution, uses RGB triple laser brightness that reaches 4800 ISO lumens (bright enough to see during the day), has a 120Hz refresh rate and gaming features to make gaming smooth, displays an 8,000:1 native contrast to make colors and blacks pop, and supports IMAX Enhanced, Dolby Vision, and HDR10+. It has an adjustable stand like the other XGIMI projectors and its own dual 12W Harman Kardon speakers with DTS Virtual:X and DTS-HD. The auto keystone is just as powerful as the other options, but the lens adds an optical zoom and a Lens Memory feature, which lets you save up to six custom lens and image setups and recall them with a click. Right now, it's down to $1,899 (originally $2,499) after a 24% discount.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, so you’re trying to pick between the $99 Fitbit Air and the $179 Fitbit Edge. Both have a lot in common — they share the same heart rate sensor, charger, and Google Health app ecosystem. But there are also a lot of differences between the two fresh trackers. I’ve been wearing the Fitbit Air since it launched in May 2026, and I’ve recently taken it off my wrist to test the new Fitbit Edge. Read on to find out what I liked and disliked.

If you’re looking to read reviews of both trackers before Black Friday, check out our Fitbit Air review as well as our Fitbit Edge review here on Tom’s Guide.

According to recent reports, with no screen, buttons, or alerts to distract you — plus nearly a week of battery — the Fitbit Air is as easy-going as it is affordable. It’s also one of the best fitness trackers of the year and our overall favorite tracker for most Fitbit fans.

Sources indicate that the Fitbit Edge is the perfect successor to the Fitbit Charge 6. It sports a bigger/brighter display, easier-to-use controls, more accurate elevation tracking, access to Google's latest health and safety features, and better battery performance. In our Fitbit Edge review, we said it offers just the right amount of fitness tracker for most folks.

If you’re into running, walking, or cycling, the choice is an obvious one — for $80 more than the Fitbit Air, you’re definitely getting a better fitness tracker with the Fitbit Edge. It has built-in GPS, which means you can leave your phone at home, and a 1.34-inch AMOLED display, which allows you to see live feedback as you move.

The Fitbit Edge also has an altimeter, which tracks your elevation during workouts and how many stairs you’ve climbed during the day, and an ECG monitor.

Despite being bigger and heavier than the Fitbit Air, the Fitbit Edge still does a good job of disappearing on the wrist. It’s dainty, and Google has released a huge range of swappable straps to suit every style. If you want a fitness tracker that’ll disappear, this isn’t quite as tiny as the Fitbit Air, but it still ticks that box.

At 32g and 11.58mm thick, the Fitbit Edge is by no means bulky on the wrist, especially compared to the likes of the Apple Watch Ultra 4 I’m normally wearing. That stated, compared to the Fitbit Air, it’s still not as comfortable to wear overnight. One of the main selling points of the Fitbit Air is its ultra-light design. It weighs in at 12g, and the textile band is fast-drying, so unlike others on the market (cough, Garmin Cirqa) you won’t be left with a soggy wrist after showering, swimming, or washing the dishes.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

There’s a reason why screenless trackers seem to be a growing trend: once you lose the non-stop buzzing on your wrist, it’s really hard to go back. Again, the Google ecosystem and the fact that these two Fitbits share a charger allows you to swap between the two, but if you’re looking for health, recovery, and sleep tracking and already own a regular watch, the Fitbit Air is the obvious choice.

It’s also worth noting here that, from a health perspective, you’re getting the same experience with the Fitbit Air, and it’s nearly half the price.

Fitbit promises seven days of battery life on both devices, and while I found that to be true with the Fitbit Air, no matter how many workouts I did, it was a different story with the Fitbit Edge.

Of course, this is largely down to the built-in GPS. Out of the box, the GPS on the device is automatically set to dynamic, which means it switches between using your phone’s GPS and the built-in GPS. When you switch the tracker to using the built-in GPS, I found it takes a hit on battery life, using around 11% for an hour-long run, and it didn’t last a full week.

When you switch the tracker to using the built-in GPS, I found it takes a hit on battery life, using around 11% for an hour-long run.

That remarked, for most casual runners, dynamic GPS is more than enough, and you’re probably not clocking hour-long workouts every day.

As I’ve mentioned before, I’m frustrated by how little the Fitbit Edge’s button actually does. Sure, I love a physical button on a fitness tracker, but I’m not sure why Google didn’t give the Fitbit Edge’s button more functionality.

For example, you’d expect the button to start a run, not just stop it; instead, you still need to tap the screen before you start moving. Any runner knows nothing’s more frustrating than trying to swipe a touchscreen with sweaty fingers, especially on the start or finish line of a race.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • More than that, VSCO Studio Pro integrates with the firm’s broader ecosystem of photography tools, allowing consumers to manage their workflow from importing and editing photos to delivering finished images to clients through VSCO Galleries, without having to manually export and upload them to another app.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, VSCO today released Studio Pro Desktop, its first native photo editor for Mac, bringing many of the organization’s familiar editing tools to macOS, alongside new features aimed at photographers working with large numbers of images. Here are the details.

Professional and amateur photographers just got a new alternative for editing and managing their photos on Mac with the release of VSCO Studio Pro, a native macOS app that brings the firm’s popular editing tools to the desktop for the first time.

More than that, VSCO Studio Pro integrates with the firm’s broader ecosystem of photography tools, allowing consumers to manage their workflow from importing and editing photos to delivering finished images to clients through VSCO Galleries, without having to manually export and upload them to another app.

It also supports keyboard shortcuts similar to those found in other popular photo editors, making it easier for photographers familiar with those apps to get started.

Here’s Eric Wittman, CEO of VSCO, on today’s launch:.

Recent findings suggest that “Photographers deserve tools built around how they actually work. […] 75% of VSCO Pro members have used our presets in the last six months. Now those looks live on the desktop, with one connected workflow from camera to client delivery and nothing getting in the way.

In a recent development, the first thing owners will notice, and then continue to notice when using VSCO Studio Pro, is how fast it is. From changing the grid size, to sorting images, to applying presets by rolling the cursor over each of the 200+ presets, pretty much everything about VSCO Studio Pro feels as real-time and instant as it can be when dealing with large numbers of images.

As for importing photos, VSCO Studio Pro supports Apple Photos, local folders, SD cards, and external drives, and offers RAW compatibility with more than 800 cameras from 20 brands. Users can also choose whether to work with files in their original location or copy them elsewhere.

Under the hood, VSCO Studio Pro Desktop combines Apple’s Core Image RAW processing with the company’s own Reflex image processing engine, which handles presets and editing adjustments.

Batch editing in VSCO Studio Pro Desktop can handle anywhere from two to 500 images at once, which is great for quickly applying the same preset or film-inspired look (including Kodak Portra, Kodachrome, Fujifilm Velvia, and Kodak Tri-X), or making adjustments to an entire set of photos simultaneously, with changes appearing across all selected images in real time.

And speaking of presets, VSCO Studio Pro packs an exclusive one called IOE1 Pro, developed with photographer Joe Greer. IOE1 Pro, as well as VSCO’s other presets, allow customers to adjust the strength, color, tone, and contrast, further helping them fine-tune each look to their liking.

VSCO Studio Pro’s editing tools include the usual suspects photographers might expect from photo editing software, including exposure, contrast, fade, highlights, shadows, whites, blacks, skin tone, temperature, tint, hue, saturation, lightness, sharpening, clarity, vignetting, and grain adjustments for strength, size, and color.

VSCO is also working to expand its toolset to include bloom and halation effects, curves, masks, and a remove tool for owners looking for more control over their edits and to make more precise, localized adjustments to their images.

Also in the works are new organizational features, including projects for managing groups of photos, as well as culling tools that will allow consumers to rate images with stars and mark them as accepted or rejected, making it easier to sort through large photo collections.

Once users are happy with their adjustments, they can export their photos individually or in batches, choosing the file name, format, resolution, and compression quality. VSCO Studio Pro also offers resizing presets for web, social media, and client delivery, as well as the option to save the finished images to a folder of their choice.

And speaking of client delivery, customers can publish their edited photos directly to VSCO Galleries, allowing them to share full-resolution images without having to export them and upload them separately elsewhere.

Sources indicate that VSCO Studio Pro Desktop is available today as a free download for Apple Silicon Macs, with full feature access requiring a VSCO Pro membership, starting at $4.99 per month or $59.99 per year, or a VSCO One membership. You can see it in action below:.

The 5 Most Unwatchable Thrillers Released Since 2000, Ranked

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The thriller is one of the most timeless and popular genres in cinema.
  • However, on the opposite end of the spectrum, the most unwatchable thrillers are lame, uninteresting, and ultimately unworthy of your time.
  • Industry observers note that basic Instinct 2 is a sequel to, you guessed it, Basic Instinct, and sees Sharon Stone reprising her role as the murderous temptress Catherine Trammell.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The thriller is one of the most timeless and popular genres in cinema. Who doesn't love to be shocked and challenged by tales of danger, betrayal, deceit, and murder? Indeed, many of the all-time greatest movies belong to this riveting genre. A great thriller can keep you on the edge of your seat, second-guessing every move, every line, until the very end, when a cathartic reveal makes everything worthwhile.

However, on the opposite end of the spectrum, the most unwatchable thrillers are lame, uninteresting, and ultimately unworthy of your time. Whether because of their silly stories, misguided performances, bad direction, or a combination of multiple factors, these thrillers fail to impress and instead settle for mediocrity. The entries on this list are the most unworthy thrillers released this century, and while some might not rank among cinema's all-time worst, they are certainly not worth watching either.

Industry observers note that basic Instinct 2 is a sequel to, you guessed it, Basic Instinct, and sees Sharon Stone reprising her role as the murderous temptress Catherine Trammell. This time, she's in London and comes under Scotland Yard's suspicion when her latest boyfriend dies in a car crash. Court-appointed psychiatrist Michael Glass (David Morrisey) treats her for "risk addiction" (lol) and becomes trapped in her web of seduction and danger.

Industry observers note that the original Basic Instinct isn't exactly great cinema, but it has value, not only as a solidly crafted erotic thriller, but also as a sordid noir powered by a terrific Stone. This baffling sequel has no redeeming quality, and saying so is no exaggeration. The plot is weak to the point of ridicule, and the acting isn't much better. Morrisey and Stone are usually great actors, but here, they're unconvincing at best and genuinely bad at worst. It's not like the script is giving them anything to work with, but they are also doing next to nothing to sell, much less elevate, what's there, delivering each line with all the subtlety of a chainsaw.

Industry observers note that heather Graham and Joseph Fiennes star in Killing Me Softly, one of the worst erotic thrillers this century. The film follows Alice (Graham), an American woman who leaves her boyfriend for Adam (Fiennes), a mysterious mountain climber. After a whirlwind romance that ends in a quick marriage, Alice begins suspecting Adam, questioning his elusive past and the fates of his previous lovers.

Killing Me Softly is director Chen Kaige's only English-language film, and it's no wonder why. Based on the eponymous 1999 book, this cheap effort is the erotic thriller at its laziest and most salacious. Even worse, it's not even entertaining in a so-bad-it's-good kind of way — in fact, it's boring, and so nonsensical that one can't help but roll one's eyes once the "mysteries" start taking shape. Hollywood has never known exactly what to do with Graham and Fiennes, but the truth is, they are simply too talented to be stuck in such mediocre thrillers.

John Travolta steps into the shoes of gangster John Gotti in a biopic that might just be as infamous as its real-life subject. Appropriately titled Gotti, the film chronicles decades in the mobster's life, including his rise as the head of the Gambino crime family, his many legal troubles, and his contentious relationships with his wife, Victoria (Kelly Preston), and son, John Gotti Jr. (Spencer Lofranco).

In a recent development, gotti has been ridiculed enough, and it's not hard to see why. It's the typical movie that sees itself as "serious" and "heavy"; alas, the only thing that's "heavy" here is the mounting prosthetics on Travolta's face. Director Kevin Connolly is hilariously out of his depth here, struggling to maintain the barest sense of momentum and drowning the film in a dull pacing only livened by moments of unintentional ridicule. For some reason, Travolta and the script try hard to glorify Gotti, and the result is a movie that is outright problematic. Chances are you won't make it past the first thirty minutes, so this puzzling biopic truly amounts to the cinematic equivalent of a whisper into the void.

It has been revealed that directed by Daniel Farrands and starring Hilary Duff (who should really know better), The Haunting of Sharon Tate is as offensive and terrible as the offensively terrible title implies. The plot follows Tate (Duff) in the days leading up to her murder as she has visions of the attack she'll suffer at the hands of the Manson Family. The film also stars the once-Aaron Samuels, Jonathan Bennett.

This borderline insulting movie is what happens when people sacrifice their decency for a check. Indeed, The Haunting of Sharon Tate is outright offensive, an insult to one of Hollywood's biggest victims that exploits the very real, very tragic circumstances of Tate's death in service of a cheap movie that shouldn't even exist. The acting is bad, the screenplay ridiculous, the directing clumsy, and the "twist" ending is the stuff of cinematic nightmares. Sloppily made and in offensively poor taste, few movies are as morally bankrupt and utterly contemptible as this one.

Let's end with a true cinematic dud, shall we? The Last Days of American Crime stars an ensemble cast led by Édgar Ramírez and is set in a near-future United States, where the government will soon launch a "synaptic blocker" that will prevent people from willingly committing crimes. A group of thieves races against the clock to pull off one last, ambitious heist before the signal activates. The film is based on the eponymous 2009 comic.

It has been revealed that the premise is intriguing, but sadly, the execution is truly terrible. The Last Days of American Crime is among the worst movies of the 21st century; there really is no other way to put it. At a whopping 149 minutes, the movie is so dull it's unbearable, offering violence for violence's sake and ultimately amounting to a hollow, cheap, and shameful experience. It was also a victim of a woefully bad release date, coming out at the height of the 2020 police protests, a fact that made it seem all the more out of touch and tone-deaf.

Recent findings suggest that for well over two decades, One Piece has held on tight to its status as one of the "Major Three" shonen anime. And yet, there is no denying that One Piece has skyrocketed in popularity in the last couple of years. For the most part, Netflix's live-action One Piece series is what has catapulted the franchise into never-before-seen mainstream popularity.

That stated, arguably well before the Netflix live-action could come around, the introduction of Gear Five in the anime and the Wano Arc's jaw-dropping animation was already pushing many towards giving One Piece a chance or finally catching up to all the new good stuff. And, now, in only a few more weeks, One Piece's most revolutionary arc is going to be a whole lot easier to stream.

Sources indicate that in a recent post on X, Netflix officially confirmed that One Piece's Wano Arc is finally making its way to the platform on December 15 across multiple regions, including the United States. The final batch of One Piece's Whole Cake Island Arc (Episodes 878–891) only just dropped on Netflix on November 15, 2026. And in just 4 weeks, the widely loved Wano Arc will also finally be available on Netflix as well, finally rounding out its One Piece offerings.

Recent findings suggest that for the longest time, One Piece's Wano Arc was only available on Crunchyroll. Netflix has gradually been licensing One Piece's anime since 2020, rolling out arc after arc starting right from the beginning. As of the Egghead Arc, the anime's newest episodes began making their way to Netflix a week after their release.

But still, even though Netflix had the newest episodes, its One Piece collection was still largely incomplete, missing a good chunk in between, including the Wano Arc, which concluded with Episode 1085 around this time, three whole years ago, and first aired seven years ago, kicking off in July 2019.

Granted, in view of One Piece's newest arcs, it's hard to still call Wano One Piece's best arc. Be it in terms of storytelling or animation, the Egghead Arc easily surpasses Wano with its masterful portrayal of Kuma and Bonney's backstory or even the more refined depiction of Gear Five.

Even so, this does not take away from the fact that the Wano Arc is still One Piece's most revolutionary arc. The grand scale of Wano's story, its distinct art direction by the late Tatsuya Nagamine, and its discernible boost in quality all make the arc a major turning point for One Piece's anime.

Sources indicate that wano set the bar higher, and trying to surpass that bar is what has given fans such spectacular anime adaptations of the Egghead and Elbaph arcs. As such, the Wano Arc holds a special place for many, especially with how Gear Five famously broke the internet with its anime debut. And finally, fans can revisit this nostalgic moment and more when One Piece's Wano Arc finally makes its way to Netflix on December 15.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, we’ve come a long way since Katniss Everdeen volunteered as tribute in “The Hunger Games.” It’s been almost 15 years since Jennifer Lawrence delivered that line and became an iconic action heroine. “The Hunger Games” brought the young adult genre to new heights and proved that these movies could be legitimate blockbusters by every measure.

Recent findings suggest that after four flagship movies and one prequel, the franchise heads back to the past again in “The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping.” The prequel revisits Haymitch Abernathy (Joseph Zada) as a teenager competing in the 50th Hunger Games. Where does Haymitch’s outing rank among the franchise’s best movies? Let’s get into the rankings.

In a recent development, by the time “The Hunger Games” reached its conclusion, the franchise had run out of gas. After saving a brainwashed Peeta (Josh Hutcherson), President Coin (Julianne Moore) tasks Katniss and her band of rebels with liberating District 2 before retaking the Capitol. It's the final push to overthrow President Snow, but as Katniss pursues revenge, she begins to question the rebellion’s true intentions.

“The Hunger Games: Mockingjay – Part 2” isn’t necessarily a bad movie. The familiar group-on-one-last-mission trope builds to an exciting conclusion. However, it’s more concerned with reaching the finish line than saying anything latest.

Recent findings suggest that splitting “Mockingjay” into two parts made financial sense, as the two movies combined to gross over $1.4 billion worldwide. Story-wise, a 390-page novel doesn’t need more than four hours of screen time. Whenever you end a movie on an unresolved cliffhanger, more often than not, fans are going to reject it. Guess what? Many fans, myself included, rejected the ending of “Mockingjay – Part 1.”.

Recent findings suggest that after being rescued from the arena in “Catching Fire,” Katniss is taken to the secret underground city of District 13. There, President Coin convinces Katniss to live up to her mockingjay reputation and become the face of the rebellion. Katniss eventually agrees to Coin’s request because she wants to save Peeta, who is being held captive in the Capitol. It’s the first movie in the franchise without the chaos of the arena, so expect less action. However, “Mockingjay – Part 1” is the best political thriller of the bunch, as it emphasizes its anti-war and anti-fascist themes the best.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Coming after the success of the four “Hunger Games” movies, “The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes” had low odds of achieving success, though not as low as some of the tributes entering the arena. A upcoming cast meant the absence of Lawrence, Hutcherson, Hemsworth, and the rest of the original ensemble. Second, it’s a prequel set before the days of Katniss Everdeen. Most importantly, it’s a story about a young President Snow — yes, the same tyrannical dictator who would rule Panem for decades. How are audiences supposed to sympathize with and grow attached to the future villain of the main trilogy?

It has been revealed that that’s the best trick “The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes” pulls off: no sympathy for Snow. You don’t feel sorry for him. Instead, it explores how trauma and grief can send a man down a path where embracing evil seems preferable to enduring hardship.

In the film, a young Coriolanus "Coryo" Snow (Tom Blyth) mentors District 12’s Lucy Gray Baird (Rachel Zegler) in the 10th Hunger Games. It’s the most grounded arena battle in the franchise, and the violence feels worse than ever before. It’s a fascinating origin story that had no business being this effective.

Recent findings suggest that “The Hunger Games” is known for having a deep bench of talented supporting actors. Woody Harrelson famously played Haymitch Abernathy, a former winner of the Games who mentored Katniss and Peeta in District 12. Haymitch was first introduced as a drunk and despondent former victor who wanted nothing to do with the Hunger Games. As the movies progressed, viewers learned that Haymitch was one of the rebellion’s allies and had been for a long time.

Sources indicate that why was Haymitch depressed all those years? “The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping” fills in the blanks, as it revisits Haymitch’s win in the 50th Hunger Games, the second Quarter Quell. Zada stars as the 16-year-old Haymitch, who is much happier thanks to the love of his family and girlfriend, Lenora Dove Baird (Whitney Peak).

Sources indicate that after witnessing the Capitol’s hostility, Haymitch becomes the key figure in a plot to sabotage the Games once and for all. It’s a tad too long, but this movie soars because of Zada, who injects so much life and passion into his portrayal of Haymitch. It’s a true movie-star-in-the-making performance. Don’t be surprised if Marvel or DC is calling Zada to put on a cape in a few years.

Recent findings suggest that the movie that kicked off the young adult dystopian movie wave was 2012’s “The Hunger Games.” On the day of the reaping, Katniss volunteers to take her younger sister’s place in the 74th Hunger Games. Katniss and Peeta, her fellow District 12 tribute, enter the arena with little hope of surviving. As the Games progress, Katniss reluctantly becomes a symbol of hope, and her defiance lays the foundation for a rebellion.

“The Hunger Games” was revolutionary for its time. It proved a young adult action franchise could be a profitable endeavor ($695 million worldwide). Lawrence became a legitimate star and rose to A-list status, which she maintains in 2026. The movie depicts a battle to the death, but its messages about authoritarianism, exploitation, and inequality are very sophisticated for a teen drama. Plus, it breaks an unwritten Hollywood rule—don’t kill kids. I commend the film for having the guts to show Rue’s death. Throw your 3s in the air!

There was only one answer. I consider myself a “real fan” of “The Hunger Games,” and real ones know that “Catching Fire” is the best book and movie in the franchise. It’s the best action movie of the bunch, with the most innovative arena, a top-notch supporting cast, and riveting twists. After Katniss and Peeta defy the Capitol, President Snow makes the duo parade around the districts to eliminate civil unrest.

When that doesn’t work, Snow announces a twist for the 75th Hunger Games: All tributes will be former winners. In other words, it’s back to the arena for Katniss and Peeta. “Catching Fire” has by far the best in-arena sequences, with my favorite scene being the opening of the Games, where Katniss teams up with her new ally (Finnick) to save Peeta. Forget the young adult genre; “Catching Fire” is an excellent action movie that improves upon its predecessor in nearly every way.
