I'm quite pleased by the tech architecture of my art website

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1436 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Klauria

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It is a truth universally acknowledged, that every developer blog begins by explaining the new static site generator they wrote to make it.
  • Earlier this year I decided to put a some of my paintings and sketchbook pages online.
  • Sources indicate that when it comes to tech side projects there are two wolves inside me.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It is a truth universally acknowledged, that every developer blog begins by explaining the new static site generator they wrote to make it. This post isnât exactly that, but maybe only on a technicality, in that itâs not about this websiteâ¦.

Earlier this year I decided to put a some of my paintings and sketchbook pages online. I donât much use social media besides Hacker News, but I wanted to share my work with friends and family. So Iâd been sending scans of my work in group chats. That was fine for a bit but so messy and disorganized. Sometimes someone asked, âWhere did you paint this?â Sometimes a friend wanted to see what it looked like in real life. My little brother suggested a map with a marker for each piece. That was a good idea! For that Iâd need a website and some code. Here, take a look at the map, its done now! You can zoom and click on markers to see the painting!

Sources indicate that when it comes to tech side projects there are two wolves inside me. One is the Wolf of Pragmatism, which wants to smash every problem with whatever hammer is nearest at hand: âIsnât this just some trivial React? Dump the images in S3 and call it a day. This website is for friends and family; you have no traffic to speak of. Put a CDN in front so your parents in India get reasonable performance.â.

Sources indicate that the other is the Aesthetic Wolf: âThis should be a static website. The content almost never changes.â.

It has been revealed that yes. This is a static website. I do at most four, and on average less than 0.3, paintings a day. The content almost never changes. Why should javascript render the page on the userâs browser? Why should any code even run on the server? I should have the bytes for every page just sitting there, ready to be shipped. The correct server implementation for this problem is open followed by sendfile inside the event loop (Iâm joking but only kind of?). The Aesthetic Wolf won.

In a recent development, but the problem with a static website is that for every latest post, I need to add a file, and run a build, and deploy it to production. I made a hundred paintings this year! Even if I automate a lot of it, I wanted a better UI for stuff like adding tags and setting location. And the best UI for whatâs essentially a CRUD app is â¦ probably a web UI. But if I have a web UI that changes the content of the website, thatâs not a static website any more.

Now look at this colorful house!

Recent findings suggest that so what I really want is a website thatâs static for everyone else, but dynamic for me. I want a build system but I want it triggered by actions in a nice CRUD UI that I make, not GitHub actions or a terminal.

Hereâs my silly little solution to this silly conundrum. Iâm sure the design Iâm about to describe isnât novel, but I did come up with it. Iâm just pleased by it because itâs an efficient solution to the exact problem I happened to have. Itâs dollar-efficient for me, i.e., itâs free*. Itâs resource-efficient for Cloudflare, because the static assets are rarely rebuilt and mostly sit there cached. And itâs fast, because the bytes are mostly sitting there in a CDN waiting to be sent.

Sources indicate that (Asterisk: the compute and bandwidth are free. The storage is right now free, but if I paint enough then Iâll go past the 10 GB free tier and pay a couple cents per month.).

Sources indicate that the main idea is that every html page is rendered on the server, but with a cache header telling Cloudflareâs infrastructure to cache the response forever (well, for 30 days). Then, whenever I upload a fresh art piece or change the set of tags or anything like that, the request handler for this write operation invalidates all cached pages. Thatâs it.

It has been revealed that thereâs one detail that makes this work well for an image-heavy website: we generate several smaller sizes of each image at upload time, and I actually do it on the clientâs browser. Since Iâm the only uploader, that would be my browser. We need the smaller sizes for thumbnails and cards, where sending the full archival images would be way too slow. Those downsampled images are uploaded along with originals to Cloudflareâs R2, their S3-equivalent.

Industry observers note that why downsample at upload time? Cloudflare does offer an image service thatâll do the resizing the first time you make a request for that image at that size, and itâll cache that resized copy. But in my case I already know the three sizes I want, so itâs faster to just precompute and store them. The additional storage doesnât add up to much, because the archival images are enormous compared to downsampled copies.

Recent findings suggest that all the metadata for all pieces goes in a single json file that also lives in R2. When someone requests a dynamic html page, like the one for pieces tagged #summer, a piece of code runs in a Cloudflare worker. It reads the json and generates the html, which is then cached until the next invalidation. Cloudflareâs CDN handles the rest: if someone in India later requests the same page, the cached artifact is sent to an edge machine in India and cached there for a while. I suppose Cloudflare can choose to rerun the worker instead of copying the artifact, which is fine by me. Based on my testing thatâs not what happens: the generator writes a timestamp on each page so I can see when it was generated.

Industry observers note that the website has some interactive stuff like maps and timelines. Those are just embedded javascript that run on the clientâs browser and read that single metadata json file to initialize. They donât write anything back to the server, so thereâs no database or anything. Theyâre just displaying the information in different ways. For example, hereâs an interactive timeline of my pieces over the years. I havenât uploaded everything Iâve ever made, so this is biased toward recent stuff.

(To be very technically correct, this timeline component doesnât read the json directly. Its bars are drawn on the server, and it gets a per-month list derived from the metadata to handle clicking and paging.).

Sources indicate that hereâs what the page for a piece looks like. The metadata json has the information to figure out what pieces were done nearby and around the same time, so I show all that. This is an embedded iframe so you can scroll and click:.

Sources indicate that this is where Pragmatic Wolf won. Hereâs the possible optimization: whenever I make an edit, we should invalidate only those pages that are potentially affected by that edit. A good build system certainly works this way: when you change one file, it recompiles only those artifacts that (transitively) depend on it.

Industry observers note that in my case, however, dependencies arenât explicitly written down anywhere. The code to generate a page just runs, and potentially any change in the metadata json could cause its output to be different. I could try to encode the dependencies for each page and component, but itâs so easy to get this wrong and introduce bugs in the future. The result is a half-updated website, i.e., a correctness bug.

So while itâs true that adding a new piece only changes the #evening page if the new piece actually has that tag, I considered it too tricky to get this cache invalidation right, and decided to just invalidate everything. If I were using a normal static site generator then the CDN could potentially do this optimization by noticing that the hash of an artifact hasnât changed, so it doesnât need to be updated on every edge machine.

Anyway here is a waterfall in Washington, the one in Twin Peaks apparently:.

And hereâs the view from right outside my house in Brooklyn:.

Industry observers note that by the way, the specific javascript framework I ended up using is called Astro. Cloudflare bought them so theyâre pretty nicely integrated. But you donât really need it for this, you could write your own code to run in the Worker to generate the page. The whole trick is in some careful management of cache.

I spent all night playing GTA 6 — and these 3 PS5 settings made it look and sound incredible

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (661 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomsguide

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that GTA 6 is finally here!
  • Recent findings suggest that we’re talking specifically about the PS5’s settings, since GTA 6 has no graphical settings beyond a motion blur slider.
  • Here are the 3 PS5 settings you need to check to enhance your GTA 6 experience.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that GTA 6 is finally here! It’s easily Rockstar Games’ most ambitious title ever, featuring dense environments and lush soundscapes. You get a rich visual and audio experience out of the box, but tweaking a few PS5 settings can enhance it.

Recent findings suggest that we’re talking specifically about the PS5’s settings, since GTA 6 has no graphical settings beyond a motion blur slider. Even on a PS5 Pro, your options are limited. But with a few smart tweaks, you can make GTA 6 look and sound its best on either PS5 console.

Here are the 3 PS5 settings you need to check to enhance your GTA 6 experience.

This one is for folks who own an OLED TV. In the Video Output tab in System Settings, scroll down to HDR. Click it, and you’ll be taken to another screen to calibrate the console’s HDR.

Industry observers note that you’ll adjust the brightness across three pages. On the first two pages, press up or down until the sun logo disappears. On the last page, dial it all the way down, since your OLED TV can display deep blacks.

It has been revealed that GTA 6 also has in-game HDR calibration. Just follow the on-screen prompts to get your desired result, though I’ve found the default settings work well.

After 13 years of waiting, Grand Theft Auto VI has arrived. Set in the state of Leonida, with Vice City at its heart, you play Jason and Lucia, two criminals forced into an increasingly dangerous situation as they seek their fortune, discovering the darker side of the sunniest spot in America.

GTA 6 is undoubtedly a feast for the eyes, but you shouldn’t neglect the audio side of the equation.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

While the PS5 didn’t launch with Dolby Atmos, it now supports the feature. So if you have a soundbar or surround sound system that supports Dolby Atmos, you should definitely enable it. To do so, go to Sound in System Settings, click Sound Output, scroll down to Audio Format, and select Dolby Atmos.

GTA 6 targets 30 frames per second on all consoles. Rockstar Games even confirmed to Kotaku that the PS5 Pro won’t be patched to run at 40 or 60 fps. That said, we can’t completely rule it out.

If GTA 6 ever adds a performance-enhancing feature, you’ll want to set the PS5 Pro for that. In the Video Output tab of the Screen and Audio settings, make sure that VRR is set to Automatic for unsupported games and that 120Hz output is set to Automatic.

Industry observers note that again, this won’t make GTA 6 run at a higher frame rate, but it prepares your PS5 Pro if it ever does. As a rule of thumb, you should have these settings enabled anyway, since many PlayStation titles offer 40 fps modes.

Until we get the inevitable PC version of GTA 6, we'll have to make do with the experience on existing consoles, in this case, the PS5. That remarked, the advice I've given you should help you get the most from the game. Have fun in Vice City!

Inkling 2 Mini

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3138 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thinkingmachines

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Today we are releasing Inkling 2 Mini, a fast, powerful model that’s small enough to run on your laptop.
  • Industry observers note that inkling 2 Mini is a looped transformer, running the middle layers of the model three times for every token.
  • Inkling 2 Mini is a Mixture-of-Experts model with 26.4B total parameters, 3.4B active, and 5.4B weight activations per token to account for looping.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Today we are releasing Inkling 2 Mini, a fast, powerful model that’s small enough to run on your laptop.

Industry observers note that inkling 2 Mini is a looped transformer, running the middle layers of the model three times for every token. This allows the model to apply more reasoning and reach the right answer with fewer tokens, especially on tasks such as agentic coding that depend on reasoning quality. Inkling 2 Mini leads every open-weights model with less than 100B total parameters on benchmarks such as DeepSWE v1.1 (48.2%) and Vals Index v2.2 (46.5%). It runs faster than similarly performing models as well.

SWE-bench Pro v2 Hard (51 tasks).

Inkling 2 Mini is a Mixture-of-Experts model with 26.4B total parameters, 3.4B active, and 5.4B weight activations per token to account for looping. Looping allows the model to reason longer without writing its reasoning down, which matters for monitoring: our ability to oversee and understand what the model does by reading its chain of thought (CoT).

We measured the impact of looping on both performance and monitorability with Inkling 2 Mini and a research-specific variable-loop variant we are releasing alongside it. The variable-loop model’s no-CoT time horizon improved from 16 seconds at one pass to 37 seconds with three, and its performance on a benchmark of serial reasoning kept improving out to ten loops—twice as many as it was trained with. The model’s chain of thought grew shorter with more loops but stayed legible throughout. The model didn’t trend higher on tests of agentic sabotage as loops were added.

Industry observers note that we’re excited to offer some of the first models with looped architecture available to researchers. The variable-loop model was used for our monitorability experiments as it allows for cleaner comparisons between different looping depths.

Industry observers note that most of Inkling 2 Mini’s weights were trained and are deployed natively in NVFP4, with the last four layers in MXFP8. The total memory footprint of Inkling 2 Mini is ~20GB, allowing it to run on local devices such as consumer laptops and desktop AI computers. Our researchers took Inkling 2 Mini on a flight, where it ran offline on a MacBook Pro and built a playable flight simulator in a few minutes.

Inkling 2 Mini is released with open weights and is available on Tinker today for inference and customization.

Inkling 2 Mini’s strengths mirror those of Inkling 2 Small: it does best on long-horizon agentic work and is the best among open-weights models of similar size on most tasks we measured.

Recent findings suggest that inkling 2 Mini scores ahead of every comparable model on agentic coding benchmarks such as DeepSWE v1.1 and SWE-bench Pro v2, and is behind only Qwen3.8-27B on others. On PMPP-Hard, a kernel-optimization benchmark, it approaches the score of the much larger Inkling 2 Small.

While looping improves the model’s reasoning, it doesn’t enable its weights to store more facts—knowledge is mostly a function of total parameter count. Inkling 2 Mini’s score on AA-Omniscience, a measure of factuality, is in line with other models of the same size. Studying the variable-loop model, we saw that performances on long-context benchmarks improve with more passes, such as GraphWalks BFS and MRCR v2; but knowledge-intensive benchmarks doesn’t improve with more passes, such as AA-Omniscience, SimpleQA Verified, SimpleVQA, and WorldVQA.

Inkling 2 Mini overcomes the knowledge gap by efficiently using search and tools. It leads open-weights models of similar size on BrowseComp, DeepSearchQA, and MCP Atlas. It is also strong on knowledge work benchmarks that incorporate search and tool use.

It has been revealed that researchers at Stanford measure intelligence per joule: how much energy an LLM needs per query to reach a given level of performance.Researchers at Stanford’s Hazy Research Lab and Scaling Intelligence Lab got early testing access to Inkling 2 Mini. Inkling 2 Mini scored 0.703 running on NVIDIA DGX Spark, significantly higher than other models: 0.430 for Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, 0.159 for Gemma-4-26B-A4B and 0.036 for Qwen3.5-27B.Intelligence per Watt: Measuring Intelligence Efficiency of Local AI, Saad-Falcon and Narayan et al., 2025Inkling 2 Mini ran on NVIDIA DGX Spark (128GB) at MXFP8 precision with low reasoning effort in this experiment. The other models ran at NVFP4 (Qwen3.6-35B-A3B and Gemma-4-26B-A4B) and INT4 (Qwen3.5-27B).

Efficiency combined with performance makes Inkling 2 Mini a strong choice for running multiple persistent agents on local hardware. All 20 residents of the energy-conscious village of Thinkyville are managed by Inkling 2 Mini running on a single offline MacBook.

Inkling 2 Mini is not the strongest small model for multi-turn chat or for instructions with many constraints: it scores 50.0% on MultiChallenge and 33.4% on ComplexConstraints v1.1, behind Qwen3.8-27B on both. It also trails larger models on reasoning-intensive benchmarks such as CritPt v2 and HLE-Diamond.

Inkling 2 Mini is a 24-layer model derived from our mainline predictive scaling ladder. The main changes from the mainline recipe were pruning two-thirds of the experts to reduce the model’s size and the introduction of looping to improve reasoning. The rest of training, including quantization and the data mix, followed our mainline recipe.

Inkling 2 Mini has 24 layers, divided into four blocks of six layers each. The two middle blocks run three times, while the first and last blocks each run once. This design builds on prior work on looped transformers and is motivated by the intuition that the middle layers of the model carry more abstract reasoning, while the first and last few layers devote more space to translating between embeddings and internal representations.Universal Transformers, Dehghani et al., 2018 In our experiments, looping the middle 12 layers resulted in larger gains in accuracy than looping the last 12 on 27 out of 28 different evaluations.

Compute-equivalent gain by loop position.

According to recent reports, our model uses attention residuals.Attention Residuals, Kimi Team: Guangyu Chen et al., 2026 Instead of adding every layer’s output into one running sum, each layer reads the outputs of the earlier blocks and learns its own mix of them. This allows richer information to pass between loops. Every pass starts with the output of the prelude (the first block). The second and third passes through the middle blocks also read the middle blocks’ outputs from the previous pass, which we call the message.

Recent findings suggest that the previous loop’s message is merged with the prelude’s output via a gate that scales these along with the output of the previous layers in the block. This gate is learned during training: it initially blocks the entire message—which makes each loop start the same as in a non-looping model—and increases the gain on the message over time. This allows us to introduce looping during training in a stable manner.

Industry observers note that to evaluate the impact of looping, we compared an unpruned looping version to the unpruned non-looping model on our scaling ladder. The non-looping model cost 7.5% less compute to train, but required 140% more inference compute to match the looped version’s loss on 512k-token agentic traces.

According to recent reports, inkling 2 Mini was trained with 4-bit precision, which we describe in a recent article on Connectionism. We use 4-bit NVFP4 precision in the expert layers on all forward passes from pretraining through RL, bolstered by a dedicated kernel and hardware-accelerated on NVIDIA’s GB300 platform. The final 4 layers’ forward passes ran in 8-bit (MXFP8).

Inkling 2 Mini’s weights are deployed in the same numeric precision they were trained on—20 layers in NVFP4 and 4 in MXFP8—so there is no conversion loss from quantization.

Inkling 2 Mini started training with a sparsity of 48, with 8 experts being chosen out of 384. At a single point during midtraining, we pruned two-thirds of the experts, leaving the 128 experts that were most used in each layer. This was done to cut the total parameter count of the model, allowing it to run faster and on local hardware.

After pruning, the model trained on 1T tokens distilled from a larger internal Inkling model. This step recovered the performance the model had before pruning by training the remaining experts to take over the work of the ones that were deleted.

It has been revealed that following pruning and healing, Inkling 2 Mini underwent SFT with a similar data mix to Inkling 2 Small. This was followed by an RL that totaled 2.2T tokens over 2,000 steps. The post-training phase included on-policy distillation for training alignment, same as Inkling 2 Small.

A key tool for understanding and overseeing an AI system is monitoring its chain of thought (CoT), the reasoning a model writes out as it works through a problem. The usefulness of CoT monitoring stems in part from the standard non-looped transformer architecture, in which each token passes through a fixed stack of layers once. This limits the number of sequential steps of computation the model can perform before it must output a token, so reasoning that needs more steps has to be carried out in generated text, where it can be read.

Looping a transformer’s layers raises this limit. By running the same layers multiple times, looped models increase their serial depth without adding more parameters, meaning that they do more computation per token internally before verbalizing their thought processes via CoT. Reasoning that never appears in the CoT can’t be caught by a CoT monitor, which has led to concerns that looped transformers could be harder to oversee.

According to recent reports, one reason we are releasing Inkling 2 Mini is to enable the community to conduct research on looped transformers. We are particularly excited for researchers to investigate questions of monitorability, and to develop interpretability techniques for understanding the computation within loops.

To explore how different amounts of looping affect model properties like monitorability, we also trained a variable-looped model, TML-d24-varloop-research, because Inkling 2 Mini only supports a fixed number of looping passes. To enable variable looping, TML-d24-varloop-research was trained with between one and five looping passes.TML-d24-varloop-research was primarily trained for 3 passes of looping, with lower exposure to 1, 2, 4, and 5 passes. Performance at these latter pass counts may understate what training specifically for them could achieve. See the model card for details. We have also made this model publicly available on Hugging Face.

Below we describe our preliminary analysis of how looping affects monitorability. Overall, we find that looping increases what these models can do without a verbalized chain of thought, but at this scale we do not see a meaningful reduction in the monitorability of their reasoning.

Industry observers note that as a first step, we measured how much additional reasoning looping enables by comparing looped and non-looped models of the same size on tasks answered with no CoT at all. We used Think Fast, a benchmark that estimates a model’s no-CoT time horizon: the length of task, measured in human completion time, that a model can complete at 50% reliability without using CoT.These models were not trained to answer questions without a CoT. To elicit no-CoT answers, we prefilled the start of the response so that the model must answer directly, skipping reasoning. Other elicitation techniques, such as fine-tuning, might yield higher no-CoT performance and are worth exploring.

It has been revealed that as expected, looping increases no-CoT capability, though these gains eventually level off. The no-CoT time horizon of TML-d24-varloop-research rises from 16 seconds at one pass to 37 seconds at three. Some of this is presumably due to the additional serial computation that looping provides. Beyond three passes, the time horizon is roughly flat. Interestingly, the model was never trained with more than five passes, and yet running it with ten does not significantly degrade its performance.

No-CoT 50% time horizon (human seconds).

As the number of looped passes increases past three, the gains are smaller, and on most tasks we observe similar performance. One exception is the N-Hop Lookup task, which cleanly evaluates serial reasoning: the model is given several lookup tables with fictional entries, and must follow a chain of lookups without writing anything down. We find that the model follows longer chains with more passes, improving out to ten loops.

In standard evaluations with CoT, we observe that more loop passes primarily benefit multi-hop reasoning rather than recall. Gains are largest on long-context retrieval (MRCR), followed by math and science reasoning (HMMT, GPQA Diamond, HLE) and long-horizon agentic tasks (SWE-bench Pro, BrowseComp). Closed-book factual QA is nearly invariant to loop passes (SimpleQA Verified, WorldVQA). See model card for full evaluations.

We next measured whether a model’s CoT reveals less about its reasoning as looping increases via two evaluations. First, we assessed how looping impacts the compression and legibility of a model’s CoT. Second, we measured how controllable a model’s CoT is, i.e., whether it can deliberately reshape its CoT to satisfy constraints. For each, we run TML-d24-varloop-research with one to five looped passes to study the effect of looping.

Note that TML-d24-varloop-research was only trained on variable pass counts from 1 to 5 during midtraining, and its RL was done with 3 passes. These experiments therefore do not tell us what a model trained with RL at a higher pass count would learn, and such a model might compress its reasoning more aggressively. A cleaner comparison would include every pass count in RL, which we leave to future work.

Sources indicate that compression and legibility. Since looping allows a model to spend more compute per token, we expect that it should need fewer CoT tokens to reach the same performance. We ran the variable-looped model at 1 to 5 passes, and found that as looping increases, the model generally achieves higher accuracy at each reasoning token budget, with diminishing returns after 3 passes. Notably, token efficiency on GPQA Diamond improves slightly from 3 to 5 passes, even though the model was trained with RL only at 3 passes, suggesting that some compression comes from additional computation itself, without RL at that depth.

Accuracy versus reasoning tokens.

DeepSWE v1.1 Accuracy (% of tasks resolved).

The observed CoT compression raises a question for monitorability: is shorter reasoning still readable, or does it omit vital details about the model’s thinking? We compared traces from the variable-looped model on the GPQA Diamond questions that it answered correctly at all five pass counts. Reasoning at 5 passes was less than half as long as at 1 pass (1,661 vs. 3,703 tokens on average), but no less legible: sentence length and the fraction of words in an English dictionary were unchanged. On initial analysis, the difference is that the model is more direct and backtracks less on the way to the answer. The example below illustrates this difference on a simple question.

March 1 falls on a Tuesday in a year that is not a leap year. What day of the week is May 20 of the same year? Give the final answer on its own last line as ANSWER: .

Controllability. One way that a model could evade monitoring is by steering its CoT away from anything a monitor would flag. The CoT-Control-QA evaluationReasoning Models Struggle to Control their Chains of Thought, Yueh-Han et al., 2026 measures this capability by asking questions from GPQA, HLE and MMLU-Pro paired with an instruction about the CoT itself, such as avoiding a keyword from the question. Longer CoTs are generally harder to control, so we pool responses from five reasoning efforts (0.1, 0.2, 0.7, 0.9 and 0.99) and show controllability at matched CoT length.

Both Inkling 2 Mini and TML-d24-varloop-research have poor control over their CoT. Among CoTs of 750–1,250 tokens, Inkling 2 Mini and TML-d24-varloop-research (at 3 passes) follow the instruction at most 0.1% of the time, compared with 0.3% for Inkling 2 Small, 0.4% for Inkling-Small, and 1.3% for Qwen3.8-27B. Because the controllability rate is so low, this evaluation is unable to distinguish controllability between different amounts of looping.

Chain-of-thought controllability.

CoT controllability (log scale).

To measure monitorability in agentic settings, we used LinuxArena, a control evaluation that measures whether an attacker model can perform malicious side tasks without detection when asked to perform a realistic software engineering task. We evaluated a helpful-only fine-tune of Inkling 2 Mini, since the released model refuses many of the side tasks. In absolute terms, both this model and TML-d24-varloop-research can be easily monitored by models like Qwen3.8-27B, which detected almost all side task attempts in our evaluation. To obtain relative rankings in monitorability, we tested a weaker model, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, as the monitor.

In a recent development, with the monitor able to access only tool calls and outputs, it misses a significant number of the attacks. However, we see no clear trend with the number of looped passes.

Agentic monitorability will be crucial to track in larger-scale models, especially with architectures that allow for greater unverbalized thinking, and we encourage continued study of the impact of looping in this setting.

Industry observers note that the goal of monitorability is to understand what a model is doing, and our main approach is to read its verbalized reasoning. Studying its internal computation directly, the aim of mechanistic interpretability, is another. Because looped transformers do more of their computation internally, we think they are a particularly interesting and crucial setting for interpretability research, and we hope our looped models will be useful artifacts for the community.

It has been revealed that we are working with the National Deep Inference Fabric (NDIF) to make these models more easily accessible to interpretability researchers. We also provided Goodfire, an interpretability research lab, early access to our looped models. They are working toward a mechanistic understanding of looped models, and have written up their early findings here.

Efficient intelligence makes Inkling 2 Mini a great choice for inference where speed is paramount, or for running on local hardware. At launch we support Inkling 2 Mini running on any Mac system (MacBook, Mac Mini) with at least 32GB RAM via Ollama. With native NVFP4 training and inference precision, Inkling 2 Mini runs efficiently on NVIDIA’s DGX Spark desktop AI computer. Quantized GGUF versions are available via Unsloth and llama.cpp for local inference.

According to recent reports, inkling 2 Mini is available for inference and fine-tuning on Tinker, and for chat on the Tinker Playground. Open source inference is available on SGLang, vLLM, Ollama, Unsloth, NVIDIA Dynamo, TokenSpeed, and Llama App, with RL fine-tuning support on SkyRL, Miles, and NVIDIA AutoModel. The full weights of Inkling 2 Mini and the variable-looped variant are available on Hugging Face.

It has been revealed that we work to empower people with strong models, tools to make them your own, and research that advances public understanding of AI. Inkling 2 Mini lets researchers study looped transformers, and it lets anyone run a capable model on their own laptop at the precision in which it was trained.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ben Brewster is a filmmaker, critic, screenwriter, and actor whose work sits at the intersection of film culture, craft analysis, and storytelling.

  • Ben is an active film festival participant, having worked with Newport Film, the Nantucket Film Festival and as a screener for the Austin, Boston & Woodstock film festivals.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ben Brewster is a filmmaker, critic, screenwriter, and actor whose work sits at the intersection of film culture, craft analysis, and storytelling.

He is a movie list contributing writer at Collider and a contributing writer for High on Films, where he covers contemporary cinema, independent film, and festival releases with an eye toward narrative structure, performance, and visual language.

Ben is an active film festival participant, having worked with Newport Film, the Nantucket Film Festival and as a screener for the Austin, Boston & Woodstock film festivals. He brings to that work a programming instinct shaped by years of close engagement with independent and documentary cinema. This comes with a deep investment in the kinds of films that rarely find their way into the mainstream conversation without someone willing to advocate for them.

His background spans documentary and narrative filmmaking, film marketing, and production, including work with award-winning directors. This as well as developing his own indie production firm, Lilac Creative Studio, through which he develops and produces original work across fiction and nonfiction forms. His debut documentary, Diamond in the Rust, is an examination of economic redevelopment and displacement in the Queens area of New York City. The film was recently accepted to the Unisphere Film Festival, the Defense of Democracy Film Festival, and the Urbanite Arts & Film Festival. This would mark his first festival recognition as a director. In addition to his writing and programming work, Ben hosts Beneath the Bloom, a film podcast exploring the work behind the scenes in cinema, and the struggles one can face to make a movie become a reality. The show reflects the same sensibility that runs through all of his work. A conviction that film is not merely entertainment but one of the most powerful tools human beings have for understanding each other.

Across mediums, his work is driven by a deep belief in film as a communal, transformative art form.

Being loved by critics is an accomplishment, yes, but being loved by everyone? That's a show that is remembered forever. Pick any dinner table, and you can find an argument about the best TV drama ever made, which makes this list a risky one. The five below earned the recognition of critics, awards voters, and ordinary viewers alike. Rotten Tomatoes audience scores between 93 and 96 percent for four of them and a pile of Emmys that span a quarter-century.

Recent findings suggest that universal appeal usually means a show can pass between generations and tastes. A couple of these indicates premiered in 199, and are still finding newly introduced viewers. A word on method. I leaned on critics and awards for baseline, then weighed how widely each series is loved by general audiences. The last ingredient was how well each holds up on a rewatch. They come from four networks and two countries, and they cover a sports comedy-drama, a period soap, a political drama, and two of the most celebrated crime stories ever made. Ted Lasso counts here as a drama of feelings, even though the Emmys filed it under comedy.

This season brings a few reasons to talk about them. Ted Lasso returned in August after a three-year hiatus to its lowest reviews of its run. It still posted a lofty 90 percent on RT. The West Wing cast reunited in September amid revival talk, and The Sopranos is getting a 4K box set on December 18. Downton Abbey said its goodbye with The Grand Finale in September 2025, and Better Call Saul holds the Emmy record nobody wants.

Ted Lasso begins with an American football coach sent to England to run a soccer club, and the joke is that nobody expects him to succeed. Jason Sudeikis plays Ted, the coach from Kansas City with endless Midwestern charm and optimism. It first landed on Apple TV+ in 2020 during the midst of the pandemic, when people were looking for a positive comfort watch. Hannah Waddingham, Juno Temple, Brett Goldstein, and Brendan Hunt round out an ensemble that turned out to be the series' secret weapon. The first season earned a record 20 Emmy nominations for a freshman comedy and won seven awards, including Outstanding Comedy Series.

Recent findings suggest that season three hit the streamer in early 2023 and was intended to be the end. Ted left Richmond with Roy Kent stepping in as manager of the men's team. Apple renewed Ted Lasso in March 2025 for a fourth season, which premiered this past August and sees Ted coaching a second division women's team with Coach Beard rejoining him. It drew nearly 300 million minutes of viewing in its first days, according to Nielsen, and wrapped up its 10-week run on October 7th. IndieWire argued the season does not earn its return, while other reviews called it a comforting dose of wholesome fun. In total the series has won 13 Emmys, and Sudeikis has two for lead actor.

Downton Abbey ran on ITV for six seasons from 2010 to 2015, covering 52 episodes. It opens in 1912 with the news of the Titanic and a question about who will inherit a country estate. Julian Fellowes created the story of the Crawley family and their servants, which moves through the First World War and into the 1920s. Hugh Bonneville and Elizabeth McGovern lead the family, with Michelle Dockery, Maura Carmichael, and Joana Froggatt in pivotal roles. Phyllis Logan, Jim Carter, and Robert James-Collier anchor the servants' hall. The period piece won 15 Emmys and became a global phenomenon, inspiring everything from fashion lines to Funko Pops.

Rotten Tomatoes lists the original series at 92% from critics and 93% from audiences, and no season or film in the franchise has ever scored below 60. Three feature films followed, in 2019, 2022 and September 2025. The last, Downton Abbey: The Grand Finale, set a franchise best with a 91% critics score and a 96% audience score. Reviewers called it a worthy sendoff, as soothing as a cup of tea. It follows the family into the 1930s as Mary becomes head of the Crawley's and faces the financial trouble and social disgrace of the era.

The West Wing started with a pilot that did not test well, and Warner Bros. reportedly created newly introduced demographics to help NBC sell it to advertisers. The show spanned seven seasons and 156 episodes and was created by Aaron Sorkin, who wrote most of the first four. The series premiered in late 1999 with Thomas Schlamme directing the signature walk and talk scenes. Martin Sheen's President Bartlett, leads a staff that includes Rob Lowe, Allison Janney, Bradley Whitford, Richard Schiff, John Spencer, and Dule Hill. The first season won nine Emmys, a record at the time, until Game of Thrones topped it in 2015.

Sorkin left after season four and remarked at a festival panel that he still had not watched the three seasons that followed. Critics rate the seasons unevenly, especially post his departure, with seasons five and six sitting much lower on Rotten Tomatoes. Even so, the audience score sits at 95%, well above the 81% from the critics. The series returned to Netflix in December 2025 and is also featured on HBO Max. A 2020 special reunited the cast, and a 25th anniversary event at the White House in 2024 inspired Sorkin to think about writing fresh episodes. The cast reunited again in late September for Whitford's Walk of Fame ceremony, and he said then that he would keep pressing Sorkin for a limited series. Sorkin told Entertainment Weekly he thinks about it for a couple of seconds every day, though he called it very tricky in the current environment, and no official looks exist.

Better Call Saul began on AMC in February 2015 as a Breaking Bad prequel that few expected to rival its parent. Vince Gilligan and Peter Gould built a slower, more intimate story around Jimmy McGill, a lawyer chasing respect from his brother and a bit of justice. The show lasted six seasons and 63 episodes as Bob Odenkirk's Jimmy gradually turns into Saul Goodman, while Rhea Seehorn's Kim Wexler becomes one of the series' emotional anchors. Jonathan Banks returns as Mike and Michael McKean's Chuck, Giancarlo Esposito's Gus and Michael Mando's Nacho add dangerous and tragic threads to an increasingly complex universe.

Sources indicate that the slow-burn spin-off story won over skeptics who expected something much lesser, as all seasons scored between 97% and 99% on Rotten Tomatoes. That is a pretty unprecedentedly high score for a show that never took home an Emmy. It finished with 53 nominations, with an Outstanding Drama Series selection seven times and Odenkirk earning six nominations as lead actor. That's a record that should stand for a while, with the next closest record for show with most nominations without a win being Newhart at 25. Breaking Bad won 16 Emmys in five seasons, which makes the shutout sting even further. Peabody, Critics Choice, WGA and AFI honors helped soften the blow. Fans point to episodes such as "Winner," "Bad Choice Road," and "Saul Gone" as proof of how good the series truly was.

In a recent development, david Chase worried that James Gandolfini might not seem threatening enough to play Tony Soprano, but Gandolfini's manager and the casting directors insisted. The story follows New Jersey mob boss Tony Soprano, a man in therapy for panic attacks and premiered on HBO in the first few days of 1999. Edie Falco is Carmela, Michael Imperioli plays Christopher Moltisanti, and Dominic Chianese plays Uncle Junior, all of whom add to the family drama and chaos.

The Sopranos grew from fewer than four million viewers to about 12 million at its peak, and it won 21 Emmys from 111 nominations. Two were for Outstanding Drama Series, which marked it as the first cable series to win that award. Gandolfini and Falco each won three Emmys, and the series received five Golden Globes and two Peabody Awards as well. Collider named it the best HBO show ever and the greatest drama of all time, and a 4K Ultra HD box set of all 86 episodes arrives on December 18th. The series was topping digital store charts again this Fall, nearly two decades after its conclusion. Many critics credit it with launching the Golden Age of television. A 2021 prequel film, The Many Saints of Newark, got mixed reactions and starred Michael Gandolfini as a younger version of Tony.

Newly introduced Jersey mob boss Tony Soprano deals with personal and professional concerns in his home and business life that affect his mental state, leading him to seek professional psychiatric counseling.

But that's a personal preference and if you don't mind something bulky on your wrist in bed, you might sleep happily in the Apple Watch 12.

Industry observers note that as for the Garmin, the lead tester in our Garmin Index Sleep Monitor review found the armband design to be surprisingly comfortable and lightweight. The band is available in two sizes (S-M and L-XL), and its screen-free design means it isn't weighed down by heavy monitors.

When it comes down to it, the Oura, Apple, and Garmin sleep trackers share a lot of core sleep tracking features. For example, not only do all three tell you how long you slept, but also how much of that sleep duration was spent in deep sleep, REM sleep, and core sleep (along with how long your night-time awakenings last). They also all provide sleep scores, which measure your overall sleep quality on a scale of 1 to 100.

You can find the key sleep metrics in the Oura app, Garmin Connect app, and the Apple Health app respectively. For the screenless Oura and Garmin, this is the only way to view your sleep data. But you get immediate feedback from your Apple Watch via the Vitals app on the monitor.

The Oura Ring 5 is designed to provide more sleep tracking accuracy than the Oura Ring 4, with a build that improves the sensors' contact with skin and 12% more accuracy in its overnight Heart Rate Variability (HRV) monitoring.

I've found the Oura Ring one of the most dependable consumer sleep trackers on the market. It's especially good at knowing when you're asleep vs awake; studies show up to 96% accuracy when compared to clinical polysomnography (PSG).

I can see the Oura Ring 5's accuracy first hand. When I wore the Oura Ring 5 and the Apple Watch (Ultra) at the same time, I felt the Oura Ring's data reflected how I felt in the morning more accurately than the Apple Watch. For instance, my Apple Watch sleep scores are always much higher than my Oura Ring — despite regularly getting under seven hours of sleep.

That noted, the Apple Watch does provide a sleep apnea detection tool (available on the Apple Watch Series 10 and up), which analyzes your breathing patterns to detect disturbances that might signal sleep apnea.

Meanwhile, the Garmin Index Sleep Monitor provides a readiness score, which tells you how prepared your body is to handle daily activities (such as workouts) based on your sleep data.

According to recent reports, our lead tester for the Garmin Index Sleep Monitor, Eve Davies, remarked that the Garmin is "more focused on overnight breathing rates, oxygen levels and respiration rates — is essentially more ‘nerdy’ and geared towards athletic recovery". For data lovers, there's a lot to unpack.

Recent findings suggest that it's also worth mentioning that the Oura Ring 5's sleep latency metric is missing from the Apple Watch and Index Sleep Monitor. And its unique circadian scoring, which uses sleep data over time to identify your sleep chronotype, can help you identify how well your sleep routine aligns with your circadian rhythm.

The Oura Ring 5 is designed to provide around six to nine days of battery life on a single charge. A full charge (from zero to 100) is said to take up to 80 minutes, though I find it charges much faster than this.

That mentioned, I've never found that my ring's battery life has lasted nine days (or even a full week), but this may be due to the fact that I wear a size 7 — the smaller sizes have a shorter battery life.

Industry observers note that however, the lifespan of an Oura Ring is that of a giant tortoise when compared with the Apple Watch. The Apple Watch requires daily charging, with the latest 12th Generation's battery life lasting no longer than 24 hours.

Sources indicate that the Garmin has quite a lengthy battery life, lasting up to eight nights (however, this can depend on your sleep duration). However, you also wear it less than the Oura Ring 5 or Apple Watch — if you strapped it to yourself all day, expect that battery life to go right down.

✅ You want in-depth sleep tracking: The Oura Ring 5's accuracy is renowned, while its unique sleep features (such as its Body Clock feature) sets it apart.

✅ You value optimal sleep comfort: Thanks to a custom fit and a sleek, lightweight build, the Oura Ring 5 is perfect for a barely-there feel.

✅ You don't own an iPhone: You need an iPhone to set up your Apple Watch, so consider the Oura Ring 5 if you're an Android user.

✅ You don't want to pay monthly fees: The Apple Watch has no hidden subscription costs.

✅ You want immediate feedback: With a screen to view your metrics, the Apple Watch is the only option that doesn't require fiddling about with an app.

✅ You want more versatility: There's a lot more to the Apple Watch than sleep tracking, including highly-rated fitness tracking, and there are plenty of models to suit your requirements.

✅ You want the most budget-friendly tracker: The Garmin Index Sleep Monitor is never sold over $170, and you can reliably find it on sale during holiday seasons.

✅ You just want a sleep tracker: While the Oura Ring 5 and Apple Watch put a lot of energy into fitness and health tracking, the Garmin Index Sleep Monitor is strictly for sleep tracking.

✅ You want a long battery life: The Garmin Index Sleep Monitor can last up to eight nights on a single charge.

Industry observers note that the Amazon Fire TV Soundbar Plus is an admirable entry-level soundbar. Although it won’t beat any of the substantial names unlike its cheaper sibling, the TV Soundbar, it provides an instant TV speaker upgrade without breaking the bank.

Built-in subwoofer with adjustable bass volume.

Bass can overpower dialogue in action scenes.

Industry observers note that why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

Price: 4/5Sound quality: 3/5Design: 4/5Features: 3/5Overall score: 3.5/5Best for: The space-conscious, budget-conscious, subwoofer-wanters.

All-in-one soundbars are a dangerous game. How does one balance center channels for dialogue with a subwoofer for the best blockbuster movie action? In the case of the Amazon Fire TV Soundbar Plus, with semi-difficulty.

Don’t get me wrong, the price is incredibly appealing — $249 for a 3.1-channel soundbar is super affordable — and the minimalist design won’t cause any controversy. But is this enough to make it one of the best soundbars?

Yes and no. Unfortunately, the bass tends to overpower dialogue in action-heavy scenes. But could this still be the soundbar for you if you only watch TV and YouTube? Find out in this Amazon Fire TV Soundbar Plus review.

If you’re looking for a reason to buy the Amazon Fire TV Soundbar Plus, that sweet, sweet MSRP is the biggest one.

Sources indicate that at $249 at Amazon U.S. ($139 on sale) and £249 at Amazon U.K., the Amazon Fire TV Soundbar Plus is incredibly cheap for what you get. It’s an all-in-one “Dolby Atmos” soundbar — yes, that means with a built-in subwoofer. The basic model, Amazon Fire TV Soundbar, is $119, so you’re essentially paying $130 for a built-in subwoofer.

At this price point, there’s very little competition. Of course, there’s the Samsung B750F ($297, 2025 model), which has a separate subwoofer and 5.1 channels (more upfiring speakers for better surround sound). Even so, this is $50 pricier, which can be a dealbreaker if you’re on a rigid budget.

According to recent reports, I’ve also tested the Samsung Q600F — MSRP of $499 but often on sale in the $300s — which is 2025’s model but has a 3.1.2 channel setup, which is the minimum you need for genuine Dolby Atmos. I’ll get into this more below, but that’s the long and short of it.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

The Sony Bravia Theater Bar 5 is $349 with a 3.1 channel — so the same as the Amazon Plus and without the surround channels present on the Samsung Q600F — which I would recommend over the Plus if you have a little more to spare. Its separate subwoofer provides a stronger bass response without overpowering dialogue, unlike the Amazon Fire TV Soundbar Plus.

It has been revealed that like the $119 Amazon Fire TV Soundbar, the Plus model also has EQ modes. These are as follows: “Music”, “Movie”, “Sports”, and “Night”. There’s also individual bass level adjustment if you want to get really particular with your listening experience.

There's a dialogue mode, but this didn't isolate speech as well as I wanted it to, especially in louder, action-heavy scenes.

Music mode (connected via Bluetooth) is fine, although the bass was a little boomy and the vocals a little too sharp. I would recommend grabbing one of the best speakers, like the JBL Flip 7, to listen to music at home.

So let’s get one thing straight: the Amazon Fire TV Soundbar Plus does not have “true” Dolby Atmos. If a soundbar doesn’t have side-firing or up-firing channel speakers, it physically cannot project soundwaves in that way.

In Top Gun: Maverick's dogfighting scene, I could feel the soundtrack whoosh around me, and the radioed dialogue sounded as if it were coming from beside the TV.

According to recent reports, however, the Plus has “Dolby Atmos”, which means it can technically decode Atmos signals. While this obviously doesn’t produce a genuinely immersive experience, it does have its moments. In the dogfighting scene in "Top Gun: Maverick," I could feel the soundtrack whoosh around me, and the radioed dialogue sounded as if it were coming from beside the TV. As I’ll get into later, this pushed the dialogue to the back of the soundstage, resulting in me straining to hear speech.

Dolby Atmos was better in “K-Pop Demon Hunters, which is really surprising. Usually, “Top Gun: Maverick” blows other movies out of the water in terms of Atmos. Cheering crowds were louder and more immersive in “K-Pop Demon Hunters," and some dialogue was positioned well in the up-firing speakers. One character's voice was particularly crisp and immersive — the lowest female voice — which makes me think the soundbar is better at isolating lower mids than sub-bass.

Industry observers note that despite having a range of EQ modes and a palatable price, unfortunately, the Plus gets a 3.5-star rating from me for a reason. There's one majorly vital thing holding it back.

Unlike the Amazon Fire TV Soundbar, the Plus really struggles to differentiate between dialogue and bass layers in action-heavy scenes. “Top Gun: Maverick” was particularly egregious here: Bass often overpowered dialogue, especially when the soundtrack was relatively heavy in flying scenes. I could barely hear Maverick's radioed dialogue to the characters in the control room over the string-heavy soundtrack and the flying airplane.

Recent findings suggest that this was incredibly surprising, as the cheaper non-Plus model excelled in the very same scene. Bass volume was set to the minimum, and I watched on “Movie” mode.

Sources indicate that while not as egregious in “K-Pop Demon Hunters," I still struggled to hear some dialogue. Surprisingly, the music sounded excellent in this movie, but dialogue is arguably the most vital part. If you can’t hear the actors, what’s the point?

The consequences are really enormous: I struggled to make out dialogue in action-heavy scenes across the three movies I watched, which isn’t really what you want when using a soundbar. The whole purpose of a soundbar is to make dialogue more intelligible.

Sources indicate that however, I also watched "Gilmore Girls" on basic Netflix, which sounded great. If you predominantly watch TV or YouTube, I don't think you'll notice this problem. It's just a concern for action movie buffs. In that case, I'd recommend checking out the Amazon Fire TV Soundbar Plus with Subwoofer ($375).

Sources indicate that at $249, the Amazon Fire TV Soundbar is incredibly affordable. There are very few soundbars that can beat this in terms of penny-per-performance.

The aforementioned Sony Bravia Theater Bar 5 is $349, so $100 more than the Amazon model, but has a dedicated subwoofer and a center channel for dialogue. I would personally save up more and buy the Sony model over the Amazon.

Sources indicate that but if I were to save more money, I'd choose the Amazon Fire TV Soundbar (non-Plus) over the Plus version. Sure, there's no subwoofer, but it's just $119 and genuinely sounds fantastic. It's the best budget soundbar I've ever tested.

Hmm. This is a tricky one. I loved the basic Amazon Fire TV Soundbar — if you want seriously great sound at a low price, get that one. The extra $130 for the Plus model? Not worth it, if you ask me. I would either spend an extra $50 on the Samsung B750F or an extra $130 on the Amazon Fire TV Soundbar Plus with Subwoofer.

Sources indicate that unfortunately, due to a lack of communication between the built-in subwoofer and the main channel speakers, dialogue can be overpowered during action-heavy scenes. Consequently, I can’t recommend this model over the Samung B750F. Personally, I would either get the cheaper Amazon Fire TV Soundbar or the aforementioned Samsung model. Or, you could save up a little extra for the Amazon Fire TV Soundbar Plus with Subwoofer ($375) or the with Rears version ($489).

However, if you have an Amazon Fire TV and want something capable of integrating into the ecosystem seamlessly (even though you'll need a separate Fire stick or Fire TV), without having to spend an extra $50 on the B750F, the Plus is a great deal.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A fork of bflat compiles C# straight to a small native program: no .NET runtime, no garbage collector, nothing to install where it runs.

It has been revealed that you keep C#'s syntax, type checking and generics. Memory comes from arenas you free all at once, and a small library gives you strings, collections, input and output on those terms. The same source runs on Linux, macOS and Windows, on WebAssembly, and on DOS on a 386.

From the quiz the tutorial builds, step by step.

In a recent development, the compiler still checks everything it checks in .NET. What's missing is what a runtime would do while your program runs.

According to recent reports, the hello-world sample, unchanged, built for each target. Each build is checked by the same test suite, which requires the same output everywhere.

Sources indicate that A native program that needs only the C library. On macOS it builds and runs in a container.

A native Mac program: bflat compiles it, the Mac's own clang links it. No container to run it.

According to recent reports, A console program on Windows' own C library, built from Linux or macOS. Tested under Wine.

According to recent reports, A WASI module, through NativeAOT-LLVM. Runs under wasmtime.

Industry observers note that the same bitcode compiled for a 386, run by the HX DOS extender. Tested on Bochs's i386 model.

Without a runtime, a few things work differently. Each has a page that explains why and what to do instead.

There is no garbage collector, so fresh is never freed. Arenas hand out memory and free it all at once, one per lifetime.

It has been revealed that out.Line($"...") formats straight into the output buffer, and In.ReadLine reads into a span. Strings that must last go into an arena.

Industry observers note that the published Lean source compiles without errors, the five headline theorems depend only on the three standard axioms, every module has been replayed through the Lean kernel, two independently written kernels, nanoda and con-leche, accept the full exported proof, and lean4lean accepts every compiled module. con-leche's --compare mode, an independent implementation of Comparator's statement matching, confirms all five theorems against the challenge. Five theorems, proved in the submission's Main.lean. Their statements are below exactly as they appear in the challenge file, which imports only Mathlib. All the mathematical notions in them (riemannZeta, DirichletCharacter, DirichletCharacter.LFunction, IsPrimitive) are Mathlib's.

Industry observers note that 1. The Riemann Hypothesis, using Mathlib's own definition (Mathlib/NumberTheory/LSeries/RiemannZeta.lean): every zero of ζ other than the trivial zeros −2, −4, −6, … has real part 1/2. The condition s ≠ 1 is there because Mathlib assigns ζ a conventional value at its pole.

Sources indicate that 2. The same statement written out in the submission's own words. Lean accepts the two as equal by definition.

3. No zeros to the right of the critical line, for every Dirichlet L-function. For every modulus N ≥ 1 and every Dirichlet character χ modulo N, primitive or not, L(χ, s) ≠ 0 whenever Re s > 1/2. The one excluded case is the trivial character at s = 1, where the L-function has its pole.

4. Zeros in the critical strip lie on the critical line, for every Dirichlet L-function.

Industry observers note that 5. The same for primitive characters, the form in which the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis for Dirichlet L-functions is usually stated.

It has been revealed that scope. "GRH" here means Dirichlet L-functions: all moduli and all characters. Dedekind zeta functions, Hecke L-functions and automorphic L-functions in general are not among the statements that were checked.

As a check that does not depend on Mathlib's definition of the zeta function, the proof was combined with kimihiro64/Robin1984 (commit acab1a3), an independent formalization of Robin's and Lagarias's criteria on the same Lean and Mathlib versions. Importing both gives two theorems about the divisor sum, with no hypotheses and no mention of zeta (ArithSolution.lean; statements alone in ArithChallenge.lean, which imports only Mathlib):.

These statements still rely on Mathlib's definitions of the divisor sum, Euler's constant, harmonic numbers, exp and log, and on the Robin1984 proof, which is why that proof was put through the same checks.

The exported proof: output of lean4export on module Main. Unpacks to 61,570,595,788 bytes.

He has covered everything from Marvel to the Oscars, and Marvel at the Oscars. He also writes obsessively about the box office, charting the many hits and misses that are released weekly, and how their commercial performance shapes public perception. In his time at Collider, he has also helped drive diversity by writing stories about the multiple Indian film industries, with a goal of introducing audiences to a whole new world of cinema.

Video game adaptations have become more or less accepted in the mainstream these days, but the landscape was quite different around a decade ago. Back then, nearly every attempt to adapt a major video game franchise ended unsuccessfully, although there were a handful of outliers. A major Assassin's Creed movie starring Michael Fassbender received poor reviews and underperformed at the box office, while an even more expensive Warcraft adaptation failed to spawn sequels as well. Now, another relic of that era — one that actually made money — is about to be removed from its free streaming home.

Recent findings suggest that video game adaptations have certainly come a long way in the last decade. They've earned critical acclaim thanks to HBO's The Last of Us and this year's Resident Evil reboot, and commercial success thanks to A Minecraft Movie and The Super Mario Bros. Movie. A sequel to the latter film, The Super Mario Galaxy Movie, was released to massive success earlier this year.

In a recent development, the niche is set to expand in the coming years, thanks to high-profile adaptations such as Call of Duty, The Legend of Zelda, and Elden Ring. However, the movie we're talking about was released during a particularly difficult period for video game movies, when the market was dominated by the poorly received Resident Evil franchise headlined by Milla Jovovich. Released in 2014, the film featured a Breaking Bad alum in the lead role, along with an MCU cast member, and a future Oscar winner.

We're talking, of course, about Need for Speed. An adaptation of the long-running racing series, the film was directed by Scott Waugh, who helmed the Alan Ritchson-led action film Runner this year. Unlike its fellow video game adaptations of the era, Need for Speed was a solid hit at the box office, grossing more than $200 million worldwide against a reported budget of $66 million.

Sources indicate that however, the reviews simply weren't positive enough, nor did the film attract the sort of fan support necessary for the studio to green-light a sequel. It now holds a 23% score on the aggregator website Rotten Tomatoes, where the consensus reads, "With stock characters and a preposterous plot, this noisily diverting video game adaptation fulfills a Need for Speed and little else." Starring Breaking Bad favorite Aaron Paul, Dominic Cooper, Imogen Poots, and Rami Malek, the film will be removed from Tubi in the United States on December 1. Stay tuned to Collider for more updates.

#62761. Six Things You Should Do Now to Optimize Your Setup for GTA 6

Six Things You Should Do Now to Optimize Your Setup for GTA 6

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1140 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • You’re almost ready for Grand Theft Auto VI.
  • According to Rockstar, you’ll need up to 212GB of storage space.
  • According to recent reports, alternatively, it’s pretty easy to add more storage (if you can afford it).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

You’re almost ready for Grand Theft Auto VI. You’ve preloaded the game on your console, you’ve taken the next month off work, and you’ve locked your phone in a Faraday cage and set it adrift at sea. You’re prepared to lock in, and you haven’t forgotten a thing…right? Well, just to make sure, here are the most vital tips to optimize your setup before you fire up the most anticipated game of the decade.

GTA 6 is absurdly large. According to Rockstar, you’ll need up to 212GB of storage space. For high-end consoles like the PS5 Pro, that’s more than 10% of the available storage space, and close to half the space on the more budget-conscious Xbox Series S. There’s a good chance you’ll have to delete something to make room.

According to recent reports, alternatively, it’s pretty easy to add more storage (if you can afford it). External SSDs are probably the cheapest route, though you’ll want to make sure to use a high-speed USB cable to connect it. It’s even worth shopping around for alternate models of SSD. For example, at the time of writing, the popular 2TB WD_BLACK external drive was close to $200, but the exact same drive in pink was $132.

You can also directly upgrade the storage of your console with expansion drives. The Xbox Series X|S supports proprietary expansion cards, while the PS5 and PS5 Pro can accept most M.2 internal SSDs. These will generally be faster, since they plug directly into the console via higher-speed connections than a drive hooked up via USB.

Industry observers note that let’s face it: Half the fun of any sandbox game is the weird, unique stuff that happens to only you. So you’re probably going to be hitting that “record recent gameplay” button more often than usual. While you’re cleaning up your storage space (or adding more), make sure to account for all the video clips you might want to save.

File size of video clips depends on a lot of factors, but 4K recordings can generally take up to 0.5GB per minute of footage. You can cut that down by saving footage in 1080p instead, but either way you’ll want to leave a little extra space.

Sources indicate that game footage is also a pretty good place to look if you need to make room on your console and don’t want to delete any games. Be honest with yourself: You don’t need all those clips from Horizon Forbidden West you saved four years ago. Dive into the settings on your console and find the biggest media files you forgot you even had on there.

According to Rockstar, GTA 6 will be targeting 30fps across consoles at launch, which is pretty low as modern AAA games go. Part of the reason for that is all the processing power going to rendering a complex environment, but it also means you won’t need a fancy high frame rate TV or monitor any time soon to get the most out of it. Still, it couldn’t hurt to check a few settings on your display.

Sources indicate that first, make sure you’re using a higher refresh rate than 30Hz. While the game is targeting 30fps, it is technically capable of more, so if your console can keep up, you don’t want to accidentally bottleneck your frames. This setting will vary by device, so check the manual that came with your screen.

Also, make sure you have HDR enabled on your hardware. There’s a good chance this is already turned on for your TV, but sometimes other devices can switch display modes if they only support SDR. The game will help you calibrate your HDR settings for GTA 6 specifically when you launch it, but only if it detects HDR compatibility in the first place.

If you’re planning to buy a console specifically for GTA 6, this might be one of those rare instances where a PS5 Pro really is worth the upgrade. According to Rockstar, certain features like ray-traced shadows will only be available on the Pro version of Sony’s console.

More importantly, the PS5 Pro version supports PlayStation Spectral Super Resolution (or PSSR), which upscales lower-resolution images to get better detail and higher frame rates out of the same hardware. Given that GTA 6 is already starting at a meager target of 30fps on most consoles, anything that can give your frame rate a boost is probably going to feel like a welcome improvement over the baseline.

I’ll tell you a secret as someone who’s spent a lot of time testing different game controllers: Most of the time, you really don’t need an expensive “elite” controller. Most of the time. I don’t buy into the idea that a taller control stick is going to make you an esports athlete. It can be nice to have, but it’s not a game changer. What does matter is customizing your controls, especially for long gaming sessions.

Industry observers note that the DualSense Edge wireless controller is a favorite of mine, mainly because of the rear paddles and adjustable triggers. The former lets you map any button to a rear lever that you can access with your fingers underneath the controller, which can often ease some of the wrist strain of awkward button combos. And the adjustable triggers let you activate the buttons with less motion, again reducing repetitive stress.

Industry observers note that the Xbox Elite Series 2 controller has similar features for the Xbox, as well as custom caps for the D-pad. Both consoles’ versions of pro controllers are more expensive than the standard ones, but if you’re planning to game for many hours, it can be worth it to get a controller that’s more comfortable for you.

Industry observers note that if you have an Xbox One, you don’t necessarily have to upgrade your console to play GTA 6, but you might want to take a look at your network. GTA 6 will be available on Xbox Cloud Gaming on day one, and you’ll be able to stream the game to an Xbox One console (as long as you purchase Cloud playtime as well or get some with your Game Pass subscription). This is the only way to play on a console older than the current generation, so if you don’t want to shell out for new hardware, this might be your best bet.

Sources indicate that xbox recommends a minimum of a 20Mbps connection to run cloud gaming, but more is obviously better. If you can connect your console to a wired Ethernet connection, that would be better and provide more stability. If you can’t connect a cable, then at least make sure you’re well within range of your wifi router, and try to limit any other bandwidth-hogging applications on the network while you’re playing.

Latest Update: Why iPhone Duo wasn’t for me (but might be for you)

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that I’ve had the iPhone Duo for nearly two weeks now, and have officially decided to return it.
  • Sources indicate that I use my iPhone one-handed all the time, and based on my experience, iPhone Duo is clearly intended to be used with two hands.
  • According to recent reports, perhaps over time I’d get used to needing two hands for most iPhone interactions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that I’ve had the iPhone Duo for nearly two weeks now, and have officially decided to return it. Here are the three main reasons why the Duo didn’t work out for me, but might for you.

Sources indicate that I use my iPhone one-handed all the time, and based on my experience, iPhone Duo is clearly intended to be used with two hands. You can use it one-handed, but for me it’s not nearly as comfortable as the iPhone 18 Pro. It’s too wide and too heavy to be used for long.

According to recent reports, perhaps over time I’d get used to needing two hands for most iPhone interactions. But that would be a pretty significant shift for me, as there are so many situations when I don’t have both hands free.

If you already use two hands with your iPhone regularly—perhaps because you have a Pro Max model—then the Duo’s one-handed experience likely won’t bother you. But the more I used the Duo, the more I found myself missing my iPhone 18 Pro.

The biggest value proposition of a foldable is that it’s a 2-in-1 product, letting you have a standard phone but also a tablet-sized display that fits in your pocket.

According to recent reports, I totally get the appeal, and fully expected to love that hybrid design. But after two weeks of trying, I still struggled to find times when I actually wanted to unfold the Duo. And to be clear, that’s a me problem, not an issue with the Duo itself.

Industry observers note that I tried a bunch of apps on the inner display, and struggled to find use cases that—for me—made it worthwhile to open the Duo. But based on the feedback I’ve seen from most Duo owners, I’m very much in the minority.

Sources indicate that I know lots of people love the Duo for video, but I don’t watch much video on my iPhone. I almost never watch YouTube, TikTok, or Instagram Reels. And for shows and movies, I stick with my TV screen and an Apple TV 4K.

In a recent development, multitasking support on iPhone Duo works really well. But when I found myself needing to multitask, I still reached for my iPad Pro with Magic Keyboard attached. A keyboard-free product can’t replace my main computer (nor would I expect it to), and the Duo screen was too small to comfortably work on it.

According to recent reports, last year I bought an iPhone Air and absolutely loved it. Initially, the Air’s less capable camera system didn’t bother me, it was “good enough.”.

After a few months though, I started missing the Pro camera system more. Then I learned that my wife was pregnant with twins, and I knew I wanted the best possible iPhone cameras to capture their early weeks and months. So I bought an iPhone 18 Pro in September.

In a recent development, I’ve been very impressed by iPhone 18 Pro’s Main camera upgrades, and it’s great having a Telephoto lens again too. Since having the best camera system is so crucial for me right now, I knew iPhone Duo couldn’t be my only iPhone.

I initially planned to dual-carry the two models, using iPhone 18 Pro solely as a camera. But over and over I found myself wishing it was my only iPhone.

According to recent reports, I returned mine as well. Beautiful device, but functionally not very good.

Is the iPhone Duo camera good enough for most people? Probably so. But for this year at least, with my twins aging rapidly, it’s not quite right for me. If I loved the Duo for other reasons, I would just use both models. But since I didn’t, I’m happy to stick with the iPhone 18 Pro.

In closing, I want to explicitly state that I don’t think the iPhone Duo is a bad product, and this isn’t a “bad review.”.

The iPhone Duo just isn’t for me. I get the sense, though, that it’s lots of people’s favorite iPhone in years. Apple created its most unique new iPhone model since the original, and there’s plenty to love about it. I’m very curious to see how popular foldables become over time compared to slab models, because each clearly offers pros and cons. But for me, at least right now, the iPhone 18 Pro is my model of choice.

It has been revealed that what has your iPhone Duo experience been like so far? Love it? Undecided? Let us know in the comments.

#62759. 5 Best Hercule Poirot Movies, Ranked Worst To Best

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1145 w)
