General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Screenrant ↗ Open Full Page

5 Best Hercule Poirot Movies, Ranked Worst To Best

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1145 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Screenrant

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Agatha Christie is one of the most popular authors of all time.
  • Recent findings suggest that then there’s Hercule Poirot, arguably Christie’s most popular fictional character.
  • It’s no surprise, then, that Hercule Poirot was brought to movie theaters soon after.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Agatha Christie is one of the most popular authors of all time. The English writer crafted many classic stories in the 20th century, and introduced a number of iconic heroes, many of whom are still being adapted to this day. One of these characters is Miss Marple, who made her debut in 1927, when she featured in a short story titled The Tuesday Night Club, which was published in The Royal Magazine.

Recent findings suggest that then there’s Hercule Poirot, arguably Christie’s most popular fictional character. Christie first introduced the Belgian detective in The Mysterious Affair at Styles, which was written in 1916 and published four years later in 1920. Poirot was a popular character upon release, but Christie’s hero became a sensation around six years later.

It’s no surprise, then, that Hercule Poirot was brought to movie theaters soon after. The character made his big screen debut in 1931s Alibi, with Austin Trevor playing the hero. However, Trevor’s iteration of Poirot deviated greatly from Christie’s books in many ways, including not sporting the detective’s classic mustache.

According to recent reports, since then, dozens of actors have gone on to play Poirot in both movies and television. Arguably the greatest Poirot adaptation of all is David Suchet’s series, which began in 1989, but the detective has still had plenty of excellent films, too. For example, both Peter Ustinov and, more recently, Kenneth Branagh helmed Poirot mystery movies that were received with great acclaim.

Sources indicate that the most famous Poirot story, in both literature and film and television, is Murder on the Orient Express. Christie first crafted this story in the early 1930s, and it was initially published as a six-part series in the Saturday Evening Post under the name Murder on the Calais Coach. With Murder on the Orient Express, Christie created the perfect locked-in mystery, with all the characters stuck on a train for days, knowing that one (or more) of them is a murderer.

Sources indicate that kenneth Branagh took on the role of Poirot, and the responsibility of adapting Christie’s iconic work, in 2017s Murder on the Orient Express remake. Like many Poirot movies that were released in the 20th century, Branagh assembled an exciting group of actors to play the train occupants. The cast included Johnny Depp, Michelle Pfeiffer, Judi Dench, Penélope Cruz, Willem Dafoe, Daisy Ridley, Leslie Odom Jr., Josh Gad, Derek Jacobi, Olivia Colman, and Tom Bateman.

Branagh’s remake was successful in many ways. The cast was exceptional, especially Michelle Pfeiffer and Willem Dafoe. Additionally, the film looked spectacular, with a blue and white color palette radiating from the screen. Branagh is a critically acclaimed director, and he certainly brought his A-game to this movie.

Yet, Murder on the Orient Express (2017) struggled in some areas, too. For many, the film felt overly familiar, which may be a harsh criticism given that the story is nearly one hundred years old and has been told dozens of times (and in many different languages, too). Additionally, Branagh’s portrayal of Poirot was a bit of a mixed bag. He captured the essence of the character well, but was vastly different physically from how Poirot is described in the books.

Industry observers note that the best of Kenneth Branagh’s three Poirot films was his last, A Haunting in Venice. With this film, it felt as if Branagh had finally found his voice in telling a Hercule Poirot story, both as a director and as an actor. Branagh seems at his most comfortable on screen in this film, and works well within the darker tone that A Haunting in Venice provides.

At the same time, this film felt less predictable than the two that came before, in part because it wasn’t adapting one of Christie’s most famous novels (and because it took more liberties from its source material, too).

Peter Ustinov played Poirot in six films in total, three of which were released in theaters, with the others going straight to television. One of the theatrical releases was Death on the Nile (1978), a film that serves as a much better adaptation of the story than Branagh’s. Like most of the other Poirot films, this movie recruited several high-profile actors.

There was Peter Ustinov as Hercule Poirot, and he was joined by David Niven, Lois Chiles, Simon MacCorkindale, Mia Farrow, Bette Davis, Maggie Smith, Angela Lansbury, Olivia Hussey, George Kennedy, and Jack Warden. Of these, Mia Farrow, Maggie Smith, and Angela Lansbury truly stood out, all giving exceptional performances. The surrounding film was excellent, too, with amazing visuals (having actually been filmed on location) and a captivating script adaptation of Christie’s original story.

Another Ustinov Poirot film is Evil Under the Sun, which was released in 1982. This is Ustinov’s best Poirot movie, in part because the English actor finds his groove to the fullest here. He’s charming, witty, and genuinely funny, too (such as in the scene where Poirot pretends to swim in a bathing suit).

Like Death on the Nile (1978), Evil Under the Sun also has jaw-dropping visuals, having once again been filmed on location. The film itself is more playful than its predecessors, too, which makes it more entertaining overall.

Recent findings suggest that four decades after the story was first released, Murder on the Orient Express made its way to the major screen with a film of the same name. This movie is a relatively faithful adaptation of the book, telling the story of the murder of American businessman Samuel Ratchett (aka Richard Widmark) aboard the famous Orient Express. From there, Poirot is forced to investigate the crime, and prevent the train journey from getting any more deadly.

Murder on the Orient Express (1974) had a star-studded cast. Albert Finney played Poirot, and did so with his usual charm and enthusiasm. Finney was joined by a number of A-list actors, too, including Lauren Bacall, Ingrid Bergman, Sean Connery, John Gielgud, Vanessa Redgrave, Michael York, Anthony Perkins, and Martin Balsam. Upon the release of the film, the ensemble cast was praised for their respective performances.

It has been revealed that in fact, several of these performers received accolades for their work in the film. For example, Bergman won the Academy Award for Best Supporting Actress for her role as Greta Ohlsson. More broadly, the film itself was the recipient of six Oscar nominations in total, and that includes a Best Actor nomination for Finney and Best Adapted Screenplay for writer Paul Dehn.

Industry observers note that the praise that this adaptation received was well deserved, too. The film does a spectacular job of bringing Christie’s story to the substantial screen, making these characters (and Hercule Poirot in particular) truly come alive. This film may be a bit dated when watching it in the modern day, however, but Christie’s story still remains timeless in many ways.

Epic accuses Apple of withholding 122,000 documents, seeks daily fines

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (928 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: 9to5mac

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a new filing, Epic Games accuses Apple of withholding more than 122,000 documents related to its proposed App Store commissions and asks the court to impose daily fines until the company complies.
  • As a result of the lawsuit Epic Games brought against Apple in 2020, Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers ruled in 2021 that Apple would have to, among other things, allow developers to direct owners to alternative payment methods outside the App Store.
  • Apple responded by allowing external payment links, but imposed a commission of up to 27% on purchases made through them.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a new filing, Epic Games accuses Apple of withholding more than 122,000 documents related to its proposed App Store commissions and asks the court to impose daily fines until the company complies. Here are the details.

As a result of the lawsuit Epic Games brought against Apple in 2020, Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers ruled in 2021 that Apple would have to, among other things, allow developers to direct owners to alternative payment methods outside the App Store.

Apple responded by allowing external payment links, but imposed a commission of up to 27% on purchases made through them. This, in turn, led the court to find Apple in civil contempt for violating its injunction. Since then, Apple has been trying to overturn that ruling, a dispute that has now reached the Supreme Court.

Industry observers note that at the same time, district court proceedings will determine what, if any, commission Apple may charge on purchases made through external payment links. Apple submitted its proposal on August 13, calling for commissions ranging from 5% to 15%, and Epic is expected to respond after Apple completes its document production.

In a new filing, however, Epic is accusing Apple of withholding more than 122,000 documents related to how it arrived at its proposed commission rates.

One of the many aspects of the ever-sprawling battle between Epic Games and Apple centers on document production.

In its new filing, Epic claims Apple has repeatedly failed to produce documents detailing how it arrived at its proposed commission rates, accusing the company of withholding materials it deems irrelevant to the proceedings.

Epic argues that Apple previously used questionable claims of attorney-client privilege to withhold documents during the contempt proceedings, but has now changed tactics.

Apple does introduce one tactical change from its prior campaign of delay. Whereas during the contempt proceeding Apple used bogus claims of privilege to evade its discovery obligations, this time Apple withholds thousands of documents on bogus claims of irrelevance. For example, Apple is withholding well over 99% of the documents returned by running the agreed-to search terms on the files of the four custodians Apple says decided on the proposed fee (Tim Cook, Eddy Cue, Carson Oliver, and Kevan Parekh (Apple’s latest CFO)) and three other key individuals (Nate Barton, Alex Roman, and Phil Schiller). Apple claims these withheld documents are not relevant to this proceeding-even though they hit on case-specific terms such as “proffer,” “contempt,” “injunction,” and “link-out.” To put this into context, while Apple produced 632 custodial documents returned by these search terms (including families), Apple is withholding over 122,000 based on a claim of non-responsiveness. Moreover, Apple claims that it completed its production from the files of these custodians, yet its production does not include a single substantive email discussing the rates Apple ultimately proposed; any notes or communications reflecting what occurred at any meeting where these rates were discussed or decided; any internal analysis of the financial or business impact of the proposed commissions; any App Store profit and loss statements; or any support for Apple’s assertion that its incremental link-out costs are “essentially zero.”.

Epic goes on to state that “Apple cannot be trusted to fix this problem on its own,” proposing instead that the court order Apple to produce all non-privileged documents matching the search terms agreed upon by both parties, regardless of whether Apple considers them relevant.

Under this proposal, Apple would still be allowed to review documents for attorney-client privilege, but it would be up to Epic to determine which of the remaining documents are relevant to the case. Epic argues that existing confidentiality protections would prevent it from using any of the information for purposes unrelated to the litigation.

Given Apple’s position, Epic respectfully submits that the Court should order Apple to produce to Epic all non-privileged documents that hit on the Parties’ agreed-upon search terms, so that Epic itself can sift the wheat from the chaff. Doing so will avoid further delays and place no burden on Apple. Moreover, doing so would not raise any of the concerns that required Special Master involvement in the prior proceeding, namely concerns around the production of privileged Apple information to Epic. Under Epic’s proposed remedy, Apple would be allowed to continue its review for privilege. For these reasons, Epic asks this Court to order Apple to produce all non-privileged documents that hit on any of the Parties’ agreed-upon search terms by December 2, 2026 (one week after Apple’s deadline to substantially complete production), irrespective of any relevance or responsiveness assessment.

Finally, though Epic does not propose a specific dollar amount, it “asks that the Court impose on Apple a daily monetary sanction for each day Apple fails to comply after December 2, 2026.”.

Recent findings suggest that according to the court docket, a hearing on Epic’s motion was initially scheduled for November 24 before Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers. However, a new order filed today, which has yet to be made public, refers the discovery dispute to a magistrate judge and includes a notice terminating deadlines and hearings.

Breaking: 6 Best Crime Books of the 2000s, Ranked

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that feel free to connect with him or check out his work.
  • In a recent development, A great mystery book essentially turns its readers into detectives.
  • Industry observers note that now, the 2000s were a turning point for the mystery genre because it got darker and more literary.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that feel free to connect with him or check out his work. He's everywhere — Upwork, YouTube, Spotify, SoundCloud, Collider, LinkedIn, Instagram.

In a recent development, A great mystery book essentially turns its readers into detectives. The author knows that the story is meant to feel like a subtle contest between the characters and the audience, with each clue raising the question of who will figure things out first. When the payoff is great, even losing the contest feels like a reward. However, if it’s bad or delivered at the wrong time, the entire buildup falls apart in a single second.

Industry observers note that now, the 2000s were a turning point for the mystery genre because it got darker and more literary. Some of the best writers of the decade stopped asking who did it and started exploring the consequences of crime and the ways it can change people’s lives forever. That shift gave the genre a upcoming emotional depth and gave us some of the best mystery books of the 2000s. Here are the top six mystery books of the 2000s.

Sources indicate that the Curious Incident of the Dog in the Night-Time is the rare mystery that’s narrated by someone who sees the world completely differently from everyone around him. Mark Haddon’s novel follows Christopher Boone, a brilliant 15-year-old boy who loves math and hates being touched. One night, he discovers his neighbor’s dog, Wellington, lying dead on the lawn with a garden fork through it. Inspired by his hero, Sherlock Holmes, Christopher decides to investigate the crime himself and writes it all down as his own mystery novel.

It has been revealed that the joke hidden in the title is that the dog barely matters. Christopher’s detective work leads him straight to the truth about his own parents, and Haddon lets readers figure it out a few pages before Christopher does. Watching him process absolutely heartbreaking news with the innocence of a teenager is one of the most painful parts of the book, to the point where readers can practically feel his confusion and fear as his whole world falls apart. The Curious Incident is a mystery that’s really about love and honesty, and it remains one of the most original novels of the decade.

Dennis Lehane’s Shutter Island spawned one of Martin Scorsese’s biggest blockbusters, but the eerie, gothic novel deserves to be appreciated on its own. The story takes place in 1954, when U.S. Marshal Teddy Daniels and his partner, Chuck Aule, take a ferry to Ashecliffe Hospital, an institution for the criminally insane on a remote island in Boston Harbor. They go there to look for Rachel Solando, a patient who vanished from a locked room as if she had walked straight through the walls. When a hurricane traps them on the island, Teddy grows convinced that the hospital’s doctors are conducting secret experiments and hiding some very dark secrets.

According to recent reports, from there, Shutter Island works like a classic pulp mystery with coded messages and a confined setting that keeps tightening the noose on its characters. Lehane’s old-fashioned style of storytelling is the book’s greatest strength. The readers get so caught up in the mystery of Rachel’s disappearance that they barely notice the inconsistencies in Teddy’s actions. By the time the book delivers its significant twist, it’s clear that the clues hidden along the way were never really about the missing patient. Shutter Island is designed to be read twice, and is still a genre-defining book today.

According to recent reports, the Shadow of the Wind is a mystery for anyone who has ever fallen in love with a book. Carlos Ruiz Zafón’s novel is set in Barcelona in the years after the Spanish Civil War and begins when a young boy named Daniel Sempere is taken by his bookseller father to the Cemetery of Forgotten Books, a secret library hidden in the heart of the city. Daniel is allowed to choose one book, and he picks a novel by an obscure author named Julián Carax. He soon discovers that someone has spent years tracking down and burning every copy of Carax’s work — and that he may own one of the last ones left.

According to recent reports, zafón’s novel feels like stepping right into an old film. Daniel’s hunt for a forgotten writer soon evolves into a story about doomed love and family secrets. However, the most interesting part is how Daniel’s life begins to mirror the author’s in unsettling ways, especially when a brutal police inspector named Fumero starts taking an interest in him. Zafón fills the city with unforgettable characters and romantic prose that is easy to get lost in for hours. The novel became a global bestseller for good reason, given that it feels like a love letter to reading itself.

Mystic River is another Lehane murder mystery that actually feels haunted. The story picks up in 1975, when three boys from a working-class Boston neighborhood are playing on the street when two men posing as police officers drive off with one of them, Dave Boyle. Dave escapes days later, but he comes back a completely different person, and the friendship between the three boys quietly falls apart. Twenty-five years later, Jimmy Marcus, now an ex-con running a corner store, learns that his teenage daughter has been murdered. Their old friend Sean Devine is the detective on the case, and on the night she died, Dave came home covered in blood.

It has been revealed that dennis Lehane is at his very best here, and Mystic River is often called his masterpiece. The mystery of who killed Katie Marcus is gripping, but the book is really about how one terrible day can quietly shape the rest of three men’s lives. The author moves between all three men, so readers always know a little more than any one of them, and that is where the book’s primary sense of tension comes from. Lehane also captures the loyalty and suspicion of a tight-knit neighborhood, where everyone knows each other’s secrets but no one wants to say them out loud. The ending is one of the most gut-wrenching in modern crime fiction, and it lingers long after the last page. Clint Eastwood’s Oscar-winning film adaptation of the novel is excellent, but Mystic River hits even harder in its original form.

Very few narrators admit they’re liars in the first few pages, but Rob Ryan does in Tana French’s In the Woods. The story opens in 1984, when Rob was one of three children who wandered into the woods near their Dublin suburb. He was found clinging to a tree with blood in his shoes, with no memory of what happened, and his two best friends were never seen again. Twenty years later, he is serving as a detective on the Dublin Murder Squad when a 12-year-old girl is found dead at an archaeological dig in those same woods. Rob and his partner, Cassie Maddox, take the case, but the catch is that Rob keeps his connection to it a secret.

In a recent development, french’s debut reads less like a police procedural and more like a confession from someone who still hasn’t made peace with his past. The present-day murder is gripping, but the real tension comes from watching Rob slowly unravel as the woods pull him back in. His friendship with Cassie is warm and funny, and it adds to the story’s emotional stakes. The fact that the readers know he is not always honest makes the whole thing feel slightly off-balance. It’s also why the ending of the novel and its refusal to give easy answers have divided readers ever since.

In Sweden, The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo was published under a much harsher title, Men Who Hate Women. This is a big clue to what Stieg Larsson really wanted to say with this story. The novel follows disgraced journalist Mikael Blomkvist, who is hired by aging industrialist Henrik Vanger to solve a 40-year-old mystery. Henrik’s niece Harriet vanished from the family’s private island on a day when the only bridge was blocked by an accident, which means someone on the island must have been responsible. Mikael soon realizes that he needs help from the brilliant but extremely private hacker Lisbeth Salander, who trusts almost no one. The Vanger case is a classic locked-room puzzle, built on old photographs and family members who all have something to hide.

However, Lisbeth’s is the reason the book became a global phenomenon. She is a character who has been failed by every institution that was supposed to protect her, and her refusal to be anyone’s victim gives the novel a unique kind of fury. She and Mikael are total opposites, but their partnership is one of the genre’s greatest odd pairings. The book covers a solid amount of ground. Despite its size, the story never wastes a page, and every thread pays off by the end. Larsson spent years as a journalist exposing extremist groups, and that anger at powerful men who escape consequences is felt on every page. He died before the book was published, sadly never seeing it become a hit that sold millions of copies around the world. Two decades later, Lisbeth Salander is still the gold standard for the modern crime heroine, and The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo remains a cultural phenomenon that mystery fans still talk about.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Laura Hurley has been writing about the entertainment industry for more than twelve years, after a decade as a content producer and editor at CinemaBlend after writing for WhatCulture and Examiner.
  • Law & Order: Special Victims Unit generated more hype than usual ahead of season 28 thanks to a major milestone: the 600th episode.
  • Several reunions from Benson's earliest days with Special Victims will, sadly, be impossible.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Laura Hurley has been writing about the entertainment industry for more than twelve years, after a decade as a content producer and editor at CinemaBlend after writing for WhatCulture and Examiner. Attending events like SCAD TVfest and San Diego Comic-Con over the course of her career, she has been immersed in the world of network, streaming, and cable TV.

Law & Order: Special Victims Unit generated more hype than usual ahead of season 28 thanks to a major milestone: the 600th episode. The long-running drama brought Christopher Meloni back to reprise his role as Elliot Stabler for the first time since Law & Order: Organized Crime was canceled, and longtime fans could look forward to the highly anticipated reunion between Stabler and Mariska Hargitay's Olivia Benson. Unfortunately, their reunion was unsatisfying. The 600th episode rewrote elements of their past. Now, as season 28 continues, another reunion could prove to be much more meaningful.

Several reunions from Benson's earliest days with Special Victims will, sadly, be impossible. SVU handled Richard Belzer's real-life passing by giving Munch a moving tribute. Then, the show killed off Dann Florek's Don Cragen in season 27 (though Florek is still displeased about Cragen's death). After the 600th episode, it seems Stabler won't be back for a long time, if at all. Fortunately, SVU is bringing back somebody else from the old days to work with Benson again.

Recent findings suggest that alexandra Cabot, the first full-time assistant district attorney for Manhattan's Special Victims Unit, will return in an upcoming season 28 episode. While details about actress Stephanie March's return as Cabot are scarce, the confirmation that Mariska Hargitay will work with another veteran of SVU's golden years provides something to look forward to. There's no indication she'll appear in SVU's upcoming fall finale. It's safe to assume NBC will heavily promote Alex Cabot's return to Law & Order: Special Victims Unit when it arrives in the fresh year.

Even though Cabot wasn't Benson's longest-running ADA during her 28 years (and counting) in the Special Victims Unit, the two formed such a strong bond that many consider Cabot one of Benson's top love interests. They never canonically coupled up, so they can't claim a spot on any official ranking of Olivia Benson's love interests, but their relationship makes Cabot the perfect person to bring back in such a milestone season.

In a recent development, plenty of time has passed to build anticipation for a reunion between Benson and Cabot. Nine seasons have gone by since Stephanie March last appeared as a guest star on SVU, so there's a lot to catch up on. Though fans can always revisit her years as part of the cast on Peacock, Cabot's departure left lingering questions, even now, nearly a decade after her last appearance on the show.

The stakes are also lower for their reunion than they were for Christopher Meloni's arrival as Stabler. Viewers are less likely to be unsatisfied with her return, no matter how it happens. If anything, a reunion with an old, less fraught friend could be just what Benson needs to realize that she should focus on her personal life instead of dedicating herself wholly to her job.

Benson's relationship with Stabler has been messy since season 1 in 1999; her relationship with Cabot was much healthier despite their occasional differences, and it's due for a revisit in 2028. The franchise hasn't spent years building up expectations for their relationship, not the way it did with Stabler. The first story to feature Stephanie March since season 19 could be exactly what season 28 needs to shake off the concerns with the 600th episode.

According to recent reports, when the news broke that Christopher Meloni was returning for the 600th episode, the odds seemed good that the installment would celebrate Law & Order: SVU's origins much more effectively than the 500th episode did. Whether viewers were rooting for a romance or just wanted to see the old partners investigating a case again, Stabler's return could have been perfect for Benson's 600th episode. Instead, the episode rewrote some of their foundational history.

Industry observers note that the problems that made Stabler such a questionable cop by the end of his time in the franchise didn't cause problems at first, and their partnership was more solid than it was dysfunctional. The 600th episode presented his behavior as more problematic from the start than season 1 ever did, all to motivate Benson to reevaluate herself. Plus, the episode's ending felt much more like a goodbye to Stabler (and Meloni) than a fitting acknowledgment of a historic 600-episode run.

As much as Meloni deserved a better exit than the abrupt cancellation of Law & Order: Organized Crime, his major exit shouldn't have come at the expense of Benson's character in such a huge milestone. After all, Stabler hadn't been a series regular on SVU since 2011. It didn't help that the episode opened by revealing the two old partners hadn't spoken in a year and a half. Stabler even denied they were friends.

In a recent development, if it had been a setup for them to resolve their issues later in the season, the twist wouldn't have been a problem. As Stabler's final appearance in season 28 (and possibly his final appearance ever on SVU), it just wasn't satisfying. Reuniting with Cabot likely won't end in tears for Benson, and the two women will hopefully capitalize on their chemistry in their season 28 episode.

Stephanie March's episode of Law & Order: Special Victims Unit will be the ninth episode of the season. The fall finale will be the seventh, so Cabot will be back on our screens early in the fresh year.

Law & Order: Special Victims Unit season 28's fall finale airs Thursday, December 3, at 9 PM ET on NBC.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that apple could see iPhone shipments rise 7% next year, giving it a 26% share of global smartphone shipments, according to a fresh report. Here are the details.

As detailed by AppleInsider, a latest Morgan Stanley research report says Apple is poised to ship approximately 270 million iPhones in 2027, a 7% bump from 2026.

The forecast comes amid a change of pace for Apple, which launched only the iPhone 18 Pro models and iPhone Duo this fall, with the rest of its iPhone lineup reportedly set to arrive early next year.

Morgan Stanley notes that this could push some purchases from late 2026 into 2027, contributing to the projected shipment growth without necessarily reflecting an increase in underlying demand.

The report also comes as Apple and the rest of the smartphone industry continue to grapple with rising memory and storage prices, though previous reports have suggested that Apple is better positioned than many of its competitors to absorb those costs.

Industry observers note that apple raised iPhone prices in September, after keeping them stable for much of the year while competitors had already introduced price hikes. In some cases, they raised prices more than once within a matter of months.

In a recent development, back to the report, it notes that global smartphone shipments are expected to drop 5% next year, compared with a previous forecast of 3.6% growth. That remarked, it’s still an improvement over the estimated 13.8% decline in 2026.

When it comes to Apple and the iPhone specifically, Morgan Stanley notes that consumer interest in upgrading has remained largely unchanged year over year, with 37% of iPhone owners saying they are extremely likely to upgrade within the next 12 months. That’s compared with 41% of smartphone owners overall, a figure that dropped by 2 percentage points year over year.

As for the market’s reaction to the iPhone Duo, Morgan Stanley found that 22% of non-iPhone users surveyed expressed interest in switching to Apple’s foldable device, with that figure reaching 34% in China.

Importantly, Morgan Stanley’s survey was conducted after the iPhone Duo was announced, but before it debuted, so these figures reflect consumer interest rather than actual purchasing behavior.

Apple Intelligence was another factor examined in the survey, with Morgan Stanley concluding that AI features are becoming less vital in driving iPhone upgrades, while factors such as battery life and upgrade eligibility are gaining importance.

Finally, Morgan Stanley found that Apple’s customer retention rate increased three percentage points to a record 93%, while its net switching rate improved to 12%.

Huawei was the only other major smartphone brand to show a positive and improving net switching rate, while Samsung and Google remained relatively neutral, and Xiaomi, Motorola, Honor, Oppo, and Vivo recorded negative rates.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • A few months ago, WABetaInfo reported that WhatsApp was working on its own backup service as an alternative to the current method of backing up chats, which relies on Apple’s iCloud.
  • At the time, the feature wasn’t available even to beta testers, but WABetaInfo’s report provided details on how it would work, including 2GB of free storage, optional paid intends for larger backups, and mandatory end-to-end encryption for backups stored on WhatsApp’s servers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that select WhatsApp beta testers on iOS are now seeing an option to use the app’s own backup service as an alternative to iCloud. Here are the details.

A few months ago, WABetaInfo reported that WhatsApp was working on its own backup service as an alternative to the current method of backing up chats, which relies on Apple’s iCloud.

At the time, the feature wasn’t available even to beta testers, but WABetaInfo’s report provided details on how it would work, including 2GB of free storage, optional paid intends for larger backups, and mandatory end-to-end encryption for backups stored on WhatsApp’s servers.

Now, the site reports that some WhatsApp customers running the latest TestFlight build are seeing the option to switch from iCloud to WhatsApp’s own backup service, suggesting that a wider rollout may not be too far off.

Owners can switch to WhatsApp cloud storage from the Chat backup screen. Here, users will have to choose the backup provider they want to use. If they choose WhatsApp, they will have to secure their backups using end-to-end encryption. Since encryption is mandatory, users cannot skip this step. However, they can choose a different method to encrypt their backups. For example, users can secure their backups using a 64-digit encryption key. Users who do not know what to choose can opt for the passkey, which is the default method WhatsApp recommends. After users complete the setup, they can back up their chat history on WhatsApp’s servers. WhatsApp keeps the backup on its servers for four months after a subscription expires. If users do not renew their subscription, WhatsApp deletes the backup permanently.

Importantly, the site notes that backups stored on WhatsApp’s servers cannot right now be used to restore chats across platforms, meaning customers switching from iPhone to Android, or vice versa, will still need to rely on WhatsApp’s built-in chat transfer feature.

Although the feature appears to be rolling out to beta testers first, the report notes that “the latest version available on the App Store is also compatible with this functionality,” meaning WhatsApp could theoretically enable it for customers running the public version without requiring another app upgrade.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that iFixit’s teardown of the newly introduced Apple HomeView is now up, revealing a device that seems nearly impossible to take apart and repair.
  • Following last week’s launch of the Apple HomeView, iFixit today published its teardown of the device.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that iFixit’s teardown of the newly introduced Apple HomeView is now up, revealing a device that seems nearly impossible to take apart and repair. Watch it below.

Following last week’s launch of the Apple HomeView, iFixit today published its teardown of the device.

Contrary to recent teardowns, which found significant repairability improvements with greater component modularity and easier access to internal components, the HomeView put up a fight nearly all the way through.

With heavily glued or adhesive-bonded components, including the display, speakers, antennas, and logic board, the teardown proved particularly challenging, even after the adhesive securing the display’s speakers was soaked in isopropyl alcohol.

At one point, one of them broke apart during removal, while the logic board required considerable force to separate from the chassis due to the thermal adhesive holding it in place.

According to recent reports, iFixit’s teardown covered the two HomeView variants: the tabletop model and the wall-mounted version. Interestingly, there are some internal differences between them, as the wall-mounted model has a slightly wider logic board to accommodate capacitors that are housed in the base of the tabletop version.

As a result, the wall-mounted HomeView also has smaller internal speakers, which helps explain the differences in their audio systems that Apple had already acknowledged at launch.

Back to the tabletop model, iFixit’s teardown also showed that separating the display from the base requires either specialized tools or extensive, potentially destructive disassembly of the display assembly, thanks to the way Apple routed the connecting cables through the pivot mechanism.

Once iFixit was in the base, however, there was some good news: the USB-C port is modular and relatively easy to access, as are the passive radiators and the board powering the lower assembly.

Still, an extremely short cable connecting the woofer to the board underneath made disassembly difficult, with iFixit questioning how anyone would be able to reconnect it during reassembly.

It has been revealed that percentage of Apple owners who are interested in repairing their device. 0.000001%.

Percentage of Apple owners who will actually try and repair their device. 0.00000001%.

Given all these repairability challenges, Shahram Mokhtari joked that while iFixit doesn’t have an official repairability scorecard for this category of device, he would give the Apple HomeView a “BEEP this thing” out of 10.

#62743. My monitor was cutting my download speed by 75%

📅 2026-11-15 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1548 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Tymscar ↗ Open Full Page

My monitor was cutting my download speed by 75%

📅 2026-11-15 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1548 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tymscar

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Somehow I am one of those few very lucky people to have the opportunity of owning a 2.5 gig symmetrical line for my internet.
  • Industry observers note that my ISP is pretty cool.
  • I didn’t have time for debugging, because I needed to travel 2000 km to the other side of the continent for a family emergency.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Somehow I am one of those few very lucky people to have the opportunity of owning a 2.5 gig symmetrical line for my internet. But one day, when I wanted to brag to my equally nerdy friends, shock and horror: 600 Mbps down? Luckily my upload speed was still 2.4 Gbps, so I didn’t lose all my bragging rights, but that’s weird, right? If anything, you’d expect the opposite!

Industry observers note that my ISP is pretty cool. It’s run by this one guy (Hey Keith!), and I know I can always message them and they respond promptly, as they did this time. We tried to run through a few debugging steps, they checked on their end, and everything was normal. I tried my work laptop too, same speed.

I didn’t have time for debugging, because I needed to travel 2000 km to the other side of the continent for a family emergency.

But as soon as I got back, I got curious again. What could it be? In retrospect, I now know when it started: when I moved all my connections onto my Studio Display XDR. I wanted to have a one-cable setup, and the monitor offered me that. I’ve had it for half a year now, and I don’t think I’ve ever run a speed test through it. 600 Mbps was more than fast enough for me to never realise I wasn’t getting three quarters of the speed I was paying for 🤦.

Recent findings suggest that pings to other wired computers during a download would fail 10% of the time over Ethernet through the adapter plugged into my screen, and 0% of the time over Wi-Fi. What made it stranger was that there were no dropped frame errors in macOS’s logs at all. This was the big hint for me: the adapter was dropping them before the computer could know.

Sources indicate that I then plugged the adapter straight into my Mac instead of the monitor, and ran an iperf3 server on my UDR 7: 2.3 Gbps. So the cable, the router and the adapter are all fine? What about fast.com? Perfect speeds there too! 2.2 down and 2.3 up when connected straight in. As soon as I connected it to the display, it was back to 600 down again.

According to recent reports, so it’s the display, right? Well, I would find out: sort of yes, sort of no, which is why I wanted to write this blog post. I couldn’t find anything online explaining the exact cause, and it’s quite a cool reason.

The adapter uses a Realtek RTL8156B, which on macOS binds to Apple’s generic USB networking driver. But Realtek ship their own driver on their website, so I thought I’d give that a go! I installed it and, to my surprise, it almost doubled the download speed to 1.1 Gbps, but that was still nowhere close to 2.5. First hint that it couldn’t just be the monitor’s fault.

Sources indicate that then I tried flow control. I had never truly looked into this before, and I think it’s quite neat to know about if you were also ignorant of it like me. Basically, when a device receives Ethernet frames it can’t keep up with, it just drops them. With flow control (it’s something your router or switch has to support), it can send the sender a “pause” frame, and the sender then buffers the data on its side, instead of the receiver (the adapter in this case) on its side. I turned it on in my UniFi console and guess what, download jumped to around 2 Gbps, with upload still at full speed! Yay! Well, not so fast….

Recent findings suggest that I don’t like it always being on, because it can add latency to other systems like my gaming PC. Can you work around it? For sure, you can disable it on those computers, but it’s janky, and it’s another thing I need to remember when my Sauerbraten game starts lagging. I need fewer things to remember, considering I am 30 in a couple of months. My memory is not what it used to be.

Sources indicate that yeah, isn’t that weird? First of all, it looks like the port can indeed do 2.5 in both directions. I already knew that, because I get much more than that from my external SSD through the monitor’s Thunderbolt port. So the glitch is not the monitor again? But it has to be!

Well, I had another idea. How about I connect to my Linux box, which is also on 2.5, and send perfectly smooth UDP traffic at a fixed rate with flow control off? Then I can check the chip’s own counter of dropped frames:.

So basically no drops whatsoever when connected straight to my Mac, but loads of drops after about 168k frames per second (roughly 2 Gbps). Remember that number. That number comes from the adapter’s own counters: however much I sent, the number of frames it managed to hand over to the Mac each second flattened out at about 168,000, and everything above that was dropped.

It has been revealed that why did this not happen on my SSD? What was the only difference I could find? Bursts!

Industry observers note that when the Mac reads data from a USB 3 device, the device sends some packets, then has to wait for the Mac to say “lgtm, send more!”. The SSD enclosure sends 16 packets before needing a go-ahead message back. The RTL8156B in my Ethernet adapter sends 4.

Here is a diagram of my best understanding of why this is an concern. I made this diagram 100 times, and I think I can probably improve it more, but if it helps you understand the issue, I have done my job.

Industry observers note that as you can see, the speed of packets coming into the adapter is 2.5 Gbps. That’s what the router pushes in. The speed going out is around 2 Gbps. The reason is that if you add up the average time it takes to get the go-ahead through my monitor’s hub, which is around 7.6 µs, to the average time it takes to send 4 KB, around 8.2 µs, you can find what the maximum speed is.

It has been revealed that well, if the speed of the drain from my adapter to my Mac is half a gig slower than the speed of the input, then you can imagine the buffer getting filled more and more until it overflows. Those are dropped packets, which result in a hard backoff when the router resends them, so you drop loads in speed. And that’s the reason for all of this.

Industry observers note that I have a cupboard full of USB-C Ethernet adapters. Don’t ask.

The problem is they’re all 1 gig adapters, so any of the tests I made would not tell me anything, because the problems don’t start at 1 gig. They start at around 2… If I run my 2.5 gig adapter at 1 gig speeds, I get 1 gig downloads with the official driver. If I run it at 1.5, I get 1.5. If I run it at 2, well, I get 1….

Industry observers note that so I thought I would do what any human would do, and I spent more money on a newly introduced adapter. Another UGREEN, but this time it’s one that promises 5 Gbps and uses the RTL8157 chip instead: UGREEN 5G USB-C Ethernet adapter. My reasoning was that if this one could get me better speeds, it would help me understand how. And that it did!

With this adapter, I dropped 0 frames:.

Why? Well, looking through what each adapter tells me about itself:.

Industry observers note that I can see that instead of sending 4 1 KB packets per burst, it would send 8! And the speed of the link was also 2x faster, so those 8 KB would go 2x faster to the Mac. That means the time spent was 8 times lower to send the same data, and while the wait for the go-ahead was identical, the theoretical speed from the adapter to the Mac, including the wait for the go-ahead, was a maximum of 4.5 Gbps. That’s much bigger than the 2.5 coming into the adapter, so the buffer would never fill up, packets would never drop and everything was great, even if the “go-ahead” response was still much slower than when connected directly to the Mac.

I think the significant takeaway from this is that all the things you think are quite easy to understand, such as transfer speeds, have so many cool intricacies that it’s worth diving deep every so often. Who would’ve thought that the speed of the link between the adapter and the Mac was defined not only by the link speed itself in Gbps, but also by the time it took your Mac to reply, by the amount of packets, by the speed of those packets, by the number of packets in a burst, and by the size of those packets?

See you next time, when I will spend just as much time on another trivial thing that we can all learn from!

They're also lighter and thinner than the X4, though there is a trade-off involved: They drop the USB-C charging port in favor of magnetic pogo pins that require a separate adapter (included).

These upgrades also increased the cost: The X4 Classic typically retails for $89, $20 more than the discontinued X4 and only $10 less than the X4 Pro, while the X3 launched at $79. But right now, the X4 Classic is just under $55, or around 38% off, and the X3 is about a dollar more. Either is a great option for those who prioritize crisp, readable text above the conveniences of a built-in light or touchscreen, as those add extra layers between the inner screen and outer glass. It's also crucial to understand what you're getting into: These devices support only e-books without Digital Rights Management (DRM), which means you can't use it to read your existing library of Kindle books. On the plus side, there's no longer a need to worry about flashing upcoming firmware if you don't want to, as the native version has been totally overhauled and is now one of your best options (though the new firmware, called "Licorice," isn't available on the X3 quite yet).

Sources indicate that these exercises aren’t just for seniors. It’s never too early to start thinking about your balance, so give them a try during your next workout. They’re appropriate for any fitness level and you won’t need any equipment to do them (but adding a dumbbell or two will always make things more challenging).

Check in with your doctor before trying any new workout, especially if you have balance concerns.

These exercises aren’t hard, but doing them correctly is important. Beginners should consider meeting with a personal trainer or physical therapist for feedback and guidance on form, and to get modifications if needed.

Recent findings suggest that you’ll just need some room and an elevated platform, like a stair step, for this workout. Hang onto a chair or another stable surface for additional support if you need it.

It has been revealed that start by doing each exercise for one set of 10 reps. As your balance improves, you can add an additional set and increase your reps to 12. You can also use small dumbbells for the step-up to balance to ramp up the difficulty.

These exercises can be done on their own or as a warm-up for other activities.

You may feel muscle fatigue when doing this workout, but you should never feel sharp pain. Stop the workout immediately and consult your physician if you feel sharp pain at any point.

Here’s how to do the exercises:.

The exercises in this workout force you to find equilibrium when your center of gravity is maintained over a smaller surface area – either one foot for the standing marches, step up to balance, and side step to balance, or a narrow placement of two feet for the heel-to-toe walks.

Industry observers note that during these exercises, your deep core muscles like the rectus abdominis and internal obliques engage to stabilize and support your entire body. Your glutes and hip stabilizing muscles also work to keep the hips in a level position. The stronger these muscles are, the more conditioned they’ll be to keep you upright and sturdy during everyday movement.

Additionally, exercises like the step-up to balance strengthen key muscle groups in your lower body, like the quadriceps, hamstrings, and glutes.

To be on the safe side, I'll describe Roman as a ... socially awkward character, but I think most people today would identify him as neurodivergent. He's a brilliant analyst of the law. His research is impeccable. But he has zero people skills and strong moral and ethical convictions that often lead him to butt heads with basically everyone he has a conversation with.

This forces Denzel to give a fairly uncharacteristic and complex performance. While Roman shares Denzel's proclivity for effortlessly spewing compelling dialogue, there's none of the gravitas that comes with Washington's more verbose, award-nominated performances. Roman has a well-educated, well-spoken tongue, but he doesn't have the smooth, silver tongue of someone like Alonzo in "Training Day," or even historical figures Malcolm X and Rubin "The Hurricane" Carter.

Recent findings suggest that there's also a physical element to the performance. Not that he's ever diminutive on screen; he's as often an action star as he is a dramatic force of nature and typically he's in excellent shape. But the physique of Roman is one I'd associate more with Forest Whitaker than Denzel. In fact, I couldn't help but think about what the movie would be like with Whitaker, an incredible actor in his own right, as Roman instead of Washington.

It has been revealed that perhaps it's for the best that Denzel got the role, though, because it's essentially the movie's sole saving grace. It has been revealed that I realize that I've spent a few paragraphs talking about this film's lowlights, but despite its flaws, it's still a movie I recommend watching for anyone who loves a great Denzel performance. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that apple today revealed that App Store prices for apps and In-App Purchases will be adjusted in five countries starting December 3, following changes in taxes and foreign exchange rates. Here are the details.

In a newly introduced post published on its developer portal, Apple today declared a series of changes to App Store pricing, as well as updates to tax rules affecting developers and customers in several countries, including the US.

According to the organization, developers’ proceeds from eligible app and In-App Purchase sales have been adjusted in four countries, reflecting the following tax updates:.

Specific to Botswana and Rwanda, Apple said that “Exhibit B of the Paid Applications Agreement will be updated to indicate that Apple collects and remits applicable taxes.”.

Apple added that a fresh “Software as a Service (SaaS)” attribute is now available for several App Store tax categories, including App Store Software, Software Training Material, Dating, and Boosting. Developers can review and enhancement their tax category selections in App Store Connect.

Additionally, starting December 3, developers who rely on Apple’s automatic pricing adjustments will see changes to app and In-App Purchase prices in:.

Apple usually makes these adjustments to account for changes in taxes and foreign exchange rates, and notes that prices won’t change in countries selected as the base storefront, for auto-renewable subscriptions, or in storefronts where developers manually manage their prices.

The announcement does not go into detail about how much prices will change in each country, or whether they will increase or decrease.

Finally, starting January 1, 2027, apps and In-App Purchases in the SaaS, App Store Software, Software Training Material, Dating, and Boosting categories will become subject to sales and use taxes in California.

Apple noted that “prices on the United States storefront are displayed to customers exclusive of taxes, so the tax change will not affect them,” but added that while developers’ proceeds will remain unchanged, “the total amount customers are charged, inclusive of tax, may increase.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that amazon's Black Friday sale kicked off today, which means it's a good time to score some of the year's best prices on e-readers. Timing your purchase is now a bigger deal than ever (so to speak), as Amazon recently raised the price of basically every Kindle by $50 or more due to the ongoing RAM crisis.

It has been revealed that because of this, the prices aren't nearly as low as they were last year, but now is still the time to get a decent discount on a Kindle Paperwhite or Colorsoft—but if you'd rather read differently, you can also save major on a few worthy Kindle alternatives. Here are your e-reader best bets in the lead-up to Black Friday and Cyber Monday.

The Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition is the best e-reader for most people. An upgraded version of the basic Kindle, the Paperwhite adds a larger screen, temperature-adjustable lighting, water resistance, and better battery life—and if you opt for the Signature Edition, you also get double the storage and no lock screen ads. Earlier this year, it jumped in price to $250, even before the tech giant introduced a new model—but you can get the 2024 model for $179.99, 28% off the new list price.

Industry observers note that if you want a great Kindle but you don't care about paying extra for more storage or getting rid of lock screen ads, the non-Signature Edition of the Kindle Paperwhite is also a great buy right now. The 2024 model has been discounted to $129.99 from the list price of $199.99. It's available in standard black, Jade, or Raspberry colors.

If you don't need the bells and whistles of the Paperwhite, you can also pick up the standard Kindle. It's still a very capable device, with good lighting, 16GB of onboard storage, and the ability to hook up your Bluetooth speakers to listen to Audible audiobooks. The standard Kindle, which now retails for $150, is marked down to $119.99, making it the cheapest Kindle option. Though I think it makes more sense to spend $10 more on the Signature Edition, this is the way to go if you want the cute Matcha color.

If you like to read comics or you just appreciate looking at your book covers in full color, the 2024 Kindle Colorsoft is also at a strong 41% discount for Black Friday, bringing it down to around $170. For $10 less than the Paperwhite Signature edition, you get all the same perks (including an ad-free experience) and a color e-ink screen that's great for reading magazines, graphic novels, and manga. Color e-ink isn't for everyone, but if it's for you, the Colorsoft has the best color screen on the market. For an extra $10, the Colorsoft Kids Edition adds a case, a yearlong subscription to Kindle Kids+, and an extended warranty.

According to recent reports, if you're looking for a combination e-reader and e-notebook, the Kindle Scribe is a great option. With a larger screen than Amazon's other e-readers, it offers all the benefits of the Paperwhite but adds support for the excellent Premium Pen stylus, allowing you to take notes in your Amazon e-books or create handwritten documents that you can later convert to text using the onboard AI tools. The 32GB black-and-white version of the Kindle Scribe is currently $349.99, while the Colorsoft version will run you $449.99. Both of these are the newest models, released in 2025.

Sources indicate that the upcoming Kindle Scribe Colorsoft has all the same great features of the black-and-white version discussed above, but adds a full-color e-ink display. Combined with the large 11-inch screen, this makes it a great device for reading comics or magazine articles as they were meant to be read, or marking up PDFs using the included Premium Pen. This device usually costs a hefty $630, but the current Black Friday sale cuts $180 off of that price.

If you want to step outside of the Amazon ecosystem, the Kobo Libra Colour is a good bet. Discounted $30 to $229.99 at Best Buy, it's right now pricier than the Kindle Colorsoft, but you get a bit more for your money. While most of the specs are similar (they both use the same Kaleido 3 screen and offer 32GB of storage), the Kobo supports a stylus, so you can jot down notes in your books or keep a digital journal. It also has physical page-turn buttons, which the Colorsoft lacks.

Recent findings suggest that if you don't want to be tied to the Amazon ecosystem and/or you're looking for a device that's a bit more portable, consider the Viwoods AiPaper Reader, right now marked down to $200, its lowest price ever. It's got a 6.13-inch screen, so it's the same size and shape as your phone, and it has a crisp e-ink screen with a strong (if not temperature-adjustable) front light and 128GB of onboard storage. The best part is, it runs on an open Android system, so you can install multiple reading apps, including Kindle, Nook, Kobo, and Libby, and keep all of your books in one place. (Check out my review of the Viwoods AiPaper Reader for more—it's a nifty little device.).

It has been revealed that if you don't have a large Kindle library, you're moderately tech-savvy, and you praise portability above all else, I can't recommend Xteink's line of e-readers more highly. The 4.3-inch Xteink X4 Classic is at its lowest price ever, coming in at just under $55, around $34 off the list price. Meanwhile, the smaller 3.7-inch Xteink X3 is about a dollar more; that's a less-generous 19% discount. I own both, and while the Classic is definitely worth the current sale price, I actually prefer the form factor of the smaller X3 (at the moment $55.72), which is about the size of a library card.

If you're feeling tentative about trusting a seemingly no-name Chinese tech brand, read more about the devices in my review, or listen to the collected wisdom of the tens of thousands of people in the bustling r/xteink Reddit group.

In a recent development, in short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

Follow our Black Friday coverage for the latest and best deals our team finds. Another good tip is to only buy what you need. It sounds simple, but making a list of the things you want before jumping into a sale with millions of products helps you focus and make smarter decisions.

Take advantage of price matching or guarantees instead of waiting. Remember, you can always return products later if you change your mind. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that apple this week revealed the additional Siri AI usage you’ll get if you have an iCloud+ subscription. This ranges from doubled limits for a 200GB proposal to 20 times for a 12TB plan.

However, the manufacturer’s support document reveals that some countries will not get access to these increased usage allowances ….

In a recent development, apple hasn’t yet specified the standard limits applicable to Siri AI usage, instead saying that these will vary depending on anything from the feature used to the overall level of demand at the time. However, it did list the proportional increases you get with paid iCloud prepares.

However, tucked away in the small print in the organization’s support document are some exclusions. One of them is no surprise: EU countries.

Siri AI isn’t available at all in the EU due to Apple’s perception of potential antitrust problems. Essentially, Apple believes that if it launches Siri AI there, it will be required to give competing AI services the same level of access to its devices. But three other countries are specifically excluded:.

Apple gives no explanation, simply saying:.

Increased access to Siri AI with iCloud+ is subject to Siri AI availability and is not available in Brazil, the EU, UK, or South Korea.

However, I have a strong suspicion about the reason.

What all three countries have in common is that they’ve taken a strong antitrust stance with Apple on a number of occasions over a range of issues.

Sources indicate that it may be that Apple has genuine concerns about how regulators might respond if they effectively throw in free access to increased Siri AI usage. The firm may fear that this would be viewed as anti-competitive by implicitly disadvantaging other AI services.

A less charitable take would be that Apple is firing a warning shot across the bows of these countries, seeking to communicate that there are consequences for what it views as attacks on its ecosystem. If customers are angered by missing out, Apple might be hoping that these feelings would be directed at regulators rather than the iPhone maker.

What’s your take? Please share your thoughts in the comments.

“We have zero evidence or any reason to believe that any of these isolated or individual instances have anything to do with nefarious actors, with cyber hackers, with criminals, with another nation state, with a malign actor of any kind. Each of them are distinct, and they’re different in their causation.”.

The statement was backed by Senator Mark Warner.

It has been revealed that democratic Sen. Mark Warner, vice chair of the Senate Intelligence Committee, also noted on Tuesday that there’s no indication these incidents are the result of an attack.

Warner went on to say that the ability of AI systems to find vulnerabilities at “unprecedented speed” does, however, mean companies and government agencies alike need to be ready to patch vulnerabilities immediately.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that apple has three main Apple Watch "lines." There's the flagship, presently the Series 12, which represents Apple's mainstream wearable. For athletes and users who think they'll put their watches through some extreme scenarios, there's the Ultra line, currently the Apple Watch Ultra 4. And while both the Series 12 and Ultra 4 are excellent devices in their own right, they can be pretty pricey (particularly the Ultra). That's why the third category, the SE, is actually best for most people, and Lifehacker's choice for best smartwatch gift of the year. Better yet, the third-generation SE is currently $50 off ahead of Black Friday, perfect for most people asking for an Apple Watch this year.

Recent findings suggest that the SE 3 does just about everything you'd expect an Apple Watch to do. It, of course, has a heart rate sensor to keep tabs on your pulse, including high and low heart rate alerts; the ability to track dozens of different workouts and exercise types (including swimming, thanks to the device's water resistance); a sleep tracker with daily analyses available in the Health app; notification forwarding to check in on your alerts without opening your iPhone; and the ability to send and receive text messages.

It comes in two sizes (40mm and 44mm) depending on how large or small you prefer your watch. No matter which model you get, the watch comes with the S10 chip, Apple's last-generation watch processor. While it isn't as fast as the current S11 chip, the S10 is more than capable of running watchOS 27. Apple claims the SE 3 can run for up to 18 hours on a single charge, and up to 32 hours in Low Power Mode, with fast charging from 0% to 80% in 45 minutes.

Industry observers note that the majority of the features missing from the SE 3 aren't essential. Apple's other watches have things like bigger, brighter displays, additional health tracking tools like hypertension alerts and an ECG sensor, longer battery life, and Audio Intelligence—the latter of which might be a benefit to miss, depending on who you are.

In a recent development, if your giftee wants or needs any of those additional features, Series 12 or Ultra 4 might be a better choice. But for anyone who wants the essential Apple Watch experience, the SE 3 is simply the best-value watch Apple sells right now—especially at this discount. Right now, the watch starts at $199 for the 40mm watch, or $229 for the 44mm. You can also save on the cellular versions of these watches: $249 for the cellular 40mm watch, and $279 for the cellular 44mm model.

According to recent reports, yes, Apple participates in Black Friday, though you may want to compare their sales with other retailers like Best Buy and Walmart. So far, the best Black Friday sale on an Apple product is the M5 MacBook Air on sale for $200 off, the lowest price since the price hike this summer.

According to recent reports, black Friday sales officially begin Friday, Nov. 27, 2026, and run throughout “Cyber Week,” the five-day period that runs from Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday, Nov. 30, 2026. But Black Friday and Cyber Monday dates have expanded as retailers compete for customers. You can get the same Black Friday sales early, and we expect sales to wind down by Dec. 2, 2026.

I tested the Xiaomi 18 Pro Max's weird rear screen — and it's actually useful

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1396 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomsguide

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I have many gripes with modern smartphones, but one of the things that really grinds my gears is the trend of Godzilla-sized camera bumps on the backs of phones, Apple's doing it, Samsung' seems to be planning on it, and a lot of Chinese brands look like they've been hit by a rogue hockey puck.
  • Sources indicate that xiaomi has taken on the task of making the most out of that normally-wasted space on the camera bump by turning it into a screen.
  • But the question is not whether the Xiaomi 18 Pro Max's Back Display is interesting, it's whether it's able to justify its own existence.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I have many gripes with modern smartphones, but one of the things that really grinds my gears is the trend of Godzilla-sized camera bumps on the backs of phones, Apple's doing it, Samsung' seems to be planning on it, and a lot of Chinese brands look like they've been hit by a rogue hockey puck. I've been testing the Xiaomi 18 Pro Max, which also has a large, iPhone-looking camera bump, but this time things are different.

Sources indicate that xiaomi has taken on the task of making the most out of that normally-wasted space on the camera bump by turning it into a screen. This is not the first phone to feature a rear-mounted screen, or even the first Xiaomi flagship to do so, but in a world of phones that all seem to feel and look the same, it's quite exciting to see a phone company offer something that helps its phones stand out.

But the question is not whether the Xiaomi 18 Pro Max's Back Display is interesting, it's whether it's able to justify its own existence.

Looking at the 18 Pro Max, my mind immediately jumped to the cover displays on compact foldables. The way the display wraps around the two main cameras is reminiscent of the Galaxy Z Flip 8 and the Motorola Razr. It's a little smaller than those screens, measuring 2.9-inches compared to those 4+-inch screens, but all three share a common purpose.

Recent findings suggest that this is a way to use your phone without actually using your phone, using the smaller screen to look at basic information like the time or notifications on a smaller and more power-efficient display. At the same time, and as Xiaomi is keen to emphasize, it's a way to customize the look and feel of your phone in a way that cases and other accessories just can't manage.

Industry observers note that my initial thoughts upon looking at the back of the Xiaomi 18 Pro Max and playing around with the screen weren't totally positive. I couldn't stop comparing it to the cover screens on foldable phones, and the fact that those screens are front-and-center when you take out your device. Xiaomi's screen is on the back, which is not part of my phone I tend to pay very much attention to.

But the more I used it, and the more I figured out that it wasn't just a glorified clock and notification alert, the more I realized that my initial reaction was the wrong way of looking at things.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

In a recent development, the idea that this is potentially a very valuable feature clicked when I opened up the camera on the Back Display. This allows you to take selfies using the main cameras, in a similar fashion to foldable phones, using the rear-mounted screen as a viewfinder. This means you're taking selfies with the 200MP main camera, rather than the lower resolution hole-punch camera on the front.

It has been revealed that I'm not going to lie, though. This isn't a fully-fledged phone screen capable of running all the apps and services that you've got installed. It is significantly more limited than that, and the difference is like describing the difference between a smart home hub and a tablet.

The home hub may be useful for its own specific use case, but it doesn't have the same versatility or usefulness as a tablet running Android or iPadOS.

Industry observers note that the Back Display is great for glancing at notifications and the time, especially if you tend to leave your phone lying face down. It even supports Live Activities on a handful of apps, including letting you control music playback on Spotify. Plus, it's possible to customize your screen with different backgrounds and clockfaces, depending on what your own personal tastes and style might be.

So far so good, though I can't say that I've ever felt using my main screen for those tasks has ever been a particular burden — especially since I'm just not used to looking at the back of my phone.

Then again, if you already have a smartwatch, that's not going to mean much, since you already have the bulk of this information available on your wrist.

Xiaomi does seem to be hinging on Generative AI to turn this screen from a gimmick into something you'll want to use throughout the day, thanks to a built-in system that lets you vibe code your own apps.

Industry observers note that anyone that remembers the flop that was Windows Phone will know that success of a mobile platform hinges on app support. Your apps give the system value, and without developers actively contributing to an app store, there's little reason for people to actually invest in one of your devices.

Sources indicate that so how do you get app developers on board to add utility to a niche display on the back of a handful of phones? You don't. You hand that job to the owners, and let generative AI do all the hard work. So Xiaomi added a prompt-based system for creating Back Display apps from scratch, as well as an App Store of sorts that lets you see a curated selection of what other people have created.

Options I can see include workout schedules, mini games, educational tools, timers, and all kinds of different options, though I have no idea how effective or accurate they actually are compared to full-coded apps. Still, it's nice to see that there's a way to improve the usefulness of the Back Display — even if it would be nice to have proper Android apps on offer.

Industry observers note that I found that basic prompts did work, but the more detail you could offer the better the outcome. Xiaomi can "polish" your prompt to better your chances of generating a usable app.

In a recent development, however, this does not guarantee that the app would successfully generate — or that it would work. It took me multiple attempts to create a Doom clone, and even when it did, I kept getting killed off by a monster hiding out of my line of sight.

Recent findings suggest that so it's not quite as painless as having a developer-made app, and playing games on a small screen isn't ideal. But in the absence of additional features, this system is fairly good at filling that niche.

I've spent my entire life looking at the front of my phone, and never really concerning myself with what's on the back. Even in the pre-smartphone era the screen was everything, whereas the back was just... not vital. If rear screens start to take off, that could change the way people interact with their phones in a substantial way. And that's obviously going to take a lot of getting used to.

Recent findings suggest that that's probably the biggest hurdle these rear screens will face. There's certainly no shortage of utility, especially with the generative AI apps. It's just reprogramming user habits to glance at the back of the phone rather than looking at their main display. It's going to be an uphill battle to convince people that these screens are worth it, especially when they have to compete with wearables.

If it weren't for the AI apps I'd say these screens don't have much of a chance. I'm not convinced that they will take off, aside from a few niche gimmicks, but at least they have some sort of unique selling point to work with.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that after launching Moonlock for Mac last year, MacPaw is bringing its scam-detection app to iPhone today. Here are the details.

When MacPaw rolled out Moonlock on the Mac, the organization described its upcoming app as something that “complements Apple’s built-in security tools, protects from Mac-specific malware, and helps you understand cybersecurity better.”.

In practice, the Mac app includes real-time protection against potential threats. Users can also manually scan their Mac for malware, including suspicious files hidden in system folders and email attachments.

According to recent reports, beyond that, Moonlock includes a VPN to encrypt internet traffic, a network inspector that shows where apps are sending data and lets people block connections to specific countries, and an AI-powered scam detector that analyzes messages pasted into the app for signs of phishing. It also helps users review and adjust macOS security settings.

Today, MacPaw is launching Moonlock for iPhone, a move the manufacturer says “helps people recognize potential scams, understand their iPhone’s security and take practical steps to improve it.”.

Unlike the Mac version, Moonlock for iPhone doesn’t scan for malware, as iOS prevents third-party apps from accessing other apps and their files. Instead, it focuses on identifying potential scams, checking for exposed personal information, and helping users improve their iPhone’s security.

On the iPhone, Moonlock lets users swiftly check suspicious texts, screenshots, and QR codes for phishing, in addition to checking whether their email addresses have appeared in known data breaches.

Industry observers note that as MacPaw explains it, Moonlock’s Scam Detect “helps people check suspicious messages they encounter throughout the day. Whether it’s a text message, a screenshot shared by a friend, or a QR code, users can paste, scan or share content directly with Moonlock and receive an assessment explaining why something may be suspicious.”.

Here’s Oleg Stukalenko, Head of Product Management at Moonlock by MacPaw, on today’s launch:.

According to recent reports, “When we launched Moonlock, our goal was to make cybersecurity something anyone could understand and use. But so much of what people do today, from banking to everyday conversations, happens on their phones. Bringing Moonlock to iPhone felt like the natural next step. We want to help people spot a scam before they tap, see where their security stands, and know exactly what to do next.”.

MacPaw adds that Moonlock for iPhone also includes the following features:.

MacPaw’s Moonlock for iPhone is free to download, with subscriptions available for $9.99 per month or $49.99 per year.

Check out Moonlock for iPhone on the App Store.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Black Friday sales officially start Friday, November 28, and run through Cyber Monday, November 30, 2026, and Lifehacker is sharing the best sales based on product reviews and comparisons before it's over.
